News.title: Chilling signs Putin is poised to fire nuke-powered ‘Flying Chernobyl’ super weapon as aircraft mass in Arctic
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin is feared to be gearing up for a terrifying test of his perilous nuclear-powered “Flying Chernobyl” super weapon.

An influx of aircraft converging in the Arctic has sparked concerns the tyrant could fire the cruise missile which is fuelled by its own atomic reactor.



The Kremlin has long hailed the “invincible” Burevestnik missile which carries a nuclear warhead and reportedly boasts an “unlimited range”.

This means it could strike the UK should Putin ever decide to blitz the West, according to analysts.



Satellite images from across the past few weeks shows Moscow’s high-powered aircraft descending on the Novaya Zemlya archipelago in the Arctic.

The region has already hosted tests for the Burevestnik and was previously used by the Soviets as one of their main nuclear sites between 1955 to 1990.

This included the 1961 detonation of the largest nuclear weapon ever tested, the 50MT AN602 Tsar Bomba hydrogen bomb.

This week, two specialist Il-976 SKIP aircraft used to monitor missile trajectories and collect test data reportedly arrived at Rogachevo airbase.



Imagery from the archipelago already shows an A-50U airborne early-warning aircraft, four An-26 military transports, an An-74 and several helicopters at the base.

Civilian vessels previously involved in missile trials have also taken up positions in the Barents and Kara seas around the Pankovo test range.

The Kremlin, who have boasted about firing the Burevestnik before, are yet to confirm or deny the suspected test fears.



Norwegian defence analyst Thord Are Iversen says the satellite pictures are a telltale sign however.

He says they follow the same pattern seen during previous tests of Putin’s experimental 9M730 cruise missile.

He told Russian outlet The Insider: “It now appears that everything is ready for actual Burevestnik flight testing.”

The missile has reportedly been tested up to 14 times before but had only been successful twice – in 2022 and 2025.

Last year, the supposedly successful missile launch saw the weapon travel 14,000km for 15 hours, top Russian general Valery Gerasimov said.



Gerasimov added: “During the flight, the missile performed all the prescribed vertical and horizontal manoeuvres, demonstrating its high capabilities for evading missile and air defence systems.”

The previous test in 2022 only lasted for two minutes.

The chilling Flying Chernobyl nickname comes from the 1986 Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant disaster which caused irreversible damage across the Soviet Union.



Experts fears any future tests or actual usage of the weapon could lead to a similar radioactive disaster due its atomic-powered reactor.

Dubbed “Skyfall” by Nato, a top US State Department official Thomas Countryman described it as a “uniquely stupid weapon system”.

It comes as Putin’s war in Ukraine continues to rage on.

In overnight strikes, Ukraine disabled the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Krasnodar region, setting it ablaze and adding to Putin’s woes over petrol shortages.

Moscow reacted by unleashing a barrage of deadly strikes.



Civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.

More than a dozen were injured in strikes on Mena, in Chernihiv region, including four children.

Kyiv was also blitzed, with a multi-story residential building crumbling just hours after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham left the capital.



Burnham made his first visit to Kyiv as Prime Minister to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky.

The trip came just after the PM handed over crucial blueprints to help Ukraine build their own long-range Storm Shadow missiles.

Moscow responded by accusing Britain of “participating” in the war with Ukraine.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Experts told The Sun the move could provoke a raging Putin to target Britain’s defence chiefs.

Outlining how Putin could retaliate, Brit ex-Army commander Hamish de Bretton-Gordon warned that Russia’s secret service could set its sights on EU defence bosses – including those in the UK.

News.title: Horror moment tornado tears through French village leaving dozens hurt & hundreds of homes damaged as roofs ripped off
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a huge tornado sweeps through southern France injuring more than 40 people and destroying at least 300 homes.

A supercell thunderstorm sparked the wild tornado as it struck the town of Pomas with wind speeds of over 73mph uprooting trees and blowing roofs off houses.



A pregnant woman was among the injured after her house collapsed when she was inside.

She was found hiding under an overturned sofa which was buried beneath a collapsed wall, police said.



The woman was rushed to hospital with the condition of her baby unknown.

The local Aude region was under an amber alert for most of Monday evening as stormy skies descended across southern France.



Several roads were closed as heavy traffic remained late into the evening due to the dozens of fallen trees and debris.

Around 2,800 homes were left without electricity from 7.30pm until late in the towns of Fontcouverte, Camplong, Souilhe, Raissac d’Aude, Fabrezan, Montmaur, Soupex, Ricaud, Montclar and La Pomarède.

Emergency services were under intense strain as they received hundreds of calls from civilians warning of injuries and destruction.

Over 120 firefighters were mobilised along with the Red Cross and canine units hunting for any missing people.

The local prefecture said shortly after 10.30pm: “The material assessment indicates that 300 homes were affected.



“Forty one people were taken care of and had passed through the victim assembly point, including 15 people evacuated to a hospital.”

Many of the homes caught in the tornado’s path had their windows smashed and roofs blown off.

Search and rescue operations continued long into the night as the weather remained stormy.



Two shelters were opened up for displaced victims in Pomas and Limoux.

There were also major flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.

High winds reached up to 73mph in the village of Arquettes-en-Val, according to France’s national weather service, Meteo-France.

France averages several dozen tornadoes each year, which vary in intensity but are typically not deadly, Météo France reports.

The wet and windy weather comes just weeks after a summer of heatwaves and wildfires.



France’s south-west region saw an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

Across the whole of the country, an estimated 224,000 people had to flee their homes due to multiple raging wildfires.

Across in Spain, a dozen “mini-tsunamis” left sunbathers fleeing waves as waterfront restaurants were left flooded.

Elsewhere in Europe, extreme rain and winds hit Poland and Italy.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A strong cyclone ravaged Forlì in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region, with winds reaching around 75mph.



Wild footage shows extreme gusts of wind flipping over four planes at an airport as witnesses recalled the aircrafts being “thrown around like toys”.

News.title: I posed as a migrant to cross the Channel in a dinghy – French cops are giving people smugglers free lifts back to camps
News.content:
AN UNDERCOVER reporter was able to cross the Channel in a small boat while posing as a migrant – and claims French police are giving smugglers free lifts back to the camps.

Journalist Christian Drogan spent weeks posing as a British criminal who was on the run in Calais before boarding a UK-bound dinghy.



Working alongside Isabel Oakeshott from Talk TV, Drogan filmed his route back to the UK, including his interactions with the criminal gangs who have control over the route.

He says it was obvious who the smugglers behind the illegal crossings were “without a shadow of a doubt” – but French police did not arrest them.



Footage shows Drogan boarding an inflatable in shallow waters on the northern French coast along with dozens of migrants.

After setting off on relatively calm seas, footage shows a Gendarmerie patrol boat approaching the dinghy.



Officers are then heard saying in English: “The sea is very rough, here it is quiet, when you go further it’s very dangerous.

“The best way today is to go back.”



Drogan said the French police offered to take anyone back to shore if they had changed their mind about crossing.

He claims the four smugglers were the only people to accept the offer – and were dropped back on the beach to continue the work of their criminal network organising the journeys.

He says it took seven hours for his boat to reach the halfway point to Britain.



Drogan, a 35-year-old builder from Rochdale, has previously spent weeks undercover inside migrant camps in Calais.

He posed under different cover stories, including as a Kurd, an Armenian, and a small-time British criminal.

Once the dinghy had reached British waters, Drogan’s footage shows Border Force workers helping migrants onto a rescue vessel.

He says at this point it became obvious to the authorities that he was not a genuine migrant.

One worker told him: “You’re on the wrong boat”.



Drogan was then taken to Western Jet Foil in Dover where small boat migrants are processed.

He said at that point he was singled out and quizzed by counter terror cops about what he had seen.

Official Home Office statistics show that on the day the reporter crossed the Channel, August 3, one boat was picked up by Border Force carrying 35 people.

So far this year 15,897 people have arrived in the UK having crossed illegally from France – which is 43.8 per cent lower than this time last year.

It is not known if Drogan’s undercover journey has been counted in the official migrant arrival figures.



The Government claimed Drogan had been “reckless” and had “made it more difficult for law enforcement officers to stop small boat crossings and save lives in dangerous conditions”.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Our partnership with France is stronger than ever, with a new deal signed by the Home Secretary delivering a 40% uplift in boots on the ground.

“Together, we are piling the pressure on the criminal gangs and preventing illegal and dangerous crossings.

“Over 1,100 boats or engines have been seized since the election, 48,000 crossing attempts have been prevented, and the number of small boats crossings are down.”

Last week footage released by the Home Office showed French police being attacked by migrants before they managed to successfully slash a dinghy as it was being launched.



Oakeshott said: “There is a very good reason no reporter has ever attempted such a mission before: because it is both extraordinarily difficult, and extraordinarily dangerous.

“Getting to the truth of what is really happening in the Channel simply isn’t possible from the safety of the beaches.”

Drogan said: “I rolled the dice with my life for this investigation, and its findings have only cemented my scepticism towards the establishment.

“This type of investigation is dangerous, but so are the people running our country.

“Truth is the most effective weapon in this fight, and that is why this kind of work has to be done.”



Drogan warned against anyone trying to copy his trip.

He continued: “I would say if anybody tries to have a go at this, It’s highly likely they could end up dead.

“France has changed since even only just sort of a year ago when I started going over.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It’s highly highly hostile now. It feels in places like a war zone.”

News.title: Afghan man, 24, charged with rape of girl, 17, in UK city centre during early hours
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'HORROR ATTACK' Afghan man, 24, charged with rape of girl, 17, in UK city centre during early hours

COPS have charged an Afghan man after a 17-year-old girl was allegedly raped in a chilling city centre attack.

Abdul Shinwari, 24, has been charged following reports the teenager was attacked in Manchester.

The alleged rape happened on Hope Street, near Piccadilly Gardens, at around 1.30am on July 14.

Shinwari, of no fixed abode, has been charged with two counts of rape and two counts of sexual assault.





He also faces charges of non-fatal strangulation and possession with intent to supply.

The 24-year-old is due to appear at Manchester Crown Court today, Greater Manchester Police said.

Specialist safeguarding officers are continuing to support the teenage victim.

Police have not released further details about the alleged attack.

News.title: Man seriously injured and two hurt after brawl involving ‘bladed article’ in UK city centre – as two arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BLADE CHAOS Man seriously injured and two hurt after brawl involving ‘bladed article’ in UK city centre – as two arrested

A MAN has been seriously injured and two others hurt after a “large” city centre brawl involving a “bladed article”.

Cops have arrested two men following the violent clash, which saw armed cops swarm to the scene.



Police said that the violence broke out on Calenick Street in Truro, Cornwall, at around 1.45pm.

The force added that one man suffered a “potentially serious injury” in the fracas.



Two others were left with minor injuries.

Police confirmed that two men, both in their 20s, have been arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent.



The force said those involved are believed to have known each other.

A number of witnesses told CornwallLive there was an extremely large police and ambulance presence in the area.

One person said: “[The road is] all cordoned off around Burger King, around 30 coppers, 12 police cars”.

A force spokesperson said there was “no wider threat to the public”.



They added: “Those involved are believed to be known to each other and there is no wider threat to the public.”

Officers are now appealing for witnesses and anyone with relevant footage to come forward.

Anybody with information is urged to get in touch with the force, quoting 50260226230.

News.title: Trump launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ on Iran as he tries to isolate regime with damaging new sanctions
News.content:
DONALD Trump has launched his crushing “Operation Economic Outcast” on Iran by threatening crippling sanctions on any country propping up the regime.

The US president last week vowed to unleash the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN” to strong-arm Tehran into accepting his peace terms.



Washington has now upped the ante with a new plan to slap severe sanctions on any country maintaining economic ties with the regime.

Iran has meanwhile vowed it will retaliate against any country participating in the US-led isolation campaign.



With the war dragging on to the six-month mark, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced “Operation Economic Outcast” as a “warning shot” to Iran‘s allies.

Bessent said that the US was giving them a chance to “remedy bad behaviour” but stopped short of naming specific countries or laying out a timeline.



“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” he said.

“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Bessent declined to answer whether the move would target China, which bought 80 per cent of Iran’s ship oil last year.

But he said: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions.



“That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”

Bessent said that the US had identified countries who continued to deal with Iran and would set individual deadlines to cut off ties or face sanctions.

He added: “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



Trump, he said, was making direct calls to world leaders to request that they “cease their interactions with the regime”.

Bessent did not elaborate on whether Trump had spoken with Xi Jinping after a successful summit in Beijing last month.

China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem.

“China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”

Xi is set to meet Trump in Washington in late September, but fresh sanctions could sour prospects for extending a deal struck last November to keep Chinese rare earths flowing and cap US tariffs.



Iran brushed the sanctions off with the country’s finance minister saying it was “fully prepared” for them.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ali Madanizadeh also accused the US of wanting to “wage economic terrorism”.

“We know how to play this game. This time, they should not think our response will be purely defensive and that we will only defend ourselves.”

News.title: Ukraine gives Britain ‘goldmine’ of secret battlefield data to help build AI weapons & protect bases from Russian spies
News.content:
UKRAINE has given Britain access to a treasure trove of top secret battlefield data to develop new AI weapons and protect bases from Russian attacks.

It comes as the UK granted Kyiv the blueprints to Storm Shadow long-range missiles, sparking a furious reproach from Vladimir Putin and his Kremlin warmongers.



Andy Burnham has now struck a deal with Volodymyr Zelensky to use Ukraine‘s coveted Avengers AI Labs, which holds millions of pieces of real-life combat data gathered from the war.

The UK will become the first foreign country to access thousands of cameras and infrared sensors that have tracked Russian tanks, troops, artillery, air defences and drones, creating a “goldmine” for training AI.



The Ukrainian military said its systems are now capable of detecting 70 per cent of all Russian targets after combing through years of data collected throughout the war.

British scientists and tech firms will now be able to use the data to develop cutting-edge defence technology.



And the first system is already about to be deployed at a UK military site to spot protesters and hostile spies trying to gain intelligence.

It turns buried fibre-optic cables into giant AI-powered sensors and could eventually be used to protect airports, prisons, railways and power stations.

Britain will in return give Ukraine access to its universities, researchers and tech firms to help Kyiv develop new battlefield technology.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security.”



The deal could also “revolutionise all parts of public life, from air traffic control to train systems,” the Ministry of Defence said.

Until now, British defence companies have relied on Ukrainian drone operations posted online, which offer just a snapshot of drone strikes and surveillance missions.

It comes at a crucial time for the UK, with Moscow orchestrating a series of surveillance operations on European military bases and nuclear sites.



Britain has also been targeted by drones trying to access sensitive facilities with drones launched from its shadow fleet vessels.

The UK and Ukraine are also collaborating on a second project to build low-power AI chips that could create more durable and intelligent drones and robotics.

Burnham hailed the “ground-breaking partnership” as he visited Kyiv on his first foreign trip as Prime Minister.

He said: “Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading innovators in defence technology, forged through courage, ingenuity and the hard lessons of war.”

The PM said the deal will give Britain “the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine.”



It comes as Russia has accused the UK of “participating” in the war and warned that there would be “consequences” over supplying weapons to Ukraine.

Kremlin mouthpiece Dmitry Peskov blasted Britain for “adding fuel to the fire” for giving Zelensky information on the components on Storm Shadow missiles so that Kyiv can manufacture the weapon itself.

But Burnham hit back and said: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?”



Foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said that Russia would target and “destroy” facilities producing the missiles.

It comes amid mounting pressure on Putin’s war machine.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ukrainian forces have repeatedly pummelled the nation’s equivalent of Amazon and are systemically blasting apart their fuel hubs.

For a third night in a row, Ukrainian drones have blitzed Ozon, Russia’s second-biggest online retailer, in an attempt to bleed Putin‘s war chest dry.

News.title: Council house tenants face the boot if they live in squalor and neglect their gardens, Reform warns
News.content:
COUNCIL house tenants could be given the boot if they live in squalor and fail to maintain their gardens, Reform UK has warned.

Nigel Farage’s party has promised a major shake-up of social housing including building more than 50,000 council homes a year.



But Reform chairman Lee Anderson said hard-up Brits expect council house tenants living in accommodation subsidised by the taxpayer to be left in a “reasonable” state.

He said: “People who live in subsidised housing – paid for, subsidised by the hard-working British taxpayer – what is wrong with expecting them to keep their house to a reasonable standard?”



Mr Anderson warned that councils failing to screen tenants properly was “creating mayhem and disturbances on these brand new housing estates.

He added: “The hard-working British taxpayer, the alarm clock people who get up at five or six o’clock in the morning, go to work and they see the house next door with four foot of weeds, dustbin not been emptied for three weeks, and a waft of weed coming out the window – it’s not acceptable.”

His comments come as Reform unveiled its plans to overhaul social housing in Britain.

Young married couples who work and have children would be moved to the front of the queue as well as veterans.

Mr Farage’s party wanted to revive the Right to Buy policy.

This is channelling an old policy put forward by Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s.



Foreign nationals living in social housing will be evicted within a short-time frame as a Reform government takes power.

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.

She says she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary.

"I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says.

While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.

But her problems didn't end there.

While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.

Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy.

"I just want somewhere peaceful for him and calm. Somewhere nice where I can bring him up," she says.

She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.

Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than Â£16bn remains to be allocated outside London.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", and the government said millions extra would be given to councils to support their housebuilding plans and help with expertise.

But the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.

News.title: Beyond China's humanoid robots, a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
News.content:
"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (Â£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

News.title: The grieving family who say the coroners' courts aren't working
News.content:
Sarah thought she knew what she was getting into when she attended a coroner's court in May 2024 to discuss the death of her second cousin.

Her day job as a murder detective meant she was used to courts, to judges, to legal argument. What she wasn't prepared for was a coroner's court. "I felt like I was on trial," she recalls of her first hearing, in Woking, Surrey. "I remember just feeling completely railroadedâ¦ It [was] far more hostile than I had ever expected."

Her cousin, Daniel Lindsay, died in 2023, aged 41. He had lived at a home in Surrey that specialises in caring for people with learning disabilities. Daniel also had Down's syndrome and type 1 diabetes.

As his death was unexpected, his case was referred to the coroner for an inquest.

What followed was one of the most stressful experiences of Sarah's life. She discovered new details about how her cousin lived, and his cause of death. The family initially thought Daniel died from a heart attack - but over the course of the inquest, they learnt that was wrong. She had expected the process to be emotional; what she didn't predict was just how complex and frustrating it would be, at times leaving her tearful and furious.

Coroners examine deaths that are not straightforward, like unexpected or violent deaths, or those that take place in state custody. Every year, thousands of British families rely on these courts for crucial answers. For many, an inquest provides the key interaction with the arms of the state at a time of trauma.

News.title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed two officers
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group. One has since been charged.

In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.

The force said:

It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning

The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area

The second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology

The Volvo has been recovered in Middlesbrough

Four of the five people in the Passat had previous convictions

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".

He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.

"We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."

News.title: HPV home-testing kits available for women in England who have missed cervical screening
News.content:
Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer â making it easier than ever for them to get tested.

"There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening â embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort â and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."

The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.

It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.

High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.

Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening â boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.

Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.

Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years â or more frequently if HPV is detected.

Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.

The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer â and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

News.title: Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
News.content:
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.

The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.

Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.

Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.

Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at Â£2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere.

"I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.

Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.

Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances.

"Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances.

"I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."

Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that.

"We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."

Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.

Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.

Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves.

The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.

Rain Newton-Smith, the chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much".

"The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.

She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

News.title: Sir Chris Hoy: Campaigning for cancer screening should not be down to me
News.content:
Sir Chris Hoy believes the onus to encourage men to get tested for prostate cancer should not just be on high-profile individuals like him.

Hoy told BBC Scotland he felt privileged to have the public platform to spread awareness and would continue to do so even if there was a national screening system in place.

But he said: "It shouldn't just be down to high-profile individuals like Jeremy Clarkson or myself or any number of men who've been in a similar situation.

"There should be a more systematic and proactive approach to let men know about their own risk."

Sir Chris was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer when was 47. He turned 50 in March.

News.title: How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump
News.content:
What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its goods to the US, actually have in this spiralling trade dispute with its southern neighbour, who also happens to be the world's largest economy?

Canada is the top customer for 26 US states, including Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin. And it is in the top three for 45 of the 50 American states, suggesting Prime Minister Mark Carney has room to manoeuvre in a trade fight.

For now, Carney's planned Canadian retaliatory duties are strategic "dollar-for-dollar" countermeasures focused on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, electronics, pulp and paper - though the list is still being finalised.

Polls suggest a majority of Canadians would be unhappy if his government went in the other direction and made significant concessions to the US. That sentiment is shared by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of Trump's most vocal critics north of the border, who responded to the tariff threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass".

Canada's Finance Department said additional measures to protect workers and businesses would be announced on Tuesday.

Here are some areas where Canada can apply economic pressure.

News.title: Letting agent accused of not returning deposits to more than 100 tenants
News.content:
Raman Kaur and her family rented a house through Morgan, Payne & Knightly (MPK) until September 2025 when they bought their own home.

They are still waiting for their Â£900 deposit to be returned and have discovered the money was not put in a registered deposit scheme.

"It's not right, he shouldn't be doing that with our money," she said. "That's our sweat, our hard work.

"It's very stressful having a young family and with the financial crisis that we're all going through.

"We've saved that money, we've budgeted and we've had to tell the kids they can't have things.

"I think he should be ashamed of what he's done. It's not his money, he didn't earn it."

Kaur says the family visited the West Bromwich branch of MPK to resolve the matter, but found it had closed, leaving them to try phoning Singh and his staff every day.

The home the family rented is owned by an individual who did not want to be named in this article. We will refer to him as Vikram.

"I'm owed Â£700 and MPK are falsely saying they're registered in a deposit protection scheme, but they're not," he said.

"I've spent months trying to get hold of Tony Singh but the offices have shut down, and nobody answers the phone or emails.

"It feels like nobody can help us, so we contacted the BBC."

Our investigation has since found that individual sums that are owed range from Â£700 to Â£16,000.

Vikram reported his experience to Trading Standards.

Sandwell Council, which covers West Bromwich, said both Singh and MPK were no longer operating in the borough.

Singh and MPK continue, however, to operate elsewhere in the West Midlands, the BBC can confirm.

News.title: Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine
News.content:
A British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.

The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.

The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.

The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

News.title: Boy, 16, arrested after four viable devices found in security alert
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been arrested under the Terrorism Act after a security alert in Omagh, County Tyrone.

Police carried out a planned search on Monday at an address in the Gardenville Avenue.

Police said four viable explosive devices were found and removed from the property for forensic examination.

Nearby residents who had been asked to leave their homes during the alert have since returned.

Det Insp Winters urged the public not to speculate about the incident.

"It's important to stress that, while the suspect has been arrested under the Terrorism Act, our investigation to establish a motive remains very much ongoing."

News.title: Man charged with murder after house fire
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder, attempted murder and arson following a fire in west London that left a woman dead and eight others in need of hospital treatment.

Pawel Kulpa, 34, faces one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

The charges come after a fire at a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday, 19 August.

A 50-year-old woman, named by the Met Police as Anna Kowalska, died in hospital while another woman, 40, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. Kulpa is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott, from Glasgow, covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Drugs dug up at Creamfields site ahead of festival
News.content:
Huge stashes of illegal drugs have been found buried underground at a festival site days before the event was due to begin.

More than 80,000 music fans will head to Creamfields Festival in Daresbury, Cheshire, from Thursday.

About 204 canisters of nitrous oxide - known as laughing gas - and large bags containing ecstasy, MDMA and ketamine tablets were dug up by police during a pre-event search of the grounds, Cheshire Police said.

Supt Andy Blizard said: "Every year, we counter a number of brazen individuals who think they can outsmart us by concealing drugs from view or burying them at the site months in advance."

"There is a zero-tolerance policy regarding drugs," he said.

News.title: Man charged with manslaughter in burglary case
News.content:
A man has been charged with manslaughter after a 75-year-old woman died following a suspected burglary in north London.

Police were called to Tollington Park in Finsbury Park on the night of 11 August after reports of a burglary.

Rose Smith was taken to hospital, where she died the following day. An 81-year-old man was also taken to hospital and was discharged the next day.

Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, of Apsley Close, North Harrow, has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary. He is due to appear at Barkingside Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

He was arrested on Friday, 21 August.

In a statement released earlier on Monday, Smith's family described her as an "outgoing woman" who loved "bingo, going to cafÃ©s with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family".

They described their loss as devastating, adding: "She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went.

"We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was - loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life."

A top beauty therapist has won over £32,000 after she was was fired because she was struggling with the menopause.

Experienced Chantelle Van Vliet was the only therapist who was not rehired when their clinic rebranded, just days after she had asked for more flexible working because of the 'severity' of her symptoms.

Ms Van Vliet, who has worked at some of the most 'prestigious' spas across the world, was let go with no warning despite the fact that she was a single mother.

She took her clinic in a Hampshire market town to a tribunal and has won over £32,000 for discrimination, saying that 'companies shouldn't get away with how they treat people'.

Ms Van Vliet was employed as a Senior Aesthetic Therapist by Footlaffs Limited - now called Always Time to be Me Ltd - from June 2022 in Petersfield, Hants.

She has 'worked as a beauty and aesthetics therapist for over 20 years' and 'apart from a period of maternity... she has never experienced any period of unemployment and has found work easily in her chosen field'.

The beauty therapist, from Chichester, West Sussex, was 48 at the time and a single parent to a 12 year old boy.

From 2022 onwards, Ms Van Vliet 'experienced significant perimenopausal/menopausal symptoms including migraines, hot flushes and recurrent urinary tract infections, which worsened through 2023 and early 2024'.

She had told Karen Dodds, the boss of the therapy clinic, about her struggles with the symptoms in April 2024, and even had discussions with her about undertaking hormone replacement therapy.

In May 2024, she even had to take a day off because 'she could not cope' with the severity of the symptoms.

open image in gallery Menopausal symptoms feel worse during a heatwave ( Alamy/PA )

A week later, Ms Van Vliet ended up emailing her manager at the clinic and Mrs Dodds requesting flexible working.

She wrote: "I would like to ask for this request to get a better work and family balance.

"I have also recently started going through the menopause which has really affected me, especially working the later shifts.

"I would be happy to agree a three month trial period."

Ms Van Vliet's manager replied a couple of days after saying they would discuss the request with Mrs Dodds but they never got back to her.

At the end of May, the manager emailed Ms Van Vliet to say that she had been taken off the rota for the following day because she had no clients booked - but that was untrue as she did have clients.

The next day, all of Footlaffs' staff were dismissed for redundancy.

However, it was heard "a large majority of the staff (including all the other therapists doing the aesthetics work), were offered new contracts so their employment could continue seamlessly with a phoenix business".

This was run by Mrs Dodds and Stephen Dodds under the name Time To Be Me, but later Always Time To Be Me Ltd.

Ms Van Vliet was the only beauty therapist who was not rehired - and no reason was given to her as to why.

She took the business and Mr and Mrs Dodd to an employment tribunal in Southampton, Hants, where Employment Judge Jonathan Burns found that the reason had to be due to the inconvenience of employing someone struggling with her menopause symptoms.

He concluded: "Mrs Dodd, who made the operative decisions, failed to give evidence and there is no or very little evidence before me to prove any alternative explanation.

"Bare assertions about redundancy have been made but no detail of this or of any other financial, operational or other non-discriminatory reasons for the relevant omission have been placed before me.

"Even if there was a redundancy situation, which is not proved, it is not shown by [clinic] that there was a lawful reason for [Ms Van Vliet's] (rather than the other aesthetic therapists’) selection.

"The flexible working request arose at least in material part from [Ms Van Vliet's] disability, which is referred to in terms in the request.

[The clinic's bosses] had at least constructive knowledge of the fact that [Ms Van Vliet] had her disability.

"[Ms Van Vliet was] at a substantial disadvantage compared to someone without the [her] disability, in that she was unable to work the late shifts due to fatigue, confusion and brain fog.

"The flexible working request was in substance a request for a reasonable adjustment for disability.

"It would have been reasonable for the [clinic's bosses] to allow [Ms Van Vliet] to change her shifts; as her request was modest and sensible, and to allow her to continue in employment so she could test out the new shifts as she had proposed."

The beauty therapist won claims of disability discrimination, wrongful dismissal, deduction of wages, failing to make reasonable adjustments and victimisation.

However further claims of automatic unfair dismissal and direct discrimination were dismissed.

It was found that the company had failed to pay Ms Van Vliet £3,228 of unpaid wages and £510 of notice pay.

She has also been awarded £12,077 for loss of salary, and because 'the dismissal had a severe emotional impact on her including loss of confidence, distress, difficulties in family life and daily functioning', she has also been awarded £16,422 for injury to feelings.

The total she is owed is £32,237 - but as the new company Always Time To Be Me is in voluntary liquidation, Ms Van Vliet is unclear as to when she will receive the compensation.

She is now self-employed and runs her own beauty therapy business.

Speaking after the judgement, the beauty therapist said: "They're absolutely awful people.

"They did it to about 20 other people too and they're now just declaring bankruptcy so I don't know what's happening with payment. It's awful.

"It's good to highlight this to other people and employers. Companies shouldn't get away with how they treat people."

Dr Xand successfully horrified his fellow guests on The One Show as he offered a breakdown of what goes into collagen supplements.

Collagen – the most abundant protein in the human body – is what gives our bodies its elasticity and resilience. As we age, its production slows down, resulting in our aged appearances and more aches and pains.

In today’s wellness industry, collagen has become a huge business, with companies peddling collagen supplements in powder, gummy, tablet and liquid form.

Appearing on The One Show last week, British doctor, presenter and broadcaster Dr Xand attempted to quell the frenzy by explaining just what collagen supplements are.

“Anyone who is into their wellness – I will tell you, I was into it too – the collagen story, I was into it too,” he said. “Collagen is the most common protein in your body… you’re held together with collagen.

“And when you get older, your collagen starts to degrade and that’s why your joints get creaky and you get wrinkly. And so eating collagen makes sense – you think, ‘Oh it’ll get into my skin, it’ll get into my joints, it’ll repair me.”

open image in gallery Dr Xand explained the sources of collagen during an appearance on The One Show ( BBC )

Dr Xand stated that he’d visited a factory in China where they “boil donkeys to make collagen supplements… the collagen industry entirely relies on the waste products of industrial meat and fish processing, so the hooves, the chickens’ claws, the pigs’ trotters, the pigs’ ears, the tails, the skin… you boil it up with hydrochloric acid and you get collagen out the other end.”

In the Nineties, he said, companies realised that rather than using this waste as animal feed, they could sell it as a beauty product.

“The research says it doesn’t work,” Dr Xand said, calling collagen “too good to be true”.

Fans were tickled by the uncomfortable reactions from comedian Judi Love and presenter Angelica Bell, with Love patting the skin on her face as Dr Xand mentioned animal waste being used to make collagen.

However, Dr Xand’s comments also sparked a fierce debate in the comments section of the clip posted to Facebook, with some viewers insisting that collagen had improved their joint pain, along with their skin, nails and hair.

open image in gallery There are now a range of collagen supplements on the market ( Independent/iStock )

Others lamented the pressure – especially on women – to maintain a youthful appearance instead of embracing aging as a natural part of life.

In an umbrella review of 113 trials involving almost 8,000 patients around the world, experts at Anglia Ruskin University found that taking collagen supplements was “consistently” linked to reducing the symptoms of arthritis, such as stiff and painful joints.

It was also associated with improvements in muscle health, although there was no evidence that it can help improve soreness after exercise.

Professor of public health at ARU, Lee Smith, said “bold claims had been made in relation to collagen supplements, particularly by those marketing the product, including that it can result in significant and rapid anti-aging.

“Collagen is not a cure-all, but it does have credible benefits when used consistently over time, particularly for skin and osteoarthritis,” he said.

“Our findings show clear benefits in key areas of healthy aging, while also dispelling some of the myths surrounding its use.”

In 2023, cattle products such as collagen, along with palm oil and soy, were linked to around 8,800 hectares of deforestation connected to UK imports between November 2021 and July 2023.

The leader of a fringe religious group in New Zealand has been sentenced to more than 10 years in jail over the death of a 70-year-old woman who had travelled from China to live in his house called the “Ark”.

Kaixiao Liu, 39, was sentenced to 10 years and five months at the high court in Auckland after being convicted of manslaughter and kidnapping in connection with the death of 70-year-old Shulai Wang.

His 38-year-old wife, Lanyue Xiao, was also sentenced to seven years and 11 months in prison.

They ran a religious community at home, and besides Liu’s parents, there were six women from China, including Wang, who the judge said “remained here illegally”.

Wang, from China’s Hainan province, arrived in New Zealand in August 2023 and subsequently lived with Liu, Xiao, and other women at their home, which was called the Ark, in Orewa in the north of Auckland, local media reported.

The prosecution described the household as tightly controlled, with the women expected to follow Liu’s rules and refer to him as “lord” or “master”.

Wang was said to have spent much of her time caring for Liu’s children, studying religious texts, and working in the garden. Court proceedings heard that she struggled with some of the household’s “suffocatingly strict” requirements and was repeatedly punished.

In March 2024, Wang attempted to leave but was captured and restrained. Prosecutors said she was held for about 38 hours, her food and water was withheld, and her mouth taped shut to prevent her from screaming, 1News reported.

70-year-old Shulai Wang travelled from China to live in the fringe leader's household, which was called the 'Ark' ( New Zealand Police )

She died later that day. Her body was subsequently transported to Gulf Harbour, where it was concealed near a marina. Liu took his children on the trip, with the court hearing that they were used “as camouflage”.

Wang’s remains were discovered days later after a fisherman found the body near the marina at Gulf Harbour. She had been wrapped in bags and rice sacks.

Police eventually connected the packaging to Liu after investigating his unusually large purchases of the particular rice brand used to conceal the body.

Justice Mathew Downs described Liu as the ringleader and said he had shown “callous indifference” towards Wang.

“Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame.”

The judge said Liu had made the major decisions surrounding Wang’s detention and punishment, making him more culpable than his wife.

The court also heard that Liu had retained objects associated with Wang’s detention and disposal of her body. Justice Downs said these appeared to have been used to intimidate the other women living in the household.

“Ms Xiao, there is no evidence whatsoever you demonstrated any empathy for Ms Wang or the other women either,” the judge said.

Mr Downs said he had observed disagreements between the couple during the trial and that there were occasions when Liu appeared to defer to his wife.

“If you had sought to dissuade Mr Liu from the offending, there is a very real prospect he might have been so dissuaded,” he said.

The couple have five children and the judge said that Xiao is pregnant with a sixth.

Liu was also convicted of interfering with human remains, attempting to obstruct the course of justice and refusing to provide police with passwords to electronic devices during a search.

Liu’s lawyer, Ron Mansfield KC, sought a more lenient sentence and said his client remained in disagreement with the prosecution’s account of what happened.

“He is not a cult leader, nor require people to follow his cult,” Mr Mansfield said.

He argued that Liu had gained followers primarily through his music rather than religious preaching. He also pointed to Liu’s role as a father and said that separation from his children had made his time in custody particularly difficult.

Liu has previously described himself as a musician.

He appeared on China’s Got Talent in 2011, where online footage showed him performing while blindfolded.

Liu and Xiao have been together for about a decade, the judge said. They met while both were living in the United States before moving to New Zealand in 2017. They have remained in the country since then and became permanent residents.

After moving to New Zealand with Xiao in 2017, Liu developed an online following through religious discussions, music and video content. He also established a project called Universal Choir, which produced orchestral music with cosmic themes.

Police told the court that at least one woman had encountered Liu and his followers online before joining the household. An officer who interviewed her said she told police she had “met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends”.

Liu’s parents were also convicted in connection with the case. His mother, Xiuyun Li, was convicted of kidnapping, while his father, Jingui Liu, was convicted of misconduct involving human remains.

They are due to be sentenced later this year.

A new campaign has been launched by easyJet as the airline seeks to recruit more mature workers for its cabin crew positions.

Since introducing a targeted hiring scheme in 2022, the business reported that staff aged over 50 have more than doubled, while crew members in their 60s have nearly quadrupled.

Research conducted by easyJet indicated that a majority of individuals changing careers past the age of 50 felt happier as a result.

The carrier added that many candidates often presume flight attendant roles are intended for younger demographics, fearing they would be the oldest members of the team.

Michael Brown, director of cabin services at easyJet, said: “It’s been incredibly encouraging to see the numbers of cabin crew over 50 more than double since 2022 – evidence that many are increasingly viewing cabin crew as a fantastic career pivot regardless of age.

“We want more over-50s to apply as they not only bring their existing skills to excel in a career at easyJet, but also a wealth of life experience that is appreciated by our customers and colleagues alike, which is at the heart of the fantastic service our crew are known for.”

Cabin crew members Pilar Roman Palomino, Andrew Hampson, Francesca Hicks, Elane Vass and Mehdi Lamrani gather at London Gatwick Airport as easyJet launches a new recruitment drive encouraging people aged over 50 to become cabin crew ( PA )

Employment minister Andrew Western said: “Supportive employers like easyJet know the breadth of experience over-50s can bring to the workforce and it shows what can be achieved when this is valued.”

Applications open from September, with opportunities available across the airline’s UK bases.

The recruitment drive comes as easyJet is to be bought by private equity firm Apollo in a £5.7 billion deal after rival suitor Castlelake walked away from a bidding war for the budget airline.

EasyJet was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer a low-cost alternative to British Airways and it has since expanded to be one of the largest networks across Europe.

Sir Stelios and his family, who own around 15 per cent of the business, have given the takeover their support.

“I am pleased with Apollo’s strategic intentions for the easyJet business, which aim to create more growth,” he said.

“My family and I intend to remain invested as long-term major shareholders of easyJet for the next chapter in the company’s journey.”

Sir Stephen Hester, non-executive chairman of easyJet, said: “The easyJet board has carefully evaluated the proposal from Apollo alongside easyJet’s standalone prospects.

“While we remain confident in the strength of our business and the opportunities ahead, we believe this offer appropriately recognises the quality of the business we have built and delivers immediate, certain and attractive value for shareholders.”

News.title: These high street bags give a nod to Mulberry, Goyard, DeMellier and more
News.content:
Finding the perfect work bag that’s comfortable, stylish and fits all of your essentials, from your lunch to gym kit, can be a challenge. Fortunately you don’t need to spend a fortune to commute in style, with plenty of affordable high street options now available that take cues from designs we’ve seen on the runway.

One brand that’s caught our eye is Katie Loxton, whose latest range of work bags nod to details seen on designs from the likes of Mulberry, Balenciaga, Goyard and more. From structured totes to slouchy, croc-style designs, these bags start from £60 and won’t set you back more than £100.

We’ve put a range of Katie Loxton’s latest work bags to the test, using them for our commutes and after-work drinks, packing in all our office day essentials such as laptops, chargers, make-up bags and more to see how they hold up.



open image in gallery This is a timeless design that won’t go out of style ( Sabrina Sahota/The Independent )

Rating: 4.5/5

This clean tote design evokes the classic styles seen at Mulberry and Goyard, but for a fraction of the price. The subtle, distressed material gives it that lived in feel and the deep cherry colour is the perfect transitional tone to take you into autumn.

The interior is spacious enough to my fit my 13in laptop, lunch, make-up bag and lots more. There are plenty of inner pockets to keep your belongings organised, including a zipped pocket for valuables. There’s even a discreet sleeve on the outside of the bag to slot your phone or card. The only downside is that the straps are quite thin, so it may start to feel uncomfortable if you’re carrying lots in it.

Why we love it: Classic and timeless design, monogram detail makes it feel extra special, plenty of inner pockets to keep essentials organised

Take note: Straps are quite thin

Reviewed by Sabrina Sahota

open image in gallery The gold twist-lock takes cues from DeMellier’s Hudson bag ( Isabella Howells/The Independent )

Rating: 4.5/5

This elevated tote is the perfect transitional piece for autumn. The rich cherry shade feels seasonal, while the gold twist-lock detail takes cues from DeMellier’s Hudson bag. It’s generously sized without being so roomy that your essentials disappear at the bottom, and the secure zip-top closure keeps everything safely in place.

The timeless suedette finish is also reportedly waterproof, although we didn’t get to put this to the test during the heatwave. Available in the shades 'bitter chocolate’ and ‘cherry,’ it’s an easy everyday work bag that goes with any autumnal outfit. The only downside is the thinner straps, which may become uncomfortable if you’re carrying a lot at once.

Why we love it: Colour options are perfect for autumn, generous size without being overly bulky, zip-top closure keeps belongings secure

Take note: Thin straps may become uncomfortable when the bag is heavily loaded

Reviewed by Isabella Howells

open image in gallery This feels straight out of Serena van der Woodsen’s wardrobe ( Hollie Brown/The Independent )

Rating: 4.5/5

The Maddie work tote is very Serena van der Woodsen. The grey faux-croc finish feels sleek and expensive, while the spacious design fits all your essentials. The relaxed tote shape and belt design feels very much inspired by Prada’s buckle bag.

I love the dedicated laptop compartment, especially as I’m guilty of throwing mine anywhere in my bag. The three-section design makes it easy to keep everything separate, while the back pocket unzips to create a handy pass-through for your suitcase handle – such a useful feature for commuting or travelling.

Why we love it: Fits up to 15in laptop within the main pocket, back pocket unzips to attach to a suitcase handle, stylish without sacrificing practicality

Take note: Only neutral colourway options available

Reviewed by Hollie Brown

open image in gallery There are two main compartments inside the bag ( Niki Cottrell/The Independent )

Rating: 4/5

For a simple work bag, the Victoria suedette from Katie Loxton really goes above and beyond. It has the structure of an Hermès Kelly bag with a relaxed, flap top opening inspired by the Balenciaga Rodeo. Made from sleek vegan leather, the design features two main compartments, an outer pocket on the back and a small interior sipper pocket that make staying organised in the office feel effortless.

My 13in laptop slipped in smoothly, though the structured design does limit the amount you can pack into it. However, the side-snap extensions easily pop open on both sides to give you a few extra inches of space for those heavier packing days.

Why we love it: Clasped top keeps items completely secure, plenty of compartments for organisation

Take note: Not the most spacious

Reviewed by Niki Cottrell

The Champions League returns next month, and this Thursday sees the league phase draw confirmed with a ceremony in Monaco.

Three months on from PSG retaining their title on penalties against Arsenal in Budapest, this season’s competition takes shape, as each of the 36 teams discovers their eight league phase matches.

Arsenal, Manchester City, Manchester United, Aston Villa and Liverpool are the English teams involved, with Celtic hoping to make it six British teams by winning their play-off tie against LASK. They won the first leg 3-0.

Other big-hitters in pot one include PSG, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Inter Milan, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid.

Here’s everything you need to know about the Champions League league phase draw.

When is the Champions League league phase draw?

The 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase draw starts at 5pm BST (12pm ET) on Thursday, 27 August.

The draw will arrange the eight matches each team contests in the 36-team first phase – facing two teams from pots one, two, three and four. Half of the matches will be at home, the other half away.

Where can I watch the Champions League draw?

The draw will be broadcast on TNT Sports 1 and HBO Max in the United Kingdom, the joint host broadcasters in the UK of the Champions League alongside Prime Video.

How does the Champions League league phase work?

The top eight all automatically qualify for the last-16, while teams positioned ninth to 24th place qualify for the knockout-phase play-off. Teams finishing between ninth and 16th will be seeded and will host the second leg.

Teams who finish the league phase 25th or lower are out and do not drop into the Europa League.

News.title: Iran claims there is a $10 million bounty on Barron Trump
News.content:

Iranian state media has claimed there is a $10 million bounty on Barron Trump, President Donald Trump’s 20-year-old son, according to a new report nearly six months into the U.S. war with Iran.

Footage broadcast on Channel 3, which is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, was titled “Where and how should we kill Barron Trump?” Euronews reported Monday.

It reportedly displayed the location of his university, as well as Secret Service positions and escort vehicles, while claiming his whereabouts were “fully monitored.”

The clip also claimed that an unnamed young woman had evaded Secret Service protection, met privately with Barron Trump and relayed information about him to the video’s creators. It also claimed he uses Xbox to communicate privately.

Euronews reported that it did not independently verify the claims. The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

open image in gallery Iranian state media has claimed there is a $10 million bounty on Barron Trump, the president's 20-year-old son, according to a new report ( C14 News )

Barron Trump, the president’s youngest son and his only child with First Lady Melania Trump, is a college student. Compared to the president’s other sons, he has kept a relatively low public profile. He has attended some official events, including the president’s UFC cage match at the White House in June and the State of the Union address at the Capitol in February.

This is not the first time he has been targeted by Iran. Last month, an Iran-linked video threatened both Barron Trump and the first lady. The clip, titled “Where to kill Melania” shows a mock up of the first lady’s motorcade and calls on “freedom fighters” to take action against her. It concludes with: “Barron Trump, wait for us!” ​

“The Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees,” an agency spokesperson told Newsweek.

open image in gallery Compared to his older brothers, Barron Trump has kept a relatively low public profile. Pictured: President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Barron Trump watch during an indoor inauguration parade at Capital One Arena on January 20, 2025 in Washington, DC ( Getty Images )

The president also has faced repeated threats from Iran over the years, with U.S. officials warning that Tehran and its proxies could seek retaliation for his 2020 order to kill Iranian General Qassem Soleimani. The threats have led to heightened security for Trump and several former members of his administration, though Iran has denied plotting to kill him.

This year, Asif Merchant, a Pakistani business owner, was convicted after authorities accused him of working on behalf of Iran with the intention of carrying out assassinations, with Trump being a target. And in 2024, federal authorities charged Farhad Shakeri, an Iranian national, with taking instructions to develop a plan to kill Trump.

Following the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, threats have intensified. At a NATO summit last month, Trump reportedly ditched Air Force One and departed Turkey on a military plane amid concerns about threats from Iran.

The 80-year-old president has said he has “left instructions” if he is killed by Iran “to just literally bomb them at levels that they’ve never seen before.”

open image in gallery Earlier this summer, a large billboard also cropped up in Tehran depicting Trump being strangled alongside the statement: ‘Revenge is inevitable’ ( AFP via Getty Images )

The newly reported threat against Barron Trump comes as the U.S. war with Iran shows no signs of abating.

Early in the conflict, U.S. forces killed Iran’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with multiple other senior officials. Trump has since claimed that so many Iranian leaders have been killed that there is “nobody” left to negotiate with.

To date, 18 U.S. service members have been killed in the war and hundreds more have been wounded, the Pentagon has said. Thousands of Iranians have been killed, according to HRANA, a U.S.-based human rights group.

Multiple recent polls indicate a majority of Americans are opposed to the war.

News.content:
