Every day, the Russian Federation launches dozens of ballistic missiles at peaceful neighborhoods of Ukrainian cities. What kind of readiness for the end of the war can we talk about?

We will be able to talk about when the war will end, when the fighting will cease. As you know, the Ukrainian side has repeatedly proposed holding negotiations on neutral grounds – in Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Qatar. However, Russia is not interested in negotiations, which is why every time they find new excuses not to accept President Zelensky’s proposals. Russia is only interested in capturing, killing, raping and stealing.

Unfortunately, this is exactly what the documented crimes of the Russian Federation in Bucha, Irpin, Olenivka, Kherson and a number of other Ukrainian cities testify to. People were killed, tortured, raped – all this solely because they are Ukrainians…

Q. How important is the mediation of other countries in the humanitarian issues of this war? Do you see the potential for involving Africa in the negotiation process on the humanitarian track?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: We are grateful to all those who, to varying degrees, are joining in helping Ukraine and its citizens. This applies to both the states located on the same continental shelf with Ukraine, such as the states of the European Union, Norway, North Macedonia and others, and the United States of America, Canada, the states of South America, as well as Qatar, the UAE, Japan, and South Korea.

At the same time, we are convinced that the potential for involving African states in the humanitarian track in this regard is more than significant. First of all, we are talking about assistance in the return of Ukrainian children and the Coalition of the same name – unfortunately, the issue of abduction of children, their loss of ties with their family and homeland – many African states have gone through these trials and their experience in resolving complex humanitarian issues is extremely important right now, when thousands of Ukrainian children were illegally taken away by Russia and placed in foster families in the Russian Federation, which is one of the most egregious crimes of this war unleashed by the Russian Federation.

Q. How do you assess the current state of Ukrainian-Liberian relations?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: Liberia is a friend and ally of Ukraine in the West African region in particular and on the African continent as a whole. Official Monrovia shares the same postulates as official Kyiv – respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, as well as for human dignity and freedom, and this is what allows our countries to develop a mutually beneficial partnership.

At the same time, we are sure that we still have something to offer each other in a significant number of areas. For example, Ukraine remains open to students from African countries and Liberia in particular – the high quality of Ukrainian education is a well-known factor in African students choosing Ukraine as the country where they prefer to acquire new skills and competencies.

Currently, a simplified online system for submitting documents to Ukrainian higher education institutions is operating. We already have a significant number of students from West Africa who have received permits to enter Ukraine and are preparing for the start of the new academic year. We are convinced that the educational component is a solid foundation for the development of further cooperation.

In addition, we believe that the potential for cooperation in the field of agriculture remains untapped. Ukraine has unique experience and expertise, primarily in the context of crop management systems, GPS monitoring of equipment and precision agriculture. Moreover, all of the above is currently functioning during the period of active hostilities on the territory of Ukraine, which indicates the stability of the Ukrainian development system to external factors and the possibility of its implementation in states interested in the development of the agricultural sector.

Another important direction is the digitalization of state databases and systems for providing public services. Ukraine has something to offer in this regard, in particular in the light of the automation of the provision of certain consular services to Ukrainian citizens abroad (approximately 7-9 million people – ed. note), access to online state registers, etc.

Q. How does the Russian Federation operate in Africa? Have you encountered cases of disinformation directed against you?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: The Russian Federation does not have a strategy specifically allocated to the African continent – Russia has always pursued the same policy towards everyone with whom it considers it necessary not to cooperate, but to exploit.

This is exactly how Russia cooperates with African states – it does not offer solutions, it sows discord and, in fact, does not hide it.

For example, almost on a monthly basis, we receive new information about African students who went to the Russian Federation to study, but ended up in the combat zone against their will – they are forced to sign a contract drawn up in Russian, that is, a language they do not even speak sufficiently. If they are lucky, they manage to surrender to the Armed Forces of Ukraine and not die. Unfortunately, such cases are rather an exception to the rule, because for the most part, those whom Russia uses as cannon fodder die in the first days of entering the front line – they are thrown into battle after a week of training.

From open sources, we know about cases of criminal recruitment by the Russian Federation in Kenya, Uganda, South Africa, and Zambia. In our region, citizens of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Ghana have become victims of Russian manipulation. Fortunately, there is currently no information about citizens of Liberia who have become victims of Russian recruitment. We hope that this trend regarding Liberia will continue in the future, because it is very important to make it clear to the Russian Federation that, unlike Russia itself, people are not expendable in other countries.

Citizens of African countries should weigh all the risks when they come into contact with Russians. If there are any doubts, victims of Russian recruiters have repeatedly highlighted the nature of the Russian Federation’s attitude towards people (Malik Diop (Senegal), Richard Kanu (Sierra Leone), etc.). Think twice before signing up for certain death – until a contract with the Russian Armed Forces is signed, you will not find yourself on the battlefield. As soon as the contract is signed, you automatically become a war criminal who violates the territorial integrity and sovereignty of another state and falls under the relevant norms of international law. There is no way back.

As for disinformation, just as Russia hides its inability to advance on the battlefield in Ukraine, Russia hides its crimes behind manipulations and lies in the media. Ukrainian Embassies in Africa are constantly accused of recruiting local citizens, assembling drones right in the Embassies, looking for sorcerers who would poison Putin and his henchmen… This style is nothing new – Ukraine has coexisted and fought against Russia for survival for centuries, so we know very well how Russia seeks to eliminate rivals. But readers should be very careful with such narratives – our African partners have repeatedly debunked Russian lies (for example, in Ghana, when an agent of Russian influence placed Nazi literature on a shelf with Ukrainian books, or in Côte d’Ivoire, when the Russians invented a story about “assembling drones at the Ukrainian Embassy in Abidjan”), which indicates an increasingly better understanding by African countries of the deceitful nature of the Russian Federation.

Q. Turning to the prospects of bilateral relations between Liberia and Ukraine, what, in your opinion, should be the next steps on both sides for the further development of mutually beneficial interstate dialogue?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: Ukraine and Liberia are partner countries. Countries that value and respect each other. And this is not only within the framework of international organizations, as I said above. In the bilateral direction, among other things, we are working on agreeing on the draft Agreement on the Establishment of a Joint Commission on Economic and Trade Cooperation between the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine and the Government of the Republic of Liberia, on the Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Liberia on cooperation in the field of education, as well as on other equally important draft bilateral documents.

In addition, we continue to work on the possible organization of an official visit of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Liberia, Ms. Sara Beysolow Nyanti, to Ukraine, within the framework of which both states could sign these documents and agree on other specific steps, as you say, of mutually beneficial cooperation between Ukraine and the Republic of Liberia.

These elements of the contractual and legal framework could form the basis, as you ask, of a new stage on the track of Ukrainian-Liberian relations.

World.title: Liberia: Koijee Warns Boakai Against ‘History’s Warning’ as Drug Probe Intensifies
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Monrovia City Mayor Jefferson Koijee has sharply criticized President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s recent expression of confidence in Liberia’s security leadership, warning that history offers cautionary lessons when political leaders place heavy reliance on security forces amid growing national tensions.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Koijee’s statement comes as President Boakai has publicly expressed confidence in Liberia’s security apparatus, including Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman, amid heightened public scrutiny surrounding the ongoing investigation into major cocaine seizures with a combined estimated street value of more than US$336 million.

In a strongly worded statement, Koijee invoked Liberia’s turbulent political history, referencing former presidents Charles G. Taylor and Samuel K. Doe and the specialized security units associated with their administrations.

“Mr. Boakai’s declaration of confidence in his security team should come with a warning from history,” Koijee said.

He cited Taylor’s confidence in the Anti-Terrorist Unit (ATU) and Doe’s reliance on the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit (SATU), arguing that excessive reliance on security structures can become a warning sign for political leadership.

Koijee alleged that when political leaders reach a point where loyalty from security forces becomes their primary source of reassurance, it can reflect growing fear and political vulnerability.

The former mayor accused the Boakai administration of intimidation and condemned what he characterized as abuses by state security personnel.

He said the opposition and the Liberian public do not need the confidence of security officials whom he accused of acting like “state-sanctioned militias.”

“What we have is far greater, the popular will of the people,” Koijee declared, describing that will as enduring and ultimately capable of determining the country’s political direction.

Koijee Challenges Security Leadership

Koijee’s remarks come against the backdrop of an increasingly contentious national debate over the handling of Liberia’s cocaine investigations.

The probe has generated intense political reactions, particularly following the seizure of a major cocaine consignment in the VOA community in Paynesville and a separate interception at Roberts International Airport.

The combined seizures have been valued at more than US$336 million by Liberian authorities.

The investigation has also drawn scrutiny following the detention and subsequent charging of former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor and other individuals in connection with the drug-trafficking investigation.

President Boakai has continued to defend the work of his security and law-enforcement institutions, while opposition figures and other critics have raised questions about the conduct, transparency and direction of the investigation.

Koijee, the Secretary-General of the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), portrayed the president’s confidence in his security team as an insufficient response to growing public concerns.

He described the president’s latest position as “a conspicuous and empty bluff,” arguing that political authority ultimately derives from the Liberian people rather than from the executive branch or security establishment.

“The People Endure”

Koijee warned security officials against becoming overly confident because of the authority temporarily entrusted to them by the state.

“Security officials intoxicated by temporary authority are transitory; the people endure,” he said.

He further argued that presidents, security commanders and political regimes do not permanently possess political power.

“Authority does not permanently belong to presidents, security commanders, or political regimes,” Koijee said, adding that the Liberian people remain the “true custodians and givers” of political authority.

Analysts say Koijee’s statement is likely to further intensify the political debate surrounding the government’s handling of the cocaine investigation, which has increasingly become a test of public confidence in Liberia’s security institutions and the administration’s commitment to accountability and due process.

Koijee concluded with a warning that political power that loses sight of its constitutional source—the people—will eventually be reminded of that reality by history.

World.title: Tingban Urges Boakai to Launch Emergency Reform at University of Liberia
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Assistant Minister for Mines, Mineral Resources Development and Conservation at the Ministry of Mines and Energy, Carlos E. Tingban Sr., has called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to make an urgent national intervention into the prolonged stalemate at the University of Liberia, warning that recurring disputes between university authorities and organized faculty and staff groups are threatening the institution’s academic mission.

In an open letter dated August 23, 2026, Tingban urged President Boakai to treat the situation at Liberia’s premier public university not simply as a labor disagreement, but as a broader national education and institutional crisis requiring decisive intervention, comprehensive reform and what he described as an institutional reset.

Tingban, who is also Chairman Emeritus of the Vanguard Student Unification Party/SUP and Executive Director of GeoMining and Environmental Consultancy Inc., acknowledged the rights of university workers to organize, negotiate and advocate for improved working conditions.

However, he argued that those rights must be balanced against the rights of students to receive uninterrupted education.

“No group should be allowed to hold the academic future of an entire generation hostage indefinitely,” Tingban said, stressing that prolonged disruptions affect not only university administrators but students, parents, families and the country’s broader development.

He said repeated academic delays, disagreements and work-related disruptions at the University of Liberia have created a pattern that should compel the government to examine the institution beyond individual administrations or university presidents.

Calls for Review of ULFA, ULSA

At the center of Tingban’s proposal is a comprehensive legal and institutional review of the University of Liberia Faculty Association (ULFA) and University of Liberia Staff Association (ULSA).

He called for an examination of the organizations’ mandates, structures, collective bargaining arrangements and relationship with the statutory authority of the university.

According to Tingban, if such a review determines that existing arrangements have become incompatible with the university’s ability to function effectively, the government should consider restructuring, replacing or dissolving those arrangements in accordance with Liberian law.

He emphasized that such reforms should preserve legitimate workers’ rights while preventing prolonged disruptions of academic activities.

Tingban stopped short of declaring that any particular conduct by university employees constitutes treason or another criminal offense, noting that such determinations belong to Liberia’s constitutional and legal authorities.

He nevertheless argued that deliberately or repeatedly disrupting higher education can cause serious national damage.

Performance Accountability for Faculty

Tingban also turned his attention to academic professionalism, calling for a stronger system of performance evaluation for lecturers and academic staff.

He proposed that faculty members be assessed annually against measurable standards, including classroom attendance and punctuality, course completion, teaching quality, student supervision, examination preparation and grading, research output, publications, professional development and service to the university.

He argued that university employment should be linked to measurable professional responsibilities and that lecturers who demonstrate exceptional teaching, research and academic leadership should be appropriately rewarded and promoted.

Tingban also raised concerns about reports of some lecturers allegedly spending excessive time in entertainment venues during periods when they should be engaged in teaching, research, preparation or student consultation.

He stressed that his position was not intended to regulate employees’ private lives, but to promote professional accountability during official working hours.

Pushes Removal of Bars, Entertainment Businesses

In one of his more sweeping recommendations, Tingban called for an immediate review of bars, drinking establishments, entertainment centers and other recreational businesses operating on University of Liberia property or within university-controlled facilities.

Where such establishments do not directly serve the university’s educational mission, he recommended their removal or abolition, subject to legal and contractual review.

Tingban said university property should primarily accommodate classrooms, lecture halls, laboratories, libraries, digital learning centers, innovation hubs, student study areas, faculty research offices, academic conference facilities, counseling services and legitimate student recreational activities.

He also called for a comprehensive review of businesses, concessions, leases and commercial activities operating on university property to determine whether they comply with contractual requirements and provide fair value to the institution.

Proposes Emergency University Reform Initiative

Tingban proposed that the Boakai administration establish a National University of Liberia Emergency Reform Initiative to address the institution’s longstanding challenges.

Among his recommendations are mechanisms to guarantee uninterrupted academic operations, an independent institutional, academic, financial, administrative and property audit, and a legal review of the status and operations of ULFA and ULSA.

He also proposed the creation of a rapid labor-dispute resolution mechanism that could resolve disagreements without automatically shutting down academic activities.

Other recommendations include strengthening research programs, modernizing infrastructure, improving laboratories and libraries, expanding digital learning, and developing a multi-year transformation plan for the university.

Calls for International Faculty Recruitment

Tingban further urged the government to recruit qualified international lecturers to address critical faculty shortages while simultaneously investing in the development of Liberian academics.

He suggested that, where legally and financially feasible, Liberia could recruit substantial numbers of qualified African and international academics, including potentially 300 to 400 Nigerian lecturers.

He cautioned, however, that foreign recruitment should serve as a bridge to local capacity development rather than become a permanent substitute for Liberian scholars.

He called for scholarships, postgraduate training, research fellowships and faculty-development programs to strengthen Liberia’s academic workforce.

One-Year Shutdown Not Ruled Out

Tingban also raised the possibility of temporarily suspending operations at the University of Liberia for a defined period—even up to one academic year—if an objective assessment concludes that such a step is necessary for comprehensive restructuring.

He argued that a carefully planned period of institutional reform could be preferable to years of recurring academic disruptions.

However, he stressed that any such decision would have to be legally grounded, carefully planned and accompanied by alternative academic arrangements to ensure students do not become victims of the reform process.

“Students Are Asking for Classrooms”

Tingban said the concerns expressed by students should remain at the center of any national response.

He argued that Liberian students are not demanding luxury but basic academic necessities—including functional classrooms, competent lecturers, laboratories, libraries, examinations, research opportunities and degrees earned on time.

“Every semester lost is more than a calendar entry,” he said, warning that repeated disruptions translate into delayed careers, increased financial burdens on families and lost opportunities for young Liberians.

He urged President Boakai to place the University of Liberia at the center of the government’s development agenda and ensure that the institution becomes a stronger engine of national intellectual and human-capital development.

“The Time for a Permanent Solution Is Now”

Tingban concluded by urging the president to treat the University of Liberia as a national institution requiring presidential attention rather than another government entity experiencing a routine labor dispute.

He said the government must protect the rights of workers while equally protecting the educational rights of students, parents and the Liberian public.

“The ARREST Agenda must not leave the University of Liberia behind,” Tingban said, calling on President Boakai to use the current crisis as an opportunity for a historic intervention aimed at strengthening the institution rather than targeting any particular group or individual.

“The time for another temporary solution has passed,” he declared. “The time for a permanent national solution is now.”

World.title: When “Let the Law Take Its Course” Is Not Enough
World.content:
The Arrest of Jewel Howard-Taylor and a Warning for a Nation That Knows the Cost of Politicized Power

By Clarence R. Pearson, Sr., PhD

There is a phrase increasingly heard in Liberia whenever a politically prominent person is arrested, investigated or accused of wrongdoing: “Let the person face the law and exonerate themselves.”

Sometimes it becomes, “The law is the law.”

At other times, “Let the person go through the process.”

The formulations differ, but the underlying argument is often the same: once the state invokes the law, questioning the manner in which it exercises its power is somehow equivalent to opposing justice.

That proposition should trouble every Liberian who believes in the rule of law.

No one is above the law—not a former vice president, not a senator, not a minister, not a police chief, not a political party leader, and certainly not an ordinary citizen. If credible evidence implicates a person in narcotics trafficking, money laundering, conspiracy or any other serious crime, the state has both the authority and the responsibility to investigate and, when the applicable legal threshold is satisfied, prosecute.

But there is another principle of equal importance:

The government is not above the law either.

And that is why the arrest of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor deserves scrutiny that goes considerably deeper than the comforting refrain, “Let the law take its course.”

The Question Is Not Whether She Can Be Arrested

Howard-Taylor, who served as Liberia’s vice president from 2018 to 2024, was stopped on August 19 while attempting to leave Liberia through Roberts International Airport and was taken to Liberia National Police headquarters. Authorities subsequently announced serious charges against her, including drug trafficking, money laundering and conspiracy in connection with an alleged transnational narcotics network. International reporting has confirmed the arrest and charges.

The government has publicly portrayed its evidence as substantial. Police Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman reportedly said investigators had reached a point at which they believed they possessed sufficient evidence and did not need first to interview Howard-Taylor. He further indicated that authorities learned of her intended travel and acted to prevent her departure. Attorney General and Justice Minister N. Oswald Tweh has said that the case would proceed to a grand jury for indictment.

Those statements raise an important question—not necessarily about whether the police possessed legal authority to act, but about how that authority was exercised.

The distinction matters.

Police may, under circumstances permitted by law, make an arrest based upon probable cause without first obtaining an arrest warrant. The absence of a warrant therefore does not, standing alone, establish that an arrest was unlawful.

Nor must prosecutors necessarily obtain a grand-jury indictment before every lawful arrest.

But saying that government can exercise a power does not end the inquiry into whether it exercised that power wisely, proportionately and professionally.

If the Evidence Was Already So Strong, Why the Airport Spectacle?

That is the question Liberia’s authorities should answer clearly.

If investigators had been monitoring Howard-Taylor; if they possessed what they characterized publicly as sufficient or overwhelming evidence; and if authorities became aware that she intended to travel, then why—assuming circumstances permitted it—was judicial process not sought before the confrontation at the airport?

Why not place the preliminary evidence before a neutral judicial officer and seek an arrest warrant?

And if investigators believed their completed evidentiary package was already sufficiently developed for prosecution, why was the matter not first presented to a grand jury for consideration of an indictment, if that procedural course was legally and practically available?

These questions do not establish that the arrest was illegal.

They establish something different: that the government should explain why it chose the most abrupt exercise of police power when less publicly damaging mechanisms of lawful compulsion may have been available.

That distinction is especially important because this was not an unknown suspect discovered unexpectedly crossing a border.

Howard-Taylor is a former vice president of the Republic of Liberia, a former senator and a nationally recognizable political figure. She was not entitled to immunity from criminal investigation merely because she once occupied high office. But precisely because of her political prominence, law-enforcement authorities should have understood that virtually every aspect of their conduct would be examined for evidence of professionalism, impartiality and political motivation.

The higher the political temperature, the greater the institutional discipline required.

Probable Cause Is a Floor, Not a Standard of Statesmanship

Law enforcement must be careful not to confuse the existence of legal authority with the quality of its exercise.

An arrest can conceivably satisfy the minimum requirements of criminal procedure and still be executed in a manner that unnecessarily damages institutional credibility.

A government confident in its evidence should ordinarily have little to fear from judicial scrutiny. Indeed, obtaining prior judicial authorization where feasible can strengthen rather than weaken a politically sensitive prosecution. A warrant issued after independent review allows the state to say something important to the public:

We did not simply decide among ourselves that this person should be arrested. We presented our evidence to an independent judicial authority, and that authority determined that the legal threshold had been satisfied.

Likewise, where indictment by a grand jury is available and appropriate, presenting evidence through that institution can provide another layer between investigators and the immense coercive machinery of the state.

None of this means that a warrant or prior indictment is invariably required before police may lawfully arrest a suspect.

It means that legality represents the beginning of the inquiry, not necessarily its end.

Professionalism matters.

Proportionality matters.

Institutional restraint matters.

And in a politically polarized society, appearances of impartiality matter because public confidence is itself an indispensable asset of criminal justice.

“Let Her Exonerate Herself” Gets the Law Backwards

There is an even more fundamental problem with the language surrounding politically charged prosecutions.

An accused person does not enter a criminal courtroom carrying a legal obligation to prove innocence.

The state carries the burden of proving guilt.

That distinction is not semantic. It is one of the great protections separating constitutional government from arbitrary power.

The proper democratic formulation is therefore not:

“Let Jewel Howard-Taylor face the law and exonerate herself.”

It is:

Let the government present admissible evidence before an independent court and prove the allegations against Jewel Howard-Taylor according to law, while affording her every protection guaranteed to an accused person.

If the evidence is compelling, prosecute the case vigorously.

If it proves guilt beyond the legally required standard, impose the punishment prescribed by law.

But until then, accusation is not conviction, police confidence is not judicial proof, and a government press conference is not a verdict.

Process Can Itself Become Punishment

This principle extends far beyond Howard-Taylor.

A state does not need to secure a conviction to inflict enormous damage upon a political opponent.

An arrest can dominate newspapers.

Images can travel internationally within minutes.

A person’s name can become permanently associated with narcotics, corruption or organized crime long before a witness takes the stand.

Legal fees accumulate. Political organizations become destabilized. Families suffer. International reputations collapse. Supporters and opponents retreat into hardened camps.

Years later, an acquittal may occupy a fraction of the attention generated by the original accusation.

That is why democratic societies impose restrictions upon prosecutorial and police power.

Due process is not designed merely to protect guilty people from punishment.

It exists to prevent government from substituting accusation for proof and procedure for punishment.

Liberia Has Special Reasons to Be Careful

For Liberia, these principles carry historical weight.

This is a country whose political history has repeatedly demonstrated what happens when institutions lose credibility, when political disagreement becomes personalized, when state power is perceived as partisan, and when citizens cease believing that public institutions operate according to neutral rules.

Liberia’s civil conflicts did not arise from a single arrest or prosecution, and it would be irresponsible to suggest otherwise. But the country’s history should make its leaders particularly sensitive to the cumulative consequences of institutional distrust.

Peace is not preserved merely by preventing gunfire.

It is strengthened when citizens—including citizens who oppose the government—believe that the police will treat them fairly, prosecutors will follow evidence rather than political instructions, courts will remain independent, and political prominence will provide neither immunity nor a target on one’s back.

That is why the Howard-Taylor prosecution is larger than Jewel Howard-Taylor.

It is becoming a test of Liberia’s institutions.

The Government Can Answer the Doubts With Evidence

There is a straightforward way for the Boakai administration, the Ministry of Justice and the Liberia National Police to reduce legitimate suspicion:

Build the case in court.

Not principally through press conferences.

Not through political surrogates.

Not through partisan social-media warfare.

And certainly not through declarations that the public should simply trust investigators because “the law is the law.”

Present the evidence.

Establish the evidentiary chain.

Identify the alleged acts.

Demonstrate the alleged connections.

Protect witnesses.

Preserve physical and digital evidence.

Respect defense counsel.

Meet every procedural deadline.

Permit independent judicial scrutiny.

And ultimately prove the allegations to the standard demanded by law.

If the evidence against Howard-Taylor is indeed overwhelming, rigorous judicial scrutiny should strengthen the government’s case rather than threaten it.

One Standard for Everyone

Liberians should reject two equally dangerous propositions.

The first is that Jewel Howard-Taylor’s former office or political influence should protect her from legitimate criminal investigation. It should not.

The second is that because police have accused her of exceptionally serious crimes, Liberians should suspend critical examination of how the government investigated, arrested, detained and intends to prosecute her.

They should not.

A mature democracy can hold both principles simultaneously.

No political immunity from prosecution.

No governmental immunity from scrutiny.

Those principles belong together.

And perhaps the most dangerous cliché in a fragile democracy is the suggestion that citizens must choose between supporting law enforcement and questioning law enforcement.

They do not.

Citizens strengthen institutions by demanding that they perform their functions lawfully, professionally and impartially.

Liberia should prosecute narcotics trafficking relentlessly. The scale of recent cocaine seizures and the possibility of penetration of state institutions demand nothing less. But the more serious the alleged crime, and the more politically consequential the accused, the more meticulous the government must become—not less.

The Howard-Taylor case therefore presents Liberia with an opportunity.

The government can demonstrate that a former vice president is not above the law.

But it must demonstrate something else at the same time:

that the police are not above scrutiny, prosecutors are not above due process, political power is not a substitute for judicial authority, and an accusation—however sensational—will never be permitted to become a conviction before the evidence reaches a courtroom.

For a nation that has paid an extraordinary price for political mistrust, that distinction is not legal technicality.

It is part of the architecture of peace.

World.title: A New Dawn for Liberia: Progress Through Freedom and Leadership
World.content:
Aristotle:https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1UmX9TnuiE/

Machiavelli:https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1HeoVC1gPt/

Socrates: https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1D5wMfsYEY/

Inspired by President Ronald Reagan — Freedom & Hope:

“Freedom is not simply the right to choose our leaders; it is the opportunity to build a Liberia where every citizen can choose hope over fear, opportunity over despair, and progress over stagnation.”

Inspired by Machiavelli — Leadership & Responsibility:

“A new dawn does not come merely because the night has ended; it comes when leaders possess the courage, wisdom, and discipline to turn freedom into progress and power into service.”

Inspired by Socrates — Wisdom & Citizenship: “A nation awakens when its people begin to question not only who governs them, but whether those who govern are worthy of the trust placed in them. Liberia’s new dawn must therefore begin with wisdom, truth, and responsible citizenship.”

Inspired by Other Philosophical Traditions — Unity & Progress: “The greatness of a few individuals will not determine the destiny of Liberia, but the courage of a united people who understand that freedom without responsible leadership is incomplete, and leadership without service is empty.”

Austin S Fallah: “A new dawn for Liberia begins when freedom becomes more than a promise, when courageous leadership transforms liberty into opportunity, justice into action, and hope into lasting national progress.”

Austin S Fallah: “Liberia’s path to a brighter future rests on two enduring pillars: the freedom of its people and the leadership to protect, strengthen, and transform that freedom into peace, prosperity, and progress for all.”

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

In the landscape of political discourse, few statements resonate as deeply as those made by former President Ronald Reagan: “Freedom and progress go hand in hand.”

This assertion encapsulates the critical intertwining of liberty, empowerment, and development, especially in contexts where nations are emerging from periods of hardship and instability.

Liberia, a nation long haunted by the specters of civil war, corruption, and economic malaise, stands on the precipice of a new chapter.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, a coalition government is poised to usher in transformative change that could redefine progress for the Liberian people.

As they seek to free Liberia from the shackles of drug cartels and foster growth through infrastructure and economic development, it is imperative to acknowledge that the country’s future is ripe with potential.

I argue that the current leadership has the opportunity in the second half of the 21st century to redefine progress in Liberia through a commitment to freedom, infrastructure, and economic empowerment, ultimately aligning the nation with the ideals expressed by Reagan.

The Historical Context of Liberia:

To appreciate the significance of Liberia’s current political climate, one must first examine its historical context.

Liberia, an area that existed in the early 19th century and was settled by settlers, has always held a unique position in African history.

However, the country’s trajectory has been marred by civil conflicts that erupted during the Yuletide (Presidential Press-Secretary Hon. Patrick Kumeh introduced me to this word in 1986, during my interactions with President Samuel K Doe) of 1989 and culminated in another catastrophic war in the 1990s and early 2000s.

These conflicts not only decimated the population but also destroyed the institutions necessary for stable governance and economic viability.

Consequently, Liberia has been left grappling with high unemployment rates, widespread poverty, and inadequate infrastructure.

The aftermath of civil conflict often leads to a culture of dependency, where the populace relies on external aid rather than cultivating local resources and governance.

The pervasive influence of drug cartels and the illegal economy further complicate the development path.

However, the dawning leadership of Fe-nya-nah- Keh-keh Boakai and Fe-Nya-Nah Pow-morh Vice President Koung offers a potential turning point in this narrative.

Their coalition government symbolizes a break from the past, fostering an environment where citizens are seen as agents of change rather than mere subjects of political maneuvering.

Freedom as a Catalyst for Progress:

The concept of freedom is foundational to any society’s evolution.

In Liberia, it is not enough merely to declare independence from corrupt systems; rather, it is essential to empower citizens to take part in shaping their destiny.

President Boakai and Vice President Koung understand that true progress is predicated on instilling a sense of ownership in the citizenry.

Freedom in this context means creating opportunities for individuals to participate actively in the economy, enabling them to contribute to their nation’s and community’s social and financial fabric.

Liberians cannot remain hostages to outdated ideologies that endorse oppression and dependence on foreign entities.

The coalition government’s agenda aims to dismantle the economic structures that thrive on corruption and illegal activities (such as drug trafficking and cartels), instead promoting lawful trade and investment as foundational pillars of progress.

When citizens feel free to engage in legitimate business without fear of exploitation or violence, they can cultivate innovation and contribute to the economy, laying the groundwork for sustainable development.

Infrastructure Development: Paving the Way for Progress

One of the most pressing issues facing Liberia is its severely inadequate infrastructure.

Poor road conditions hinder access to markets, restrict transportation of goods, and stifle economic activity. Ma-sa-noh Ben-dor Keh-Keh Boakai and Ma-sa-noh pow-morh fe-nya-nah pow-morh Koung’s administration has recognized that infrastructure development is not merely an ancillary concern; it is central to the nation’s sovereignty and prosperity.

With plans to asphalt interior roads, the coalition government signals its commitment to enhancing connectivity across the country.

Asphalted roads will significantly impact agricultural development, a cornerstone of the Liberian economy.

By facilitating transportation, farmers can access larger markets, ensuring their produce reaches consumers efficiently.

This will not only enhance food security but also boost the rural economy, lifting many out of poverty. Furthermore, improved infrastructure attracts foreign investment, which is integral to sustainable growth.

When international businesses see a commitment to modern infrastructure, they are more likely to invest in long-term projects that create jobs and build skills within the local workforce.

Economic Empowerment as a Cornerstone of Development:

Beyond infrastructure, the coalition government emphasizes economic empowerment as a fundamental aspect of national progress.

This initiative requires a multifaceted approach, including education, vocational training, and supportive policies that encourage entrepreneurship.

By equipping citizens with the skills necessary to thrive in a competitive marketplace, Liberia can foster a culture of self-sufficiency and innovation.

Education plays a pivotal role in this strategy.

Historically, access to quality education has been limited in Liberia, particularly for marginalized populations.

By prioritizing educational reforms, the coalition government can ensure that the next generation is not only literate but also capable of critical thinking and innovation.

Investment in vocational training programs will equip young adults with tangible skills for local and international markets, allowing them to pursue various income-generating avenues from agriculture to technology.

Moreover, supportive economic policies, such as microfinance initiatives and tax incentives for small businesses, can stimulate local entrepreneurship.

When citizens are empowered to establish their own enterprises, they contribute to a more diverse and resilient economy.

This economic dynamism helps to reduce dependence on any single industry, shielding the nation from the vulnerabilities associated with socio-political turmoil.

The Role of Governance and Leadership Integrity:

As Liberia embarks on this journey toward revitalization, the importance of governance and integrity must not be overlooked.

The coalition government led by Wa-na-ba-nah (Big person) Boakai and Wa-wa-ba-nah pow-mor (Small person) Koung has a unique opportunity to set a precedent for transparent leadership by actively engaging citizens in the political process.

By promoting accountability and ethical governance, they can build public trust, a critical component of successful policy implementation.

Fighting corruption is paramount in this endeavor.

The Liberian people have long suffered from the consequences of corrupt leadership, which has undermined development efforts and perpetuated socio-economic disparity.

Transparency in government processes, along with the establishment of independent bodies to oversee public officials’ activities, can help eliminate corruption and restore faith in public institutions.

In addition, fostering dialogue between the government and the citizenry is essential for inclusive governance.

By actively seeking public input on policy decisions and allowing citizens to voice their concerns, the coalition government can ensure that development initiatives align with the needs of the populace.

This approach not only strengthens the democratic process but also cultivates a sense of belonging and commitment among Liberians.

A Bright Future for Liberia:

Liberia’s current political landscape represents a watershed moment in the nation’s journey toward prosperity and stability.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, the coalition government stands poised to redefine what progress means for the Liberian people.

Freedom and progress are not abstract ideals; they are actionable principles that can breathe life into a nation long beset by challenges.

By embracing freedom as a catalyst for empowerment, prioritizing infrastructure development, and committing to economic empowerment, Liberia can rise above the shadows of its past.

The coalition government has the opportunity to build a future where citizens are no longer mere spectators in their own country but active participants in shaping a prosperous and peaceful Liberia.

As Reagan eloquently put it, “freedom and progress go hand in hand,” and it is through this synergy that Liberia can reclaim its rightful place in the annals of human history, writing a new chapter of hope and resilience for generations to come.

World.title: The Empowering Journey of Liberian Women through Education: A Pathway to Freedom and Integrity
World.content:
“The Empowering Journey of Liberian Women through Education: A Pathway to Freedom and Integrity begins when every Liberian girl understands that education is not merely a certificate; it is the knowledge, confidence, and independence needed to shape her own future and contribute meaningfully to Liberia’s development.”

“Liberian women and girls must never be used as punching bags in the fight against drug trafficking and cartels. Women must also learn not to be used as political pundits by so-called politicians seeking to score public political points. Let the accused face due process, and let us reject unnecessary political noise.”

“Liberian women must be vigilant about the company they keep. Do not allow money, political influence, or social pressure to draw you into drug trafficking, criminal networks, or destructive political activities. Protect your dignity, your future, and the integrity of Liberia.”

“In the 21st-century AI age, no Liberian woman should be left behind. Education must become her bridge to technology, innovation, leadership, and economic opportunity because an educated woman not only transforms her own life, she strengthens her family, community, and nation.”

“Liberian women deserve dignity, justice, and protection—not to be turned into political tools. Women must learn to recognize when so-called politicians are using them as political pundits to score public points. Let every accused person face due process, while we put an end to political manipulation

“A woman’s strength is reflected in the choices she makes and the people she allows to influence her. Let Liberian women reject criminal exploitation, drug trafficking, and political manipulation, and instead embrace education, integrity, peace, and responsible leadership for the advancement of Liberia.”

“Let every Liberian girl and woman embrace The Empowering Journey of Liberian Women through Education: A Pathway to Freedom and Integrity; for in an age driven by artificial intelligence, those who learn, adapt, and lead with knowledge and integrity will help determine Liberia’s place in the world.”

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

In global development and human rights, education is one of the most powerful tools for liberation, empowerment, and societal transformation.

For Liberian girls and women, this truth resonates deeply as education not only equips them with knowledge but also galvanizes their ability to discern between detrimental choices and constructive life paths.

In this disquisition, I argue that educating Liberian women is critical to their personal development and serves as a salute to the nation’s future female leaders.

Through the testimony of Ms. Abigail Musu Kpakar, an embodiment of ambition and intelligence, we will explore the transformative power of education and its role in fostering critical thinking, discerning judgment, and a refined moral compass.

From an early age, Ms.Abigail Musu Kpakar’s father instilled in her the fundamental truth of education: “Musu, please go to school and be educated, so that you will learn how to read and write not only for your betterment but that of the future female leaders, and so that one day you will not see your boyfriend’s or husband’s girlfriend letter and give it to him and say, here is your receipt.”

This advice encapsulates the essence of education as a pathway to self-awareness and discernment.

Education equips women with the ability to differentiate between intoxicating substances like cocaine and innocuous everyday products such as cooking soda or baby powder, brown sand, or brown sugar.

In a society marred by the consequences of drug abuse and fraudulent practices, an educated woman is likely to make informed choices that benefit her life and her community.

It is a salutary pursuit, an endeavor that holds “inestimable” value. Only through education can young women rise above the pangs of ignorance and resist the siren calls of corrupt influences that often seduce the vulnerable.

The transformative impact of education can be compared to a serendipitous discovery; it unveils hidden potential and talent.

For many Liberian women, the quest for knowledge has helped them uncover skills and capabilities that lay dormant because of socio-cultural constraints.

This journey is not without its challenges; they often face a noisome environment filled with societal expectations that dismiss the importance of female education.

However, those who persevere emerge as unstoppable forces for change, even in the face of opprobrium directed towards women seeking education.

In a society that has, for too long, relegated women to mendicant roles, the audacity to seek education is revolutionary.

Education allows women to assert themselves, to engage in intellectual discourse, and to create futures beyond the limited horizons previously imposed upon them.

By educating female leaders, we foster an environment where young girls can flap their wings and soar unencumbered by the limitations of traditional roles.

As Machiavelli famously asserted, “Politics have no relation to morals.” Yet education imbues women with a nuanced understanding of morality, the ability to question the status quo, and to stand firmly against injustices crafted by a system blind to ethical considerations.

This moral clarity becomes their shield, protecting them from acquiescing to corrupt practices that might otherwise lead to societal degeneration.

In contrast, those who succumb to the phlegmatic complacency that fuels corruption are outdone by educated women, who emerge as instigators of reform and advocate for justice and equality.

Furthermore, education cultivates critical thinking skills, enabling women to dissect complex issues and reach enlightened conclusions.

Armed with knowledge, educated women seize opportunities in various spheres- journalism, politics, business, leadership, and medicine- often using their positions to advocate for other women and girls.

Women of valor, not cocaine invested, drug traffickers, drug cartels, political manipulators, or corrupt individuals, can become mentors, guiding the next generation toward achievements that were once deemed unattainable.

The communities benefit immensely, as the daughters of educated women often outperform their predecessors, breaking cycles of ignorance and lifting those around them.

The road to education for Liberian women is paved with myriad obstacles.

The societal narrative that positions women as inferior not only discourages them from seeking knowledge but also reinforces systemic issues that hinder progress.

By adhering to the expectations of being obsequious and compliant, many women find themselves trapped in cycles of poverty and dependency, perpetuating the stigma that they are unworthy of education.

However, education serves as the antidote to this oppression; it punctures the enigmatic facade of societal norms and reveals an empowering truth.

In addition to breaking barriers, education also instills self-worth and confidence amongst women.

The ability to read and write transforms mundane tasks into thriving opportunities for growth and realization.

Such empowerment envelops them in a state of mental audacity; they begin to envision lives filled with promise rather than resignation.

Through education, they shed the soporific tendencies of complacency and embrace their roles as leaders and change-makers.

Promoting the education of Liberian women should not be an audacious act limited to local communities, but an international mission aimed at global systemic change. Governments, NGOs, and positive civil society must collectively foster environments for female education, tackling the barriers and societal stigmas that hinder such aspirations.

Initiatives must be formulated to provide financial backing, mentorship programs, and educational resources designed for women at all stages of life.

The education of Liberian women emerges as a powerful catalyst for transformation, allowing them to navigate their futures with maturity and insight.

The words of Ms.Abigail Musu Kpakar ring true: “Go to school and be educated” stands not just as advice but as a rallying cry for a generation on the verge of initiating monumental changes.

Education opens the mind’s eye to the dynamic interplay between knowledge and morality.

This relationship ultimately reinforces the notion that women who wield pen and paper will create a legacy far richer than those who succumb to intemperance and ignorance.

As a society, we must nurture and support the educational pursuits of Liberian women, allowing them to create communities led by informed, fearless, and morally conscious individuals.

Indeed, empowering women through education is an undeniably invaluable endeavor that promises not only their personal success but also the flourishing of future generations.

The road ahead may be fraught with challenges, yet the collective spirit of educated women will illuminate the path toward a future forged in resilience, integrity, and unyielding ambition.

Ultimately, as we invest in the minds and hearts of Liberian women, we redefine life trajectories and reshape our society’s narrative into one that celebrates strength, knowledge, and equality.

World.title: Zesco Girls ready for COSAFA Semis – Mwila
World.content:
Zesco Ndola Girls coach Florence Mwila says her side is ready to face any opponent in the semi-finals of the CAF Women’s Champions League | COSAFA Qualifier Botswana 2026.

The Ndola-based Zambian champions booked their semi-final spot in style, securing top spot in Group A with a 2-0 victory over hosts Gaborone United at the Gaborone United Stadium on Monday evening.

Zesco finished Group A with maximum 9 points from 3 games: following victories over Lesotho Defence Force (1-0) and Zimbabwe’s Herentals Queens (5-2).

After the win over the hosts, Mwila praised her team’s response.

“It is sweet three points. We are here to play the game. We knew we were facing a tough opponent, so we needed to improve in relation to the approach,” Mwila said.

The Ndola Girls are likely to face either Silver Strikers of Malawi or Mozambique’s Costa do Sol from Group B in the last four.

But Mwila insists there are no favourites.

“There are no preferences, we play any team that come our way. We are prepared. This is a tournament so you meet any opponent and you must be prepared,” she told journalists in Gaborone.

Group B concludes action on Tuesday evening.

Mamelodi Sundowns leads with 6 points, followed by Silver Strikers and Costa do Sol on 3 points each. Nsingizini Hotspurs of Eswatini are bottom with no points.

Zesco were runners-up last year after losing to Gaborone United in the final of the regional champions league.

This year, they have already beaten GU in the group stage and will be hoping to go one step further and qualify for the CAF Women’s Champions League finals.

World.title: LAZ Says Closure Timing Threatens Constitutional Rights
World.content:
LAZ Demands Explanation As Court Closures Collide With Election Petition Window

The Law Association of Zambia has raised sharp concern over the closure of courts nationwide, coupled with the presence of heavily armed military personnel around court premises, demanding a formal public explanation for the action. LAZ president Arnold Kaluba said in a statement that the closure carries immediate implications for access to justice, particularly for people requiring urgent judicial intervention, including those with pending criminal proceedings, bail applications and habeas corpus matters.

Kaluba grounded his objection in specific constitutional text. He cited Article 13(3) of the Constitution, which requires that a person arrested or detained on reasonable suspicion of having committed, or being about to commit, a criminal offence and who is not released, be brought without undue delay before a court. He said any disruption to the ordinary operations of courts must be managed in a manner that ensures affected persons do not suffer prejudice and that constitutional rights continue to receive effective judicial protection.

What makes the timing especially significant, Kaluba said, is Article 103(1) of the Constitution, which provides a strict seven-day window within which a person may petition the Constitutional Court to nullify the election of a President-elect following the declaration of results. He warned that closing the courts during this constitutionally prescribed period creates a real risk that persons seeking to exercise that right may be prejudiced by uncertainty over access to court registries, filing facilities and judicial officers.

Kaluba said LAZ is demanding an explanation from the judiciary, arguing it is imperative that the institution immediately clarify the arrangements in place to ensure no person is prejudiced in exercising a constitutional or statutory right because of the closure, including any applicable filing deadline. He was careful to acknowledge that LAZ recognises exceptional circumstances, including genuine and immediate security concerns that may require temporary protective measures for judicial officers, staff, litigants and the public.

However, Kaluba stressed that any such measures must be lawful, proportionate and implemented in a way that preserves access to justice and respects the constitutional independence and autonomy of the judiciary. He demanded the urgent restoration of access to the courts and the resumption of filing, receipt and hearing of matters as soon as it becomes safe and practicable to do so.

Pending full reopening, Kaluba said the judiciary must immediately establish and publicly communicate alternative arrangements for the filing and receipt of urgent and time-sensitive matters, and, where necessary, ensure such matters can be placed before a judicial officer without undue delay. He called for particular priority to be given to matters affecting personal liberty, including habeas corpus and bail applications, as well as constitutional, electoral and other proceedings subject to strict statutory or constitutional timelines.

Kaluba said the judiciary must ensure no person is prejudiced by the closure in respect of any applicable filing deadline, and should issue directions or make arrangements as necessary to preserve parties’ legal and constitutional rights. He further called for prompt communication to legal practitioners, litigants and the public regarding the reasons for the closure, its geographical scope, expected duration and the arrangements for continued access to justice, along with clarification of the legal and institutional basis for the security measures, to the extent such information can properly be disclosed without compromising legitimate security considerations.

LAZ’s intervention adds institutional and legal weight to concerns already raised separately by other bodies, including the Human Rights Commission and civil society organisations, over the timing of the court closures relative to the constitutional petition deadline.

World.title: Former Kanchibiya MP Chanda Says Bill 7 Vote Cost Him His Seat
World.content:
Former Kanchibiya Member of Parliament Sunday Chanda has attributed his election loss to his vote in favour of the contested Bill 7 constitutional amendment, saying constituents turned against him over the decision and that the party subsequently withheld campaign support because he was seen to have defied local sentiment.

Chanda said the practice within his party was for the leadership to consult stakeholders before major decisions, and that outcomes were meant to reflect those consultations. He said he was not deployed to campaign in Kanchibiya during the run-up to the election, a decision he linked directly to how his Bill 7 vote had been perceived among constituents and party structures.

The former legislator’s account offers a rare first-hand illustration of how constitutional reform debates, which dominated parliamentary business well before the election, continued to shape voter behaviour and party dynamics at constituency level. Bill 7 remained a politically divisive issue throughout its passage, with supporters and opponents divided along lines that did not always track neatly with party affiliation.

Chanda’s remarks suggest that his vote was interpreted locally as a break from the wishes of Kanchibiya residents, regardless of the broader political or constitutional justification he may have had for supporting the amendment at the time. He indicated that this perception hardened opposition to his candidacy well before the formal campaign period began.

He also pointed to the absence of campaign deployment as a compounding factor, describing it as a signal that the party itself had distanced itself from his position. Without that support, Chanda suggested, an already difficult path back to the seat became considerably harder to navigate.

The episode highlights a broader dynamic playing out across several constituencies this election cycle, where MPs who supported contentious legislation faced consequences at the ballot box regardless of their standing within party structures. Chanda’s case adds a personal dimension to that pattern, illustrating how quickly parliamentary votes on divisive national issues can translate into local political costs.

Chanda has not indicated whether he intends to remain active in politics or pursue any further role within his party following the loss. His comments, however, are likely to resonate with other legislators who supported Bill 7 and who may be assessing their own standing with constituents in its aftermath.

World.title: Human rights Advocate calls for unity
World.content:
Governance expert and human rights advocate Wesley Miyanda has called on Zambians to protect the country’s long standing culture of peaceful democratic transitions, urging political leaders and their supporters to place national unity above political interests.

Mr Miyanda said Zambia has enjoyed peace since attaining independence and has conducted elections that resulted in changes of government without bloodshed or widespread political violence.

Speaking in an interview with the media, the governance expert appealed to political actors, particularly those dissatisfied with electoral outcomes, to use established democratic and legal processes to address their grievances rather than resorting to actions that could threaten the country’s peace and stability.

“Petitions are very important and they are constitutional. No one can stop them. I think that is the best thing we should do. We need to follow the process and see how the issues are resolved at the end of the day,” said Mr Miyanda.

He cited Zambia’s history of political perseverance as an example of how electoral disputes and defeats can be handled within a democratic framework.

He noted that some political leaders had lost elections several times but continued to participate in the democratic process, reorganising and returning to contest subsequent elections without mobilising supporters to cause unrest.

Mr Miyanda said political leaders should consider the broader interests of the country rather than allowing political disagreements to divide citizens.

“We cannot afford to put this country on fire because of politics. We don’t have any other home apart from this home called Zambia,” he said.

Mr Miyanda urged both winners and losers of elections to demonstrate restraint, peace and unity, saying the responsibility to protect Zambia’s stability rests with every citizen.

He said Zambia should now focus on healing and reconciliation following political contestation and begin rebuilding trust among citizens.

Mr Miyanda further warned that political instability could undermine Zambia’s economic prospects by discouraging potential investors.

He argued that investment could help create jobs and business opportunities while contributing to efforts to address the rising cost of living.

Mr Miyanda called on Zambians to put aside personal attacks and political divisions and work collectively to move the country forward.

He said the responsibility of the current generation is to preserve the peace inherited from previous generations and leave behind a stronger and more united Zambia.

“We should put our heads together and forget about personal attacks. Let us become a picture of this country that we should move forward and even make it better than we found it,” said Miyanda.

World.title: LSUC gazetted as higher learning Institution
World.content:
Lusaka South University College (LSUC) has announced that it has been officially featured in the Government Gazette of Zambia, marking a historic milestone in the institution’s journey toward becoming a premier centre for higher learning and innovation.

The Government Gazette is the official legal publication of the Republic of Zambia.

Being gazetted, alongside accreditation by the Higher Education Authority (HEA), grants LSUC the legal mandate to award internationally recognised certificates and degrees, conduct high-level research, and provide expert consultancy and professional short-term training.

Speaking on behalf of the Board of Directors, Peter Chikubula noted that the recognition is a testament to the institution’s commitment to quality.

Mr Chikubala said the recognition is a demonstration of trust in the institution by the Government.

“Our official gazetting is more than just a legal formality, it is a seal of trust from the Government. It enables us to empower our students with qualifications that are respected world-over, ensuring they can compete in the global marketplace,” Mr Chikubula said.

He said over the years, LSUC, also registered under TEVETA, has been at the forefront of addressing national challenges through specialised skills training.

Mr Chikubala said the college has made a significant impact in the renewable energy sector, specifically in solar technology.

“By building local capacity during periods of national load shedding, LSUC has provided Zambians with hands-on skills necessary to achieve a sustainable energy mix and support the nation’s green energy goals,” he said.

Mr Chikubala emphasised that LSUC is dedicated to producing graduates who possess the practical skills required to transform and grow the Zambian business landscape.

World.title: Mambwe district engaged on risk management
World.content:
The Eastern Province Administration through the Provincial Planning Unit has embarked on a risk management technical assessment in Mambwe District.

Senior Planning Officer, Steven Madyabi, says the risk management was introduced with the view of improving performance in the civil service across government departments.

Mr Madyabi observed that providing technical support to districts, is necessary as it enables departments to be able to identify risks, analyse them, profile them and come up with mitigation measures to reduce and possibly, eliminate risks.

He further said after the engagement with the provincial team, the district would formulate a risk management committee.

“Mambwe District does not have a Risk Management Committee. Therefore, it is our hope that after this meeting, the district team will be able to identify Risk Focal Point Persons as well as formulate a Risk Management Committee that will bring all government departments on board,” he said.

Mr Madyabi expressed confidence that with the direction that the government is taking, many risks that various government departments were facing will be attended to.

“After today’s meeting, it is our hope that Mambwe District will be able to come up with risk mitigation measures that they, themselves can implement. We want them to be innovative and come up with solutions to the various risks that are there and where resources can’t allow, there is room for risk transfer from the district level to another level for onward submission at national level,” he added.

Mr Madyabi said government observed that the performance of the civil service was not tallying with the funding disbursed across departments.

Meanwhile, Mambwe District Administrative Officer, Diana Lupiya appreciated the step by the Provincial Planning Unit to bring the district up to speed.

Ms Lupiya said many activities in the district tended to be disrupted due to various risks that were being encountered with no mitigation measures in place.

“The only risk that the district is actively managing well is flood, a quite common situation in the area,” she said.

World.title: ZRA, Astrophysics sign contract for advanced cargo scanner
World.content:
The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) and United States-based Astrophysics Inc. have signed a contract for the supply, delivery, installation and commissioning of an advanced drive through X-ray cargo scanner at the Livingstone Border Post.

The contract was signed today at the United States Embassy in Lusaka by ZRA Commissioner General, Dingani Banda and Astrophysics Inc. Vice President of Human Resources and Organizational Development Vincent Zayek, during a ceremony hosted by U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires, Mich Coker and attended by senior government officials.

Speaking during the ceremony, Mr Banda said the initiative was in line with President Hakainde Hichilema’s call for the use of technology to transform tax administration and facilitate trade, through the implementation of the Non-Stop Border Pass concept.

“Technology, therefore, plays a vital role in facilitating trade and securing the supply chain. This underscores the importance of scanners in trade facilitation,” Mr Banda said.

Mr Banda said physical inspection of cargo without scanners can take up to five hours, while the Astrophysics scanner already deployed at Nakonde Border Post can scan a 30-tonne truck in about five seconds.

He said the Livingstone scanner will be the second scanner supplied by Astrophysics, building on the existing cooperation between the company and ZRA following the commissioning of the Nakonde scanner by President Hichilema in June 2026.

Mr Banda said Zambia’s strategic geographical position as a landlocked country situated along six major trade corridors makes efficient trade facilitation critical to the movement of goods across Southern Africa and the continent.

He said ZRA has implemented several reforms, including Coordinated Border Management, which has reduced the number of government agencies operating at borders from 18 to six, as well as Customs to Customs Data Exchange with Zimbabwe, Botswana and Malawi, with discussions underway with Tanzania.

Mr Banda said ZRA is also applying risk management in customs operations, noting that entries channeled through the Blue Lane, which is earmarked for post-clearance audits, accounted for 59 percent of revenue collected in 2025.

“We are also applying risk management in the operations of customs, meaning that not all goods are subjected to a physical inspection,” he said.

Mr Banda said ZRA looked forward to continued collaboration with Astrophysics in leveraging technology to advance tax administration, enhance domestic resource mobilisation, secure the supply chain and ensure efficient trade facilitation.

And Astrophysics Inc. Vice President of Human Resources and Organizational Development, Vincent Zayek said the agreement represented more than a contract, describing it as a shared commitment to strengthening Zambia’s border security and the continued success of the programme.

He said Astrophysics was proud to provide Zambia with the latest technologies in non-intrusive cargo inspection and looked forward to expanding its presence in the country.

Mr Zayek said the company intends to add more systems and establish a permanent Astrophysics office in Zambia to provide stronger local support.

He thanked the U.S. Embassy and commercial team for organising the ceremony, as well as ZRA for its partnership, cooperation and trust in Astrophysics.

Meanwhile, U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires, Mich Coker, said the project represented a model for modern border security by accelerating legitimate trade while making it harder for those seeking to abuse the border to succeed.

“American companies deliver not just best-in-world technology, innovation, and equipment, but an unrivaled standard of quality, of transparency, and of long-term partnership rather than a one-time transaction,” Mr Coker said.

He said the project supports Zambia’s priorities of strengthening domestic revenue collection, improving the ease of doing business and positioning the country as a reliable and secure hub for regional trade.

The initiative is aimed at strengthening border security and trade facilitation by enabling ZRA officers to inspect cargo more efficiently, accurately and safely, while reducing truck clearance times and making it more difficult to move contraband, smuggled goods and dangerous materials across the border.
