World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 25, 2026
World.content:
Two UN Peacekeepers Killed in South Sudan Ambush

Two UN peacekeepers have been killed and seven others injured after unidentified gunmen ambushed a UNMISS patrol in South Sudan's eastern Jonglei state. The injured include three peacekeepers, two national police officers and two civilian staff. UNMISS chief Anita Kiki Gbeho condemned the attack and called for a prompt investigation, warning that attacks on peacekeepers may constitute war crimes. The incident comes as renewed violence puts South Sudan's fragile peace process under increasing strain. The country remains one of the world's most dangerous places for aid workers, with at least 36 humanitarian workers killed since January.

Prince Harry Steps Down from African Parks Board

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Prince Harry has stepped down from the board of African Parks, an African wildlife charity he supported for 10 years. However, he remains a supporter of its conservation mission. His departure follows an independent investigation into allegations that rangers managed and funded by the organisation committed human rights abuses, including beatings, rape and torture, against indigenous people in Congo-Brazzaville. African Parks admitted the abuses last year and said it had since strengthened its safeguarding measures and governance. Harry's exit comes as he and Meghan prepare to relocate with their children from California to the UK.

Kagame Slams 'One-Sided' US Sanctions Over DR Congo Conflict

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has criticised US sanctions imposed over Rwanda's alleged involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He said that they add to existing problems without addressing the root causes of the crisis. The US sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force and four senior commanders in March, accusing them of supporting AFC/M23. Kigali described the measures as one-sided. Kagame said international pressure should also address the role of the FDLR, the Congolese government and other actors, arguing that the conflict cannot be blamed solely on Rwanda. He said Rwanda would continue pursuing peace while taking measures it considers necessary to protect its security.

Former DP Gachagua Vows to Contest 2027 Presidential Election

Former Kenyan Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has said that his impeachment does not automatically prevent him from contesting the 2027 presidential election. Gachagua is challenging the decision in the Court of Appeal and potentially the Supreme Court. Gachagua argued that the High Court acknowledged his right to a fair hearing was violated. However, they still upheld his removal from office, which he called a constitutional "absurdity". Gachagua insists he remains a presidential contender, declaring that he is not a "kingmaker" but a potential candidate himself. He said that his opposition to President William Ruto is driven by concerns over governance rather than personal bitterness.

Close 

Tanzania Commission Begins Probe Into Election Violence

The Presidential Commission of Inquiry into the Individuals Involved in Violence and Violations of the Law during and after the October 2025 General Election has officially begun preparations to investigate those responsible. Commission chairperson retired Court of Appeal Judge Shaban Ali Lila said it will collect evidence from the public and other stakeholders. He said the commission would receive oral testimony, examine documents, and visit locations identified as connected to the incidents under investigation. The commission, established by President Samia Suluhu Hassan, will assess the evidence in accordance with Tanzanian laws and regulations.

US Seeks Wider UN Arms Embargo on Sudan

The United States has proposed expanding the UN arms embargo on Darfur to cover all of Sudan, as the country's civil war enters its fourth year. US Envoy Massad Boulos told the UN Security Council that weapons and financial support from outside powers were fuelling the conflict and proposed including drones and related technology under the embargo, as well as increasing monitoring. Sudan has backed a technical extension of the existing embargo but warned against measures that could weaken its army. Russia has expressed concerns about expanding the sanctions. The war between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions, with Darfur among the areas worst affected by violence.

KwaZulu-Natal Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case

Acting as executor, while Peter "Gagash" Nonyane is alleged to have been involved in the fraud. World.title: Congo-Brazzaville: Congo's Wealth Is Not Yet Power
World.content:
guest column

Across Africa, the decisive economic contest lies between raw material and finished product. For cotton, it is the distance from fibre to fabric. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, it is the distance from mineral and hydropower wealth to electricity, industrial capacity and productive work. The sectors differ, but the development question is the same: who captures the value created between extraction and the final product?

The Democratic Republic of Congo contains a startling share of the raw materials on which the modern economy depends. It is the world’s leading producer of cobalt. It has vast copper deposits, one of the planet’s great river systems and a population of roughly 100 million people, most of them young. On a map of the energy transition, the country appears indispensable.

On a map of lived prosperity, it looks very different. Only about 21 per cent of Congolese people have access to electricity, according to the World Bank. Poverty remains deep, insecurity persistent and the state distant or predatory for many citizens. The country’s most important economic question is therefore not how much wealth lies beneath its soil or runs through its rivers. It is whether that wealth can be converted into power, production and broadly shared opportunity.

That distinction separates endowment from development. Congo has never lacked resources. It has lacked the durable institutions and infrastructure that allow resources to become public value.

An extractive inheritance

The origins of that failure reach back to the formation of the state itself. Under King Leopold II, the Congo Free State became synonymous with forced labour and brutal extraction. Coercive labour practices persisted after Belgium assumed direct colonial rule in 1908, and a genuinely free labour market emerged only slowly before independence in 1960, according to academic research cited in the original manuscript.

The colonial economy was designed to remove value and administer territory, not to cultivate a broad Congolese political, managerial and technical class. At independence, the country inherited immense land and mineral wealth but little indigenous administrative capacity. A World Bank historical assessment cited in the manuscript describes both the shortage of trained Congolese personnel and Belgium’s effort to retain influence through technical advisers placed alongside key officials.

The crisis that followed independence, the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, Mobutu Sese Seko’s long authoritarian rule and the Congo wars deepened those institutional weaknesses. Mobutu did not invent the extractive state, but his personalised system entrenched it: institutions weakened, patronage expanded and public resources served political survival. Later conflicts and regional interventions fragmented authority further and allowed armed groups to flourish.

This history matters not because it condemns Congo to failure, but because it explains why geology alone has proved such a poor development strategy. Resources create possibilities. States, markets and public institutions determine who captures them.

From quarry to factory

The scale of the opportunity is nonetheless exceptional. The US Geological Survey estimated that in 2024 the DRC accounted for about 75 per cent of global cobalt production and roughly 55 per cent of global reserves. It was also the leading producer of tantalum and among the leading producers of copper, diamonds, tin and other strategic minerals.

These materials sit inside the energy, electronics, telecommunications, defence and manufacturing supply chains that are reshaping global commerce. Yet the familiar model remains one in which the highest-value activity occurs elsewhere. Minerals are extracted in Congo; more sophisticated processing and manufacturing take place abroad.

The policy choice is often described as one between exporting minerals and exporting products. But moving from one to the other requires more than declaring an industrial ambition. Copper processing, battery materials, electrical equipment, construction inputs, machinery and chemicals all require dependable electricity, transport, skills, capital, enforceable contracts and access to markets.

The real transition, then, is not simply from “quarry” to “factory”. It is from an extractive system to a productive one. The measure of success is not how many tonnes leave the ground, but how much capability, employment and domestic value are created before they leave the country.

The river and the grid

Congo’s most consequential industrial asset may be the one that flows through it. The Congo River and its tributaries give the country extraordinary hydropower potential. The Inga site alone has an estimated capacity of about 42,000 megawatts, which the World Bank describes as one of the world’s largest hydropower opportunities.

That number is dazzling. The national power deficit is sobering. With electricity reaching only about one in five people, the first claim on Congo’s hydropower future must be domestic: households, schools, clinics, farms and businesses that cannot develop without reliable power. The country’s National Energy Compact aims to raise access to 62 per cent by 2030, potentially reaching about 82 million people, according to the World Bank.

Power is also the bridge between Congo’s mineral base and its industrial ambitions. A processing plant cannot run on geological promise. Mines, smelters, factories and cities need generation connected to functioning transmission and distribution networks. The Inga opportunity therefore cannot be judged only by installed capacity. It must be judged by whether electricity reaches Congolese users reliably and affordably.

Regional trade could extend the value of that system. The DRC participates in the Southern African Power Pool, and electricity from Inga has historically been supplied to countries including South Africa and Zimbabwe. The World Bank has identified stronger transmission links between Inga, Zambia and the wider southern African market as strategically important.

The proposed Inga 3 project illustrates both the promise and the uncertainty. World Bank analysis cited in the manuscript places its possible generation between 2 and 11 gigawatts, depending on the final design. Congo’s position could eventually allow power to move across southern, central and eastern African pools. But “could” is the operative word. Regional electricity trade depends on finance, transmission lines, credible contracts, regulatory alignment and political confidence—not capacity estimates alone.

World Bank/ Ai Generated Congo at the centre. Country and river geometry: Natural Earth.

Europe’s interest, Congo’s choice

The strongest European connection is not a speculative cable from the Congo River to European homes. It is the prospect of a different industrial relationship. Europe seeks secure supplies of critical minerals and lower-carbon industrial inputs. Congo needs energy, jobs and greater value addition.

If renewable power can be combined with copper, cobalt and other minerals, Congo could produce more of the intermediate goods required by the energy transition. That would allow trading partners to buy higher-value Congolese output rather than raw material alone.

But the arrangement will be developmental only if industrial capacity takes root inside Congo. Supply security for foreign buyers is not the same as prosperity for Congolese citizens. The terms of contracts, the distribution of rents, local skills, environmental safeguards and the strength of domestic suppliers will decide whether a new mineral boom merely modernises extraction or changes the structure of the economy.

A young country needs work

The urgency is demographic. A World Bank assessment cited in the manuscript estimates that almost 65 per cent of the population is under 25. About 22 million people were aged 15 to 24 in 2025; that figure is projected to reach roughly 26 million by 2030. About a third of young people are neither in education, employment nor training, while roughly 40 per cent struggle to find work.

A young population is neither automatically a dividend nor inevitably a danger. It becomes an economic advantage when education, electricity, investment and functioning markets allow people to be productive. Without those conditions, demographic scale can intensify exclusion and instability.

This is why Congo’s industrial debate must be about jobs as much as exports. Capital-intensive mining can generate revenue without employing people on the scale the country requires. Processing, construction, energy, logistics, agriculture, services and regional manufacturing offer a broader employment base—but only if skills policy and industrial policy are designed together.

Peace as economic infrastructure

No such strategy can succeed while conflict continues in the east. Violence is first a human catastrophe. It is also a destruction of economic possibility: roads go unbuilt, schools are disrupted, responsible investment becomes harder and informal or illicit systems gain ground.

The IMF has identified governance weaknesses, mineral dependence, youth exclusion, conflict and the regional dimensions of insecurity among the DRC’s drivers of fragility. The implication is that peace cannot be treated as a security file isolated from economic policy.

The DRC and its neighbours have a material interest in replacing the economics of conflict with the economics of connection. Electricity links, roads, railways, ports, digital networks, agricultural value chains and lawful cross-border trade can raise the opportunity cost of destabilisation. Integration is no guarantee of peace. But an economy organised around shared production and exchange offers a stronger foundation than one organised around contested extraction.

Finance, and the test of delivery

Development institutions have begun to finance parts of this agenda. As of September 2023, the African Development Bank’s active DRC portfolio consisted of 27 operations worth about $1.45bn across transport, information and communications technology, energy, water and sanitation, and agriculture. Its 2023–2028 country strategy focuses on industrialisation, employment, infrastructure, agricultural value chains, human capital and the business environment.

The energy commitments cited in the manuscript include $22.4mn in parallel AfDB financing alongside $73.1mn of World Bank support approved in 2014 for Inga-related technical assistance. In December 2024, the AfDB was appointed mandated lead arranger for the $340mn Moyi Power Metro-Grids project, intended to bring cleaner, more reliable electricity to more than one million people in three cities.

These commitments show that Congo’s needs are recognised. They do not, by themselves, prove transformation. Portfolios, strategies and mandates are inputs. The meaningful outputs are functioning grids, reliable transport, competitive firms, transparent institutions and work that pays.

The missing chain

Congo’s agenda is often presented as a list: better mining contracts, more roads and rail, stronger security, technical education, regional power links, a better business climate. Each item is necessary. The more difficult insight is that they are interdependent.

Electricity without transmission cannot power a factory. A railway without predictable freight may not be financeable. Mineral processing without skills and reliable energy will not compete. Investment without accountable institutions can reproduce the very extractive bargain Congo needs to escape. Peace without legal economic opportunities may remain fragile.

The country therefore needs more than projects. It needs a sequence: secure productive regions; improve public institutions and contract transparency; expand electricity access and transmission; connect mines, farms and cities to markets; build technical capabilities; and use mineral and energy policy to support industries that can compete.

None of this is quick. Nor is it guaranteed. The same resources that make Congo strategically valuable also intensify struggles over rents and influence. Large infrastructure can create debt, displacement and governance risks if projects are badly designed. Regional interconnection creates opportunity, but it also requires patient diplomacy and institutions able to enforce agreements.

Yet the alternative is not stasis. Global demand for strategic minerals is placing Congo closer to the centre of the world economy. The country can remain indispensable as a source of raw materials while its citizens remain excluded from the value those materials create. Or it can use this moment to negotiate a more productive bargain.

The real test will not be whether the Democratic Republic of Congo finally “wakes”. Countries are not giants in fairy tales. They are political economies, built through choices and constrained by institutions.

Congo already has the assets. What it has not yet secured is the chain that joins them: peace to investment, power to production, minerals to industry, and national wealth to household prosperity. Building that chain would not merely alter Congo’s fortunes. It could change the economic geography of Africa.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa Dragged to Constitutional Court, Accused of Packing Senate With Zanu-PF Politicians
World.content:
President Emmerson Mnangagwa has been dragged to the Constitutional Court over his appointment of 10 senators, with two applicants accusing him of packing the Upper House with politicians instead of independent professionals as required by the Constitution.

Thamsanqa Ncube and Ibhetshu LikaZulu are seeking an urgent order blocking the nominees from being sworn in and ultimately declaring their appointments null and void.

The respondents are Mnangagwa, the Speaker of Parliament, Justice Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi, the Attorney-General and the 10 nominees, Jabulani Sibanda, Makhosini Hlongwane, Mary Mliswa, Nokuthula Matsikenyere, Kudakwashe Tagwirei, Godwills Masimirembwa, Lucy Chitaga, Gen Gibson Mashingaidze, Brilliant Dube and Iren Mutumbwa.



The applicants argue that Section 120(1)(e), introduced through Constitution Amendment No. 3, requires the President to appoint 10 senators based on their "professional skills and other competencies" and after consultation with the National Assembly.

But they claim the nominees are predominantly Zanu-PF politicians or closely linked to the ruling party, defeating the purpose of the amendment.

The application says the appointments are "the precise opposite" of assurances given by Justice Minister Ziyambi during debate on the amendment.

Ziyambi had told Parliament: "The appointment power is not unbounded. The text requires that these 10 Senators be chosen for their professional skills and competencies."

He said the new senators were intended to bring expertise "in finance, in science, in law, in technology, in public health".

The applicants also challenge the consultation process, saying Mnangagwa's nominees were simply announced in Parliament before the Speaker declared: "Recommendations put and agreed to."

"There was no debate, no question, no point of order, and no opportunity for meaningful consultation," Ncube says in the founding affidavit.

The applicants further argue that there is no legislative or parliamentary framework regulating the consultation process, making the appointments premature and unconstitutional.

They fear the dispute will become academic if the nominees are sworn in and begin voting in the Senate.

"The ten individuals are awaiting swearing-in. Once sworn, they will sit and vote in the Senate with full rights," Ncube says.

The applicants want the court to stop the swearing-in and order that any fresh appointments only be made after proper procedures are established to ensure the nominees have the professional expertise required by the Constitution.

The case comes shortly after Constitution Amendment No. 3 increased the Senate from 80 to 90 members by creating the 10 presidentially appointed seats.

World.title: Arizona grandpa to undergo amputation after collapsing on scorching sidewalk
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An Arizona grandfather is preparing to undergo an above-knee amputation of his right leg after he tripped and fell while walking outside in Bullhead City during 120-degree heat earlier this month, according to his family.

Grant Siler, 72, fell during a walk on Aug. 3 in Bullhead City, causing his body temperature to rise to more than 105 degrees.

The family’s GoFundMe said Siler was on the ground for an estimated at least an hour before a passerby found him. The fundraiser said he suffered second and third-degree burns in multiple areas of his body, heat stroke and multiple organ shock.

HIKERS FACE URGENT GRAND CANYON HEAT WARNING AFTER TEEN’S DEATH ON POPULAR TRAIL

He was then taken to a burn ICU in Las Vegas, where he has been cared for since the incident. When he arrived at the facility, doctors discovered he was suffering from heat stroke and organ shock.

"He is in constant pain, can barely move, and has undergone two debridements. Also, he will soon need to undergo surgery for amputation, the extent is not yet known," the GoFundMe reads.

During surgery, a surgeon found that tissue in Siler’s right leg was so severely damaged it was unlikely to fully heal, according to an update posted to the fundraiser.

Siler is scheduled to have his right leg amputated above the knee on Aug. 31, according to FOX 10 Phoenix.

ESPN ANALYST MATT MILLER SAYS HE UNDERWENT LIFE-SAVING AMPUTATION OF LEFT ARM AFTER CAR ACCIDENT

"The plan now is to have an above-knee amputation. The Dr's feel he will overall heal faster and have better pain control this way," the fundraiser reads.

"We can all imagine that after any amputation, the road to recovery is long and hard...physically, mentally and emotionally," it continued.

His wife, Vicki, has been traveling one-and-a-half-hours each way to be with her husband as she continuing to work to support the family’s financial obligations. The family said the couple will also soon have to face medical bills to help with Siler’s recovery.

The family is accepting donations to help with home renovations, home medical supplies, prosthetics and other added costs.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Siler's daughter, Heather Crook, recalled an incident in which he dropped an 80-pound cinderblock on his foot but did not even take a Tylenol.

"He's hurting really bad," Crook told FOX 10. "He's the 'get up and walk it off' type."

"So for him to holler out in pain … it’s really hard to hear. That’s not the kind of person that he is," she added.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Postpartum is real, but child killing demands accountability, veteran prosecutor says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

While failures by people, medical professionals and systems around Lindsay Clancy deserve scrutiny, nothing should erase a parent’s responsibility for killing a child, according to a veteran prosecutor who said he's concerned that public support for the Massachusetts mom is overshadowing the killing of her three young children.

Clancy is accused of killing her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

But as the case has drawn national attention, Clancy has also attracted supporters both online and in-person at the courthouse, and experts have warned that that support has taken attention away from the victims.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S THREE CHILD VICTIMS FORGOTTEN AMID CROWDS OF SUPPORT: MOTHER OF SIX

"Nobody who murders children is a victim no matter what they’re suffering through," said Jonathan Hatami, a veteran child abuse prosecutor. "You're never a victim if you murder people because victims don't do something. Something happens to them."

GOT A TIP?

The defense does not dispute that Clancy caused the deaths — but she has pleaded not guilty and is contesting criminal responsibility.

Hatami has spearheaded a number of high-profile cases against child abusers in Los Angeles, California, including the murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, who was tortured and killed by his mother and her boyfriend. Gabriel's killing exposed a series of missed red flags by the county's Department of Children and Family Services and inspired a Netflix docuseries.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE SCORES ‘EXTREMELY HELPFUL’ PSYCHOSIS CONCESSION AS EXPERT FLAGS NEXT HURDLE

"Gabriel Fernandez was tortured and murdered by his mom and her boyfriend — however, there were a lot of other people...that were responsible," Hatami told Fox News Digital. "There were a lot of people that missed signs through the eight or nine months of Gabriel's torture. There were a lot of people in government, in law enforcement, social workers, who missed all these different signs that really could have saved Gabriel — and they didn't do it. However, Pearl Fernandez and Isauro Aguirre were ultimately responsible for the torture and murder of Gabriel and were prosecuted for that and they were convicted of that."

LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

In Clancy’s case, he argued, many of the people and systems around her deserve scrutiny — but that should not turn her into the central victim of the story. In his view, she's been too much of the focus.

"Instead of about the three victims who were innocent kids," he said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

While failures of government and the child welfare system were investigated after Gabriel's murder, that didn't take responsibility away from the killers, he said. And in the Clancy case, he said he sees a risk that the focus on her mental health could eclipse the three children who were killed in their own home.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I didn't see people out in the streets cheering on Pearl Fernandez because there were other people that were somewhat responsible for what happened to Gabriel," he said. "And the same thing plays in this case. Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death. She admitted to strangling them to death with exercise cords."

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Clancy's defense has said she sought help repeatedly as she struggled with depression, sleeplessness, suicidal thoughts and voices urging her to harm herself and the children.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

"If you murder your children, you need to be held accountable and responsible for that," Hatami said. "No matter what the whys are, no matter what reasons are."

SUSAN SMITH ELIGIBLE FOR PAROLE AGAIN AFTER BEING DENIED RELEASE FOR DROWNING HER 2 SONS IN 1994

If convicted of any of the three counts of first-degree murder she faces, Clancy would see a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Your children should be your life. And if you take their life, you should, as a person, want to be punished for that," Hatami said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News' Sarah Rumpf-Whitten and Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

World.title: Illegal immigrant accused of fentanyl dealing linked to Virginia high school overdoses
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An illegal immigrant from El Salvador who has faced a final deportation order since 2024 was caught and later released on bond at the Texas border in 2016 before his arrest last week for allegedly dealing fentanyl near a Virginia high school, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Isaac Melendez-Carranza, 31, was arrested Aug. 20 and charged with distributing fentanyl within 1,000 feet of a school. He is being held without bond at the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center.

"ICE lodged a detainer on August 20 for Isaac Melendez-Carranza, an illegal alien from El Salvador, with the Loudoun County Jail," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News.

An immigration judge issued Melendez-Carranza a final order of removal on July 18, 2024, according to DHS.

THE BORDER IS CLOSED THANKS TO PRESIDENT TRUMP. IN VIRGINIA, THAT DOESN’T MATTER

Melendez-Carranza was encountered in Sterling, Virginia, less than a month later, on Aug. 16, 2024, but no action was taken, DHS said.

The department cited the Biden administration for the lack of action.

U.S. Border Patrol arrested Melendez-Carranza near Hebbronville, Texas, on May 3, 2016, after he illegally entered the U.S. via the Rio Grande, according to DHS. He was released on bond on July 13, 2016, the department said.

The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office identified Melendez-Carranza as a suspected drug dealer connected to overdoses involving Park View High School students in May.

MEXICAN NATIONAL FACES FEDERAL CHARGES AFTER CBP FINDS $238K IN FENTANYL INSIDE ELECTRIC MOPED

Deputies seized about 100 pills and approximately $1,000 in cash during a search of his home, FOX 5 DC reported.

Multiple students had been hospitalized following suspected overdoses at Park View High School in May, the outlet said.

Loudoun County Public Schools confirmed at the time that two students suffered nonfatal suspected overdoses during school hours.

Additional students were taken to a local hospital for evaluation after exhibiting symptoms, district officials said.

The school system noted that it was unclear whether the incidents were connected and could not immediately confirm whether controlled substances were involved.

JEANINE PIRRO CALLS OUT 'DIRTBAGS' AFTER 14 CHARGED IN ALLEGED COCAINE RING OPERATING FEET FROM A SCHOOLYARD

Sheriff Mike Chapman called the case particularly alarming because the illicit drugs were reaching local students.

The sheriff's office said Melendez-Carranza will be turned over to ICE after he is released, Fox 5 DC reported.

"He’s here illegally," Chapman said. "I think he came in about 10 years ago. We shouldn’t be here and maybe if he wasn’t here this would not have happened, so we take that quite seriously. There is a detainer on him from ICE, so once he is done with his charges here, he will be released to ICE."

The sheriff's office said more arrests are possible, but there was no timetable.

Chapman confirmed ICE placed a detainer on Melendez-Carranza, who will be transferred to federal immigration authorities after his local criminal charges are resolved.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S.," DHS said.

World.title: Houston Uber driver caught in wild police chase as officers seen on dashcam video hitching a ride in his car
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Houston Uber driver was caught "off guard" but kept his cool when two police officers jumped into his vehicle and directed him to chase a suspect fleeing on foot, wild dashcam video shows.

Anthony Baines said he was driving for Uber at about 12:20 a.m. Aug. 8 in a Houston Heights neighborhood, when a shirtless man ran across the street in front of his vehicle with two Houston Police Department officers close behind, according to Storyful.

The video shows Baines getting waved down by an officer and stopping as she approaches and hops into the front passenger seat.

HANDCUFFED SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY SLIPS RESTRAINTS, STEALS DALLAS POLICE CRUISER WITH OFFICER TRAPPED IN BACK SEAT

"Hey, give me a ride over there please," the officer says in the video. "Go, go that way … go, go, go, go, go!"

Baines can be heard asking which way he should drive as officers point him in the direction of the suspect. After driving a short distance, the officer signals for her partner, who's carrying a flashlight, to get in the vehicle, too, and opens the car door and jumps into the backseat.

RIDESHARE PASSENGER HELD HOSTAGE FOR EIGHT HOURS DURING ARMED STANDOFF WITH POLICE IN SWANKY NEIGHBORHOOD

The officers rode with Baines for several minutes while searching the area before one of them appeared to spot the suspect. Both officers jump out of the Uber and resume their pursuit on foot.

"What the f---?!" Baines is heard saying as the officers dart from his car.

BODYCAM SHOWS POLICE K-9 LEAPING INTO ACTION AFTER SUSPECTED IMPAIRED DRIVER REFUSED TO SURRENDER

"It caught me completely off guard," Baines told Storyful. "I’ve never had anything like that happen driving. I was surprised but just did what the officer asked in the moment."

Houston police confirmed the authenticity of the video and the incident to KPRC 2, which reported officers had been responding to a terroristic threat call involving allegations that the suspect threatened to shoot a woman and her children after becoming upset over a belief that someone had stolen from him.

Police said officers tried to detain the man as he left an apartment, but he refused to cooperate and ran away. An officer asked the driver to take them around the block to the apartment complex, where the officers returned to their own vehicle, according to KPRC.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED IN IHOP RESTAURANT AFTER POLICE SAY HE STABBED A RIDESHARE DRIVER

Despite the unusual assistance, police did not locate the suspect. His identity has not been released, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Baines later appeared to confirm in a social media post that he was the Uber driver behind the dashcam footage.

"Yep, that was me," he wrote. "The Uber driver whose dashcam caught two HPD officers jumping in my car to chase a suspect."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Baines described himself as an Army veteran, husband and father of two who began driving Uber so he and his wife could save for their first home.

Fox News Digital has reached out to HPD and Uber for comment.

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed grilled on past statements on Sharia law and White supremacy, taxing the rich
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was grilled in a fiery interview on "Jesse Watters Primetime" Monday on his progressive policy positions as he sparred over his high-stakes Senate race against former Republican congressman Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed was challenged over his stated adherence to Sharia law, which was recently criticized by Vice President JD Vance, as well as previous remarks in which he linked efforts to eliminate Sharia law to White supremacy.

"Nobody is trying to push Sharia law on anyone else, just like I hope nobody is trying to push Canon law on anybody else, because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion," he told host Jesse Watters.

VANCE UNLOADS ON EL-SAYED OVER SHARIA REMARKS: ‘THAT’S NOT MY GRANDPA’S DEMOCRATIC PARTY’

El-Sayed, who said he would "never" push his faith on someone else, argued that there is evidence proving the Trump administration has targeted him because he is Muslim.

"There's statistical evidence that the president and the vice president like to target me simply as a function of my faith," he said.

The Democratic nominee condemned Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., over his proposed legislation that would prevent foreign nationals advocating for Sharia law from entering the U.S., including the No Sharia Act and Preserving a Sharia Free America Act.

"The idea, that you have somebody like Tommy Tuberville – who barely was good at coaching football – is out here trying to ban Sharia Law when there's less than 1% of the Muslim community in America, as if somehow Muslims are out here trying to push Sharia law, that seems to me to be deliberately targeting the Muslim Community, because they're different," he said.

EL-SAYED'S AGENDA PUTS ‘PERMANENTLY’ CHANGED AMERICA ON THE LINE IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE, GOP FIREBRAND WARNS

El-Sayed and Watters later clashed over the Democratic nominee’s proposal to raise taxes on the wealthy.

"I also think we got to start taxing wealth for people who know have over $100 million. I mean at that point like what are gonna even do with more money?," El-Sayed said Wednesday on "The Ansari Podcast."

"What are you going to do with more money? Whatever I want!" Watters said in response to El-Sayed’s podcast remarks.

El-Sayed, who has repeatedly railed against "the 1%" as a malign influence on American politics, defended his tax-the-wealthy stance, arguing it is aimed at improving the lives of average Americans, including in infrastructure and education.

EL-SAYED MAY BE 'FULL-BLOWN COMMUNIST' DESPITE SOCIALIST DENIAL: TOP REPUBLICAN

"The question ultimately is, ‘Do you want to drive on good roads, or would you rather have a billionaire make a second billion?’ That's what Mike Rogers wants. That's why Donald Trump wants. Apparently, that's what you want. I think the people in Michigan want something different," he said.

While El-Sayed has repeatedly criticized the influence of wealthy Americans on the campaign trail, he and his wife reported $686,069 in income in 2025, placing their household among Michigan’s top earners.

LIZ PEEK: MICHIGAN CAN STOP THE SOCIALIST FEVER RAGE — OR WATCH IT SWALLOW THE SENATE

El-Sayed accused Watters of "defending billionaires," to which the host responded, "No, I just think I have the right to the fruits of my own labor. That's America. It's not communist what you're talking about."

El-Sayed countered that billionaires would remain financially secure even if they faced higher taxes.

"If we tax you at 7%, you're still going to make what? A cool $30 million off your billion dollars? I think that's okay, they're going to be okay, Jesse," he said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

El-Sayed also took aim at Rogers, calling his opponent in Michigan’s Senate race a "beta" male who "thinks he is running against Hasan Piker."

He accused Rogers of dodging interviews, though El-Sayed himself seemed to dodge questions during his "Jesse Watters Primetime" appearance about men in women’s sports and him previous characterization of the NFL as racist.

The Democratic Senate candidate also argued that considering reparations for Black Americans "shouldn’t be a crazy thing" and that the U.S. shouldn’t be fighting wars "we don’t know how to get out of," referencing the Iran conflict.

World.title: Trump administration proposes six-figure price tag for new H-1B visas
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration unveiled a proposal on Monday to codify an unprecedented fee of more than $100,000 for cap-subject H-1B petitions for highly skilled foreign workers, replacing a charge first imposed by presidential proclamation last year that has thus far been blocked by a federal court.

The Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule would charge $103,265 as an additional fee for every H-1B petition subject to the annual statutory cap, including petitions eligible for the advanced-degree exemption.

The worker visas are heavily relied on in the tech, education and research industries.

The fee would be used to cover the federal government’s costs of administering the legal immigration system, including actions carried out by DHS and the Department of Justice, Department of State and Department of Labor.

FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers," U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a news release.

The fee, which was first temporarily imposed by President Donald Trump's administration last year, was blocked by a federal judge in June in an order that barred the federal government from collecting the money.

An appeals court is reviewing the judge's decision while a different court considers whether a challenge to the fee by a major business group was properly rejected.

The temporary fee increase expires next month, one year after it was issued. The proposed rule by DHS was posted for public inspection Monday and is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday. It would make the $103,265 fee permanent.

The charge could be finalized by the end of the year.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers with training in specialty occupations, with 65,000 of these visas offered annually under the regular cap.

Another 20,000 are offered for workers with a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. institution, generally granted for up to three years but typically extendable to a total of six years. Those visas typically came with fees between $2,000 and $5,000 before Trump's order, according to Reuters.

The proposed fee would apply to all cap-subject H-1B petitions, including petitions filed for some foreign students already in the United States seeking to change to H-1B status. It would not apply to cap-exempt H-1B petitions; routine extensions for current H-1B holders generally are not subject to the annual cap.

Trump has argued that the H-1B program is abused by many companies who replace American workers with cheaper foreign labor. But business groups and many U.S. companies have contended that the program is needed to address a lack of qualified American workers for certain jobs and to allow American firms to bring in the most skilled workers to support the U.S. economy.

According to court filings, about 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications as of late February.

The fee is being challenged by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce of Democratic-led states and a coalition of labor unions and employers.

Those complaints could be altered to challenge the rule proposed this week once it is finalized.

The Trump administration has also ordered increased vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers.

Earlier this month, DHS added fees of up to $4,500 to applications to extend the stay of H-1B workers or to transfer employees based in other countries to the U.S.

World.title: Ex-Lakers player speaks out in defense of Enes Kanter, doubles down against WNBA's trans issue
World.content:
Ex-Los Angeles Lakers forward Matt Ryan isn't staying quiet after watching Enes Kanter Freedom get escorted out of Wintrust Arena on Sunday night for standing up for female athletes.

Ryan didn't hold back in Freedom's Instagram comments after the ejection, calling out the WNBA for failing to stand up for female athletes as the league's position on the trans issue keeps falling apart.

He doesn't understand why Enes is catching so much heat.

"Just insane times we are living in," Ryan commented on Freedom’s Instagram on Monday.

"Getting demonized for trying to PROTECT women's sports and calling out the absurdity that the WNBA cannot define what the W is... just unreal and sad. Hopefully you'll force them to come to their senses, be REAL leaders, and protect the future young women."

CLUELESS WNBA ATTACKS 'BAD-FAITH' FANS WHO DON'T WANT BIOLOGICAL MEN RUINING WOMEN'S SPORTS

Ryan's support for Enes came after Freedom was booted late in the third quarter following a heated courtside exchange with Sky guard Natasha Cloud.

Kanter Freedom was sitting baseline in support of Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, an outspoken advocate for protecting women's sports.

ENES KANTER FREEDOM OPENS UP ON CONFRONTATION WITH NATASHA CLOUD THAT LED TO EJECTION, WNBA PURSUIT

Before tip-off, Freedom was met by a hostile crowd outside the arena.

Rather than walking back his words after they went viral, Ryan pulled a Sophie Cunningham, heading over to X to double down on his message.

"Yes. This is an '80-20' topic, with [more than] 80% of the country having the most basic of common sense - being able to clearly define what a woman is, and recognizing someone not born as a woman should not participate in women’s sports. There is no transphobia involved in this stance. Every human in the US is free to live as they choose. However, others should not be forced to adhere to absurdity for the sake of feelings.

"The W has a golden opportunity to be PRO- women and protect their league’s integrity. It shouldn’t be difficult. Enes has ZERO intention of stepping foot on a WNBA court - if you can’t recognize that l, I’m not sure how to help you. He’s simply, and very publicly, challenging the highest league in women’s basketball to do what is right."

In an interview with Fox News Digital's Jackson Thompson following his ejection, Freedom explained what triggered the altercation.

WNBA PLAYER NATASHA CLOUD FIRES OFF PRO-TRANS MESSAGE FOLLOWING ALTERCATION WITH ENES KANTER FREEDOM

According to Freedom, the drama began after a routine play by Cunningham.

"Sophie Cunningham shot a three, and I put my hands up to celebrate," Freedom said to Fox News Digital. "Literally, a couple possessions later, Natasha came back and started screaming and yelling and said, 'She's not gonna sleep with you.' And I was like, 'I am not trying to sleep with her. I'm just here to protect women and support her.'"

ENES KANTER FREEDOM EXPOSES NATASHA CLOUD'S PROFANE TIRADE ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE' AFTER WNBA EJECTION

Freedom said Cloud immediately escalated the exchange with explicit language in front of family audiences.

"She started to use some very heavy language, she started to actually cuss," Freedom said. "I was very shocked that there were a lot of kids and teenagers at that game... using those F-bombs in front of all these kids. That’s not a WNBA athlete reaction."

The courtside exchange nearly stole the spotlight from Indiana’s 113-90 blowout victory. Afterward, Fever superstar Caitlin Clark said she did not see the incident and referred questions to Chicago. Fever head coach Stephanie White dismissed the incident as a "social media thing," while Sky forward Azura Stevens called it a routine "fan incident."

Regardless of those attempts to downplay the scene, Freedom made clear that WNBA leadership is facing a reckoning it can no longer dodge.

ROYCE WHITE PREDICTS ENES KANTER FREEDOM WILL BE SUSPENDED FROM WNBA EVENTS AFTER RUN IN WITH NATASHA CLOUD

"The WNBA has no idea what they're about to face," Freedom noted. "They're still trying to figure out what a woman is. So let's see if they can figure that out... let's see what kind of rules that they're gonna come up with."

With players like Ryan publicly backing Freedom and calling out the league's ideological confusion, the WNBA's attempt to sweep the arena fallout under the rug is failing fast.

World.title: Rob Manfred addresses possibility of cancelling 2027 Major League Baseball season: 'We want to play'
World.content:
The 2026 Major League Baseball season is rapidly drawing to a close, and there are multiple compelling storylines to follow.

Impressively, the American League is potentially set to make the wrong kind of history with several teams under .500 in postseason position. For once, there's a legitimate competition for National League MVP, with Cubs outfielder Pete Crow-Armstrong giving now-annual winner Shohei Ohtani a run for his money.

Speaking of Ohtani, his team, the Los Angeles Dodgers, have recovered from a lengthy losing streak to put themselves in position to secure a first round bye. As baseball's new villains, the Dodgers' fate in October will be the most talked about storyline. Win a third straight championship and fans, incorrectly, will complain about competitive balance in baseball. Lose in the NLDS or NLCS? They'll be "chokers" that deserve eternal scorn.

WITH ONE MONTH LEFT, AMERICAN LEAGUE TEAMS ARE HEADING TOWARDS AN EMBARRASSING, HISTORIC LOW

And that outcome might determine the likelihood of a 2027 season too. Not for any legitimate reason, but because the league's billionaire owners are committed to using misguided fan sentiment to push for their ultimate dream: increasing profits and reducing the percentage of revenue that goes to players through a salary cap. With the Collective Bargaining Agreement set to expire at the end of the year, there's a possibility, if not likelihood, that the owners lock the players out on December 1.

During Sunday night's Little League Classic game between the Atlanta Braves and Milwaukee Brewers, commissioner Rob Manfred joined the broadcast and wasn't exactly reassuring when talking about the possibility that the lockout could drag on well into the 2027 season.

MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL HAS A HUGE PROBLEM BREWING FOR THE 2026-2027 OFFSEASON

"We're meeting regularly, which is good," Manfred said during the ESPN broadcast. "Every week, we've had days where we've met with the players. It's early, but we've got a lot of work to do, and we're at it."

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Sounds good, right? Meetings are happening. Conversations are happening. Maybe there's hope. Well, about that.

"Look, our goal is to make a deal. We want to make a deal. We want to play baseball next year. We're planning on playing baseball next year," Manfred said.

"We want," is not "we will." "We're planning" is also not "we will."

WORLD SERIES CHAMPION JOHN SMOLTZ WARNS MLB 'CANNOT AFFORD' A WORK STOPPAGE WITH CBA SET TO EXPIRE

Obviously, the two sides are engaged in active negotiations, and as such, Manfred may not want to weaken his bargaining position by giving too much away. He's also smart enough to know the position baseball is in right now, with attendance and ratings growing and the Dodgers giving the other 29 fanbases a compelling foil.

But it's still a bit disconcerting to hear "want" and "planning" when the future popularity of the sport is at stake. Baseball can't afford a lengthy work stoppage or, God forbid, the cancellation of the 2027 season. Young, exciting players like Crow-Armstrong, Bobby Witt Jr., Konnor Griffin, Paul Skenes, Jacob Misiorowski, Junior Caminero, Jordan Walker, Gunnar Henderson, J.J. Wetherholt and Kevin McGonigle are helping the league build momentum.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Losing out on a year of development, growth, and excitement is simply not an option. Hopefully Manfred realizes that, public comments aside.

World.title: California attorney general cancels talks with Paramount, accuses company of leaks
World.content:
California’s attorney general called off a meeting Monday with Paramount Skydance to discuss a potential settlement of the state’s antitrust lawsuit seeking to block the media company’s $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

In a statement Monday morning, California Attorney General Rob Bonta confirmed he “pulled down this meeting” and accused Paramount of “playing games.”

“I prefer to resolve disputes in the boardroom, not the courtroom. As I’ve also said, if the opposing party in litigation wants to meet in good faith to make a sincere effort to resolve the case, we’ll meet,” Bonta said in part.

Bonta accused Paramount of leaking “the alleged substance of settlement discussions” that were held on Friday. “But they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” the Democratic official added.

A Paramount water tower; California Attorney General Rob Bonta. Getty Images file

In response to a request for comment Monday, a spokesperson for Paramount said the company shared Bonta’s “concerns about the public discussions and misreporting that has surrounded this deal.”

“As we have assured the Attorney General’s office, Paramount has not been the source of the leaks of any of our confidential discussions with the AG’s office,” the Paramount spokesperson added.

Bonta and the Paramount spokesperson appeared to be referring to a Wall Street Journal article published Saturday that detailed some of the conversation topics at Friday’s meeting.

The back-and-forth is the latest twist in a corporate saga that has riveted Hollywood in recent months.

Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America filed a lawsuit last month challenging the tie-up between Paramount and Warner Bros., two of the country’s leading entertainment and media conglomerates.

The states contend the deal violates federal antitrust law and threatens to “extinguish” economic competition in three markets: wide-release theatrical films, anticipated top-grossing movies and basic cable television distribution.

Paramount has flatly rejected those claims, calling the states’ lawsuit “wrong on both the facts and the law.” It has argued that the merger will increase economic competition and production output across film and television.

The company has agreed to freeze the merger until either the antitrust challenge is resolved or June 1, 2027 — whichever comes first. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is presiding over the case, scheduled an antitrust trial for early March.

Paramount has already won clearance from the Department of Justice and secured regulatory go-aheads from more than 60 territories around the world, including Australia, China and the European Union.

The combined corporation would be led by David Ellison, the 43-year-old son of Oracle mogul Larry Ellison. It would encompass two movie studios, two streaming platforms, a suite of cable channels and two marquee news organizations: CBS News and CNN.

Ellison has threatened to move Paramount out of its traditional headquarters in California unless Bonta opened settlement talks, according to a source who was in a closed-door meeting earlier this month but wasn’t authorized to speak about it on the record.

If the deal hasn’t closed by Oct. 1, according to the companies’ agreement, Paramount will be on the hook for a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. shareholders, or roughly $650 million a quarter.

California political leaders have urged both sides in the legal conflict to get to a resolution.

“The continued uncertainty is not good for the workers, not good for productions and not good for the future of this industry,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat running for re-election, said last week.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed concerns that the antitrust challenge could harm California employment if the deal is blocked.

In response to NBC News’ request for comment on that report, Newsom’s office said it “doesn’t comment on anonymous sources or unverified reporting.”

In the antitrust challenge, California is joined by the Democratic attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

World.title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
World.content:
Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation.

The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv.

But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States.

While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.

The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor.

Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, center left, and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, center right, in Kyiv on Monday. Henry Nicholls / Getty Images

Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine.

European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement.

“The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said.

World.title: Multiple dead, including children, in Montana shooting and house fire
World.content:
Multiple people, including children, died when a gunman opened fire at a Billings, Montana, home that was then set alight, authorities said Monday.

Police characterized the incident Sunday evening near the city’s West End neighborhood as a family disturbance. The gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot, NBC affiliate KULR of Billings reported.

Interim Yellowstone County Sheriff Kent O’Donnell said at a news conference Monday that “multiple adults and multiple juveniles” died at the residence.

The dead have been identified, he said, but the number of those killed, their names and their ages will not be released for now.

“Because of the fire and obviously water that goes to suppress that fire, it’s going to slow our investigation of the crime scene recovery of evidence,” he said. “So we ask for patience as we complete this investigation.”

A possible motive was not available Monday.

Billings police and county sheriff’s deputies were dispatched to the shooting in the 300 block of White Star Circle at 6:01 p.m. Sunday, Billings police said on Facebook. O’Donnell said gunshots could be heard during the 911 call.

Officers and deputies reached the scene in roughly 10 minutes and at that point heard gunfire from the back of the residence, the police department said.

Three minutes later, the home was fully engulfed in flames, it said.

Video from the scene showed law enforcement officers taking cover behind patrol SUVs on the street near the home as a small tactical team behind a handheld shield moved toward the structure.

Firefighters were dispatched but may have faced water access issues and fewer fire hydrants than might be ideal, officials said.

“The delay in limited access presented significant challenges, fire conditions continued to worsen, and the residents ultimately became ... consumed by fire,” Billings Fire Chief Matt Hoppel said at Monday’s news conference.

The origin of the blaze was also under investigation.

Billings Police Sgt. Jeff Stovall said in a statement Monday that some information was being withheld “to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation.”

“There are details we simply cannot release at this time,” he said.

World.title: ‘Getting no help’: Thousands in Gary, Indiana, still without power nearly 2 weeks after storms
World.content:
GARY, Ind. — The power outages caused by storms that roared through the region nearly two weeks ago have one resident of this Rust Belt city literally gasping for air.

Joetta Walker, who is 73 and has asthma, uses a nebulizer to help her breathe. But right now it’s a useless piece of machinery, and she has had to rely on an inhaler to survive.

“I have a nebulizer where I need to take breathing treatments,” Walker said in an interview at her sweltering home. “I can’t do that without the electricity.”

Lifelong Gary, Ind., resident Joetta Walker, 73, holds her nebulizer. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Walker said the inhaler doesn’t give her the same level of relief.

“I wheeze,” Walker said and demonstrated. “You hear it now because I get too hot.”

No other place in Indiana has suffered more as a result of those Aug. 11 storms than this mostly Black city on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, best known as the hometown of Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5.

As of Monday, more than 8,600 customers were still waiting for their power to be restored, most of them in Gary, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) reported on its website.

Mayor Eddie Melton said he spoke with President Donald Trump and told him “explicitly that we needed help, that we needed resources.”

Melton said he asked Trump to sign an executive order “and move this thing forward so folks can start getting back to work and we start restoring Gary back to normal.”

“He said that he was going to do all that he can,” Melton said.

Melton said he also met with Republican Sen. Jim Banks. He hopes power for residents will be fully restored by Tuesday.

“I believe a good chunk of that will be restored today, and hopefully 100% will be restored tomorrow,” he said.

Melton’s hopeful forecast came a day after he ripped NIPSCO for failing to completely restore electricity to his city.

“Twelve days is too long for families to be without power,” he said Sunday in an address posted on the city’s Facebook page. “I have made it clear the current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

Tree Care workers from Michigan remove a tree from the front of a home in Gary on Thursday after it was toppled during a recent storm. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In an email Monday, NIPSCO, the Merrillville, Indiana-based utility provider that supplies natural gas and electricity to over 1.3 million residential and commercial customers across the northern third of the state, said it’s “focused on safely restoring power to all customers in every affected community.”

On its website, it said it expects to restore power to all of its customers in Gary by Tuesday.

Walker said that can’t happen too soon. She said she has been relying on her nieces to bring her food and charge up her cellphone twice a day. She said she has $750 worth of pork chops, spiral hams and other foods rotting in her nonfunctioning freezer and refrigerator.

“All gone, gone,” she said.

At night, Walker said, she gets around the house by candlelight.

Walker stands in front of her empty fridge, where, she says, more than $700 worth of food has spoiled. Selina Guevara / NBC News

“I feel hurt ... because I feel like they can do better than this,” she said of the power company. “But I also understand how much damage was done, and I also understand the workers have to be tired.”

Another Gary resident, Dion Thomas, 40, said Monday was the first time he’d seen power crews in his neighborhood. But they seemed to be struggling to turn the electricity back on.

“Some people’s stuff was coming on, then it went back out,” he said.

In the meantime, people have been heading to parks to cook whatever food they have left over charcoal and eat it before it spoils, said Thomas, a father of three.

“It’s been crazy,” he said.

Since the power went out, there has been a spate of generator thefts in his neighborhood, said Calvin Boone, 44, a father of four.

“The kids running around, they stealing people’s generators right now,” Boone said. “I think about the older people, the health for them.”

Boone said that everybody has been feeling hot and miserable and that some have taken to sleeping in their cars with the engines on and the air conditioners blasting.

“We ain’t getting no help,” he said.

Channie Weaver got her power back overnight. But it was too late to save the food in her fridge. She said she’d gone shopping right before the storms hit and estimates she lost $300 worth of provisions.

“All the food is gone. We about to go out and get something out to eat,” said Weaver, 50.

Channie Weaver, 50, of Gary. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Weaver said she lives with her 22-year-old daughter, Desaray Weaver, and her granddaughters, Raelynn, 2, and Riley, 1.

“Man, it’s been rough,” Weaver said. “Being hot in the house, no air conditioning, plus my daughter — she’s pregnant. But it’s definitely been rough.”

Weaver and other Gary residents said in interviews that they can’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power is getting restored last is that it’s a mostly Black city.

“I feel like we at the bottom before everybody else,” she said.

Shaquille Brewster and Selina Guevara reported from Gary and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

World.title: Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into a key challenge for Sen. Darline Graham ahead of the South Carolina runoff. Plus, Allan Smith breaks down the shifting political landscape around data centers.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

⚖️ Breaking news: The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms. Read more →

Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. — On Friday, a South Carolina Republican voter named Roger showed up to a Donald Trump and Darline Graham rally wearing a “DARK MAGA” T-shirt. He arrived early and waited hours to see the president speak.

But Trump’s endorsement wasn’t enough to convince him to vote for Graham in Tuesday’s high-stakes GOP runoff. Graham’s recent debate performance affected his perceptions after she said that “national security is not my thing” when asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are U.S. national security issues.

“Her people should have briefed her a little bit more,” he said. “Foreign policy is something that — you’re going to come in as a new senator, as a rookie, you’re gonna have to learn that.”

Glenda Clinkscales, who said she “loves Trump” and was “excited” to see him, didn’t harbor the same feelings for Graham. Like Roger, she was undecided.

“Some good answers and some not so good answers,” she said when asked what she made of Graham’s debate performance. “I’m not so sure about her right now.”

The hesitation by the two Trump supporters casts a cloud over Graham’s prospects for a six-year term as she faces five-term Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C.

Another voter, Daniel Musick of Myrtle Beach, labeled Trump “the best president we’ve ever had.” He had made up his mind for Norman even before watching Trump and Graham at the rally.

“It’s just that she’s untested. I don’t know enough about her,” he said, adding that “part of the reason” for his opposition to Graham is her debate moment. “Her answer on foreign affairs, when it came to China and Taiwan — it was really unclear that she knew her foreign policy, and to me that was the biggest issue.”

Norman has sought to capitalize on her debate blunder, but it’s not clear he is on the path to victory. Norman is 73, at a time when age is an issue for voters, and has been accused by Graham’s team of being insufficiently loyal to Trump as a member of the House Freedom Caucus that seeks to push his agenda to the right.

Graham, 62, has defended her debate moment by saying voters in South Carolina aren’t asking her about China and Taiwan.

“Now the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said at Friday’s rally with Trump. “And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job.”

Trump, for his part, said Graham was just “being honest” in the debate.

“I mean, she’s going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump told reporters Friday before the rally.

To other GOP voters who attended Friday’s event, Trump’s support was enough.

“Honestly, I don’t know as much about the platforms there, but if Trump supports her, I do too,” said Lynn Spivey, who was wearing a Darline Graham sticker.

Patrick Maguire contributed.

📱Related: MAGA Inc., the super PAC tied to Trump, has spent $830,000 on text messages and voter phone calls to boost Graham, Bridget Bowman reports.

Republicans wrestle with data center backlash as Trump promotes the benefits

By Allan Smith

As recently as last month, Republicans in some of this fall’s biggest races publicly expressed skepticism about the growing backlash to data center development.

A lot has changed since then. On Thursday, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, announced support for a one-year moratorium on data center development. In Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, Republican nominees for governor cut ads hitting their Democratic rivals for being too open to the projects.

Earlier this month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who had welcomed the developments to his state and faces re-election this fall, ordered an audit of data center projects in the state before any more can advance. And in Ohio, GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy released a plan stating that any future data center built in the state must pay the electricity bills and property taxes for nearby residents, adding that he will sign an executive order pausing development until such a plan is enacted into law.

Meanwhile, the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote a memo last week for data center industry leaders detailing how in Ohio’s Senate race, the issue is single-handedly tearing down Republican Sen. Jon Husted as his Democratic rival, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, spends millions on anti-data center ads.

Data centers are one of the few issues in American politics that don’t fall along neat ideological lines. Both parties are rapidly trying to figure out what approach works best for them at the national, state and local levels. Democrats, including some who previously offered the industry a warm embrace, are similarly positioning to be seen as champions for data center accountability and tightly regulated growth as progressives angle for state and federal moratoriums on their development.

But the challenge is equally, if not more, daunting for Republicans, who have worked to build stronger relationships with tech leaders after they gravitated to President Donald Trump during his last presidential bid. And they’re campaigning as Trump himself has promoted the benefits of data center development needed to power the growth of AI.
