03

What to See & Do

TUESDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — FREE ART IN CENTRO Museu Nacional de Belas Artes is open and free this Tuesday Start on Avenida Rio Branco at Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, open 1pm to 5pm today (last entry 4.30pm) and free. The partial reopening covers only Galeria de Moldagens 2, showing restored plaster casts of classical sculpture alongside Vicente de Mello’s photography show “Breu”; the main academic collection stays closed until the full reopening later in 2026. Reach it on Metrô Line 1 or 2 to Cinelândia station; the single journey is R$7.90 (about US$1.55). From there it is a ten-minute walk south toward the waterfront. Pair it with Paço Imperial, open today noon to 6pm with free entry, in Praça Quinze. It is a quiet, airy space for contemporary Brazilian works inside a restored colonial palace. Do not try CCBB today: it is closed on Tuesdays. Wednesday through Monday it opens 9am to 8pm free, so save it for tomorrow. For a green pause, walk up to Campo de Santana and sit under the old fig trees before the heat peaks.

OUTDOORS — BEACH AND GARDEN BEFORE THE RAIN Jardim Botânico or a morning beach stretch Jardim Botânico opens at 8am daily, with entry R$40 (about US$8) for residents and R$80 (about US$15.50) for foreigners. Go early to the palm avenue and the orchid house before the cloud builds. If you prefer salt air, Ipanema and Leblon are cleaner at the Arpoador end after days of moderate swell. Yellow flags mean wading not swimming. A late-afternoon walk on the seafront ciclovia still works, but finish by 4pm to avoid the first showers.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO AND BOTAFOGO Quiet laptops after the museum visit Curto Café on Rua São José in Centro does strong espresso and has tables near power points, with no pressure to leave quickly. In Botafogo, Slow Bakery on Rua São João Batista offers reliable wifi, natural light and Brazilian pastries, but it fills by 10am. Neither is a dedicated coworking space, so take calls outside or order a second coffee before settling in.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — EARLY WATERFRONT WALK Museu do Amanhã for the architecture crowd Museu do Amanhã in Praça Mauá is open today 10am to 6pm, last entry around 5pm, with tickets at R$40 (about US$8) and R$20 half price (about US$4). The interactive climate and technology exhibits suit a slower, air-conditioned afternoon. Reach it on the VLT light rail from Cinelândia to Parada dos Museus; the route is short and above ground. The contrast is simple: Belas Artes feels old Rio, Amanhã feels like a sci-fi set on the bay.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Botafogo or Santa Teresa for dinner, not a late-night club A Tuesday night in Rio is more bar than club. In Botafogo, Comuna on Rua Sorocaba serves burgers and craft beer, with occasional weeknight live sets but nothing heavy before 9pm. In Santa Teresa, Bar do Mineiro stays lively for feijoada plates and cachaça, but tables on the street fill fast. For a calmer close, settle at a pavement table on Rua Dias Ferreira in Leblon, where the dinner crowd starts around 8pm. Rain may return after 9pm, so keep the later part of the night indoors.

ALSO ON TODAY Museu do Amanhã — Centro — 10am–6pm, R$40 / about US$8 (half R$20), science and climate exhibits Paço Imperial — Centro — noon–6pm, free, colonial palace with contemporary art Real Gabinete Português de Leitura — Centro — 10am–5pm, free, 19th-century reading room MAR — Museu de Arte do Rio — Centro — 11am–6pm, R$20, free on Tuesdays Parque Lage — Jardim Botânico — 8am–5pm, free, gardens and café

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô Lines 1, 2 and 4 run normal Tuesday service; the single journey is R$7.90 (about US$1.55) and cards are accepted at all stations. Use Cinelândia for Belas Artes and Paço Imperial, or Praça Mauá via the VLT for Museu do Amanhã.

Rain later could push ride-app prices up after 5pm, so walk or use the Metrô for the central stops and leave the beach before clouds thicken.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Try Confeitaria Colombo on Rua Gonçalves Dias for a historic, tiled tea room feel with lunch plates around R$60–90 (about US$12–17). For faster, cheaper food in Centro, walk to Amarelinho on Praça Floriano for a prato feito around R$40.

Dinner: Stay in Santa Teresa at Bar do Mineiro for feijoada and local plates, around R$70–110 per person (about US$14–21). Alternatively, Botafogo’s Comuna serves burgers and craft beer for about R$60–90 (about US$12–17) without the hill drive.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a water bottle, a compact umbrella, and a card; nearly all venues take Pix or cards, but have R$60 (about US$12) in small notes for taxis or street snacks.

Museums can ask for ID for half-price or free Tuesday entry, so keep a passport photo or digital copy on your phone.

After dark, stick to lit main streets in Centro as you walk from metro to dinner, particularly around empty office blocks north of Avenida Rio Branco.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Expats often gather at the free Tuesday MAR entry for an unplanned midweek hangout, and the café there is a decent meeting point. Newcomers should check the Rio Expats & Digital Nomads WhatsApp groups for a possible sunset meetup near Copacabana if the rain holds off.

Coworking regulars at Goma in Botafogo and SobreCafé in Jardim Botânico are the fastest informal network for apartment leads and visa chat this week.

08

Game Day

MIDWEEK FOOTBALL WATCH

No senior Flamengo, Fluminense, Vasco or Botafogo fixture is scheduled for Tuesday August 25. The week’s pressure is on squad fitness and injury returns before weekend league rounds.

Even without a match, Comuna in Botafogo and Shenanigan’s in Ipanema keep multiple screens on for Champions League or Libertadores replays from around 8pm.

If you want to watch Brazilian league highlights, most bars switch to SporTV after 9pm, but call ahead if the rain looks heavy.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The market board from Monday’s session shows a modestly positive local session, helped by a strong performance in the materials sector, particularly Vale. This offset sharper drops elsewhere, including a steep fall in petrochemical shares after an extrajudicial recovery disclosure.

Investors are treating this week as a macro-focused stretch: Monday’s central bank Focus readout offered updated consensus on inflation and rates, and later week data includes jobs and current account prints.

The mood among expat professionals is cautious but not defensive. Travel and service businesses are watching consumer finance numbers, while importers track the dollar board for how it closes the month.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is the CCBB open today?

Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil (closed today; open Mon, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun) is closed on Tuesdays. It opens tomorrow Wednesday from 9am to 8pm, with free entry. Do not go today; choose Museu Nacional de Belas Artes or MAR instead, both open and a short Metrô ride apart.

Can I swim at Ipanema today?

Most of Ipanema and Leblon are on yellow flags, meaning moderate waves and currents. Lifeguards are allowing wading but not full swimming in some stretches near Arpoador. Water temperature is around 22°C, but rain and cloud make it a poor beach day. If you want a safer swim, .

How do I get from Centro to Barra da Tijuca easily?

Take Metrô Line 1 or 2 to Botafogo, then transfer at the integrated bus terminal for an express BRT to Barra. The total trip can take 60–80 minutes in late afternoon traffic. A ride app may cost R$70–120 (about US$14–23) depending on demand, and with rain expected after 5pm, surge pricing is likely.

World.title: Latin America Sports Daily for Tuesday, August 25, 2026
World.content:
CONMEBOL reprogrammed the tie after the earthquake in Colombia. The first leg was eventually played in Ibagué on 18 August, not the original date.

Aron Rodríguez scored the only goal as Deportes Tolima lost 0-1 at home. Independiente del Valle lead 1-0 on aggregate, so any draw tonight sends them through — CONMEBOL scrapped the away-goals rule in 2022.

The second leg kicks off at Estadio Banco Guayaquil in Quito. The altitude gives the Ecuadorian club a familiar edge against a Tolima side that must score.

What is at stake is a place in the Copa Libertadores quarter-finals. CONMEBOL has confirmed the fixture for Tuesday 25 August.

For foreign readers, this is one of Latin America’s tightest club competitions. One goal in Ibagué still leaves the series wide open.

In short — Independiente del Valle defend a 1-0 lead at home to Deportes Tolima in the Copa Libertadores round of 16.

The Continent’s Mood Today

The continent is holding its breath. Mark Carney said the US wants to destroy Canada’s steel, aluminum and auto industries, and that Ottawa is weighing retaliation.

That tension, reported by Bloomberg on Monday, ripples through Latin American economies already nervous about US policy toward Mexico, Brazil and beyond. It makes an already cautious Tuesday feel defensive.

Brazil – Poll Fever Before the Real Fight

Brazil is in an election season, and the numbers are stirring real feeling. In Paraná, Sergio Moro leads the governor race with 37%, ahead of Requião Filho at 21% and Sandro Alex at 15%.

Requião and Alex are technically tied within the three-point margin of error. Voters are not just watching; they are arguing about whether Moro, the former anti-corruption judge, can hold such a big lead. In Alagoas, Renan Filho has 42% in the first Quaest poll, while in Rio Grande do Sul, Zucco at 26% and Juliana Brizola at 23% are statistically level.

The mood is restless. People remember Moro’s role in Lava Jato, a wound that still divides families. For a foreigner living in Brazil, this means political advertising and heated talk will dominate until October, but markets are not yet panicking.

Mexico – Diablos, Tariffs and a Blood Moon

Mexico is wrapped up in playoff baseball. The Diablos Rojos forced a fifth game against the Pericos de Puebla after winning Game 4 by 15-10 on Monday.

Game 5 is set for the Estadio Hermanos Serdán in Puebla at 19:00. The series has fans on edge, and the sports pages are full of bravado and nervous joy.

Under that noise sits a quieter worry: US tariff aggression toward Canada feels close to home. Expansión also reported that Mexico will see a blood moon on Thursday. A foreigner holding Mexican assets should know the sports euphoria does not erase trade anxiety.

Argentina – Records and Rust

Argentina is proud but tired. The Central Bank reported reserves reached a record US$50.655 billion, and farm exports hit US$31.952 billion in seven months.

Yet the UIA said industrial activity fell 0.6% in July. Production remains 10% below 2022 and 2023 levels. People are pleased about the trade surplus, but they know household debt pays for food, not luxuries.

The memory of recent crisis is fresh. For a foreigner with assets in Argentina, the high reserves offer some comfort, but the industrial decline means daily life still feels tight.

Colombia – Earthquakes and Ledgers

Colombia is exhausted but organized. The government is suppressing four viceministries and ordering audits, while José Antonio Ocampo says the wealth tax should be kept to rebuild after the earthquake.

Almost 95% of mobile sites affected by the earthquake are back online. Chocó has the worst disruption at 11.7%. The mood is pragmatic and a little somber.

The US also launched a visa fast-track pilot in Bogotá. For a foreigner there, this means quicker administrative paths for some, but tax debates and reconstruction will dominate public life.

Chile – Stuck in Copper and Cost

Chile is frustrated. Long-term borrowing costs hit an 18-month high as growth stalls, and copper production remains at 2004 levels.

The Everton victory over Universidad de Concepción with a controversial disallowed goal fed a sense of injustice. The mood is sour, industrious, and a little resentful.

For a foreigner holding Chilean assets, this means credit is pricier and optimism scarce. The country feels stuck between its mining past and an uncertain future.

Uruguay – A Casino, a Union, a Fight

Uruguay is quietly combative. The Montevideo Casino Parque Hotel moved to national control, and the union rejected 150 job cuts at Frigorífico Tacuarembó.

Workers are angry, but the state is not backing down. The mood is defensive, yet proud. For a foreigner living there, this means labor disputes could disrupt services, but the social fabric holds.

The Shared Mood

Across the region, people are holding on to small joys and big worries. Baseball, art and tango sit next to tariff fears, tax fights and slow credit.

The common feeling is a guarded Tuesday: not panic, but a lowered expectation. Latin America is waiting for the next US move while tending its own messy, lively house.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is driving Brazil’s political mood today?

Fresh Quaest polls show Moro leading Paraná with 37%, Renan Filho ahead in Alagoas with 42%, and technical ties elsewhere, keeping voters tense and talkative.

Why is Mexico focused on baseball right now?

The Diablos Rojos forced a Game 5 against Pericos de Puebla after winning Game 4 by 15-10, and the decisive game is set for Monday night in Puebla.

What is the biggest cross-border concern in Latin America?

US tariff threats against Canadian steel, aluminum and autos are making the whole hemisphere nervous, even as local economies post some strong export numbers.

World.title: IKEA Maps Out Its Costa Rica Rollout in Three Locations
World.content:
IKEA has identified the first three sites it plans to operate in Costa Rica, giving the clearest picture yet of how the Swedish home furnishings retailer intends to build a physical presence in a year after signing its franchise agreement. The first will sit inside Parque Empresarial Lindora, a mixed-use business park in Pozos de Santa Ana, west of San José.

The company describes it as a hybrid site that pairs logistics support for online and telephone orders with a planning and ordering space, where customers who buy through the website can collect their purchases. Staff at that location will also advise customers on designing and organizing rooms in their homes, a service the chain offers in other markets. The site is not a conventional showroom, and the company has not described it as a full store.

Two further openings are planned after that. One is a compact-format store in Curridabat, east of the capital. The second is a medium-format store in Escazú, which will be developed alongside a distribution center of greater capacity. IKEA did not announce opening dates for any of the three. The company has said its rollout will be progressive, with online sales serving as the first commercial point of contact for Costa Rican customers.

That approach has been consistent since the beginning. Inter IKEA Systems B.V., the owner of the IKEA concept and its worldwide franchisor, announced in August 2025 that it had signed agreements with Sarton Group granting exclusive rights to explore expansion in Costa Rica and Panama.

Maria Johansson, IKEA’s expansion manager, said at the time that the agreements were part of the brand’s growth across the Americas and would “invite Panama and Costa Rica into the IKEA family.” Sarton Group already operates IKEA stores in Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and Spain’s Canary and Balearic Islands. Tony Tavira, retail manager at Sarton Group, has said Costa Rica represents a relevant market within the company’s regional development, and that assembling teams capable of bringing the brand to life in a new market would be central to the effort.

The groundwork has been visible for months. In June, the company opened hiring for roles spanning logistics, sales, customer service, communications, interior design, operations, information technology and human resources, and launched its Costa Rican site at ikea.cr, which initially displayed products without allowing purchases.

By July, heavy machinery was moving earth on a property in Guachipelín de Escazú near Route 27, close to the Sheraton hotel. El Financiero confirmed with the municipality that the project held the permits required to begin work, and a sign on the property showed environmental viability approval from the Ministry of Environment and Energy.

Whether that Escazú site corresponds to the medium-format store now listed third in the company’s sequence, or to the distribution center attached to it, has not been clarified. The company has consistently declined to give opening dates, citing the logistical complexity of the project. IKEA operates more than 500 stores across 63 markets, according to company figures for the close of its 2025 fiscal year, with retail run by more than a dozen franchise groups.

Its arrival gives Costa Rica’s home furnishings sector a competitor with global purchasing scale and flat-pack pricing and puts pressure on established local retailers to revisit their catalogs and price positions. For now, none of that has a date attached. The company’s online channel remains the only way to reach the brand in Costa Rica, and the Lindora site will be the first place customers can pick up what they order.

World.title: Two earthquakes shake Costa Rica’s Central Valley before dawn
World.content:
If you were jolted awake around 1:40 a.m. this morning you felt one of the strongest quakes to hit the San José area this year. The shaking was sharp and close, and you should expect more of it through the day. The first quake hit at 1:37 a.m. with its epicenter in Vásquez de Coronado, roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) northeast of downtown San José. A second, smaller quake followed within about three minutes. Both were shallow, which is why they hit so hard for their size.

There have been some discrepancies on how strong the first one was. The Observatorio Vulcanológico y Sismológico de Costa Rica (OVSICORI), put it at magnitude 5.0 at a depth of 11 kilometers (6.8 miles), about 8 kilometers (5 miles) from San Isidro de Coronado. The Red Sismológica Nacional revised its own reading upward to magnitude 5.4 at just 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) deep, placing the epicenter 11 kilometers (7 miles) north of Cascajal de Vásquez de Coronado. The United States Geological Survey logged magnitude 4.9 at 10 kilometers (6.2 miles).

Those gaps are normal in the first hours after a quake, and they will narrow as more data comes in. What all three agree on is the part that matters, it was shallow, and it was directly under a densely populated corner of the Central Valley. The second event registered at magnitude 4.5 on OVSICORI’s confirmed bulletin, with earlier readings listing it at 4.4. By 3:30 a.m., OVSICORI seismologist Marino Protti reported roughly 30 aftershocks.

Damage so far appears minimal as the Comisión Nacional de Emergencias said at 1:52 a.m. it had received no damage reports at all. It later confirmed a single 911 call reporting a damaged perimeter wall at a home in Vásquez de Coronado, plus a downed electrical pole in San Vicente de Moravia. Bomberos de Costa Rica and the Cruz Roja Costarricense both ruled out serious damage overnight.

Those in the area reported strong shaking in San Francisco de Dos Ríos, Tres Ríos, Moravia, Hatillo and parts of Alajuela. In Cariari de Pococí, on the Caribbean slope, people described it as mild. Expect aftershocks to keep coming as a sequence of 30 in under two hours is typical after a shallow magnitude 5, and smaller tremors can continue for days. Most will be too weak to feel. A few may be strong enough for you too feel.

As a precaution, walk through your home this morning before you assume everything is fine. Look at perimeter walls, masonry, and anywhere plaster meets a corner, because hairline cracks that appear after one quake can open further during aftershocks. Check that your water heater is still strapped and that gas connections are not leaking. A wall that shifted overnight is far easier to spot at 7 a.m. than it was at 1:40.

The Central Valley sits on top of an active fault and fold system, which is precisely why a moderate quake here produces harder shaking than a much larger one out at sea. That geology is not going to change, and neither is the answer to it. So, the useful response is not alarm but maintenance — knowing where your water shutoff is, keeping a flashlight somewhere you can find it in the dark, and checking the walls just to be sure all is in order.

World.title: Mother of five Nichole McDonald granted $800 bail after more than two months on remand; Says she took anger management classes in prison
World.content:
Mother of five Nichole McDonald granted $800 bail after more than two months on remand; Says she took anger management classes in prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Mother of five Nichole Gilda McDonald is out of the Belize Central Prison after a Magistrate granted her bail on Monday in connection with the alleged assault of a doctor at the Matron Roberts Polyclinic.

McDonald, 38, had been on remand since June 8, when bail was denied after she was charged with harm upon a doctorand aggravated assault upon a nurse stemming from an incident at the clinic two days earlier. At the time, the court found that the new charges allegedly breached conditions attached to bail she had received just days before in another case.

On Monday, McDonald was granted bail in the sum of $800 plus one surety of the same amount. As conditions of her release, she must report to a police station once weekly and must not be arrested and charged with another offence while on bail.

McDonald was also provided with 10 pages of disclosure in the harm case involving the doctor. Trial has been set for October 21, 2026.

The June 6 confrontation at Matron Roberts drew significant public attention after videos circulated on social media. The doctor later spoke publicly about the incident and called for stronger legal protection for healthcare workers.

McDonald has pleaded not guilty and maintains that she will contest the allegations at trial.

She told reporters following her release that her time in prison included a period under sanction and that she participated in the Ashcroft Rehabilitation Programme and an anger-management programme. While maintaining her innocence, McDonald said she was grateful for what she learned from the programme and was looking forward to returning home to her children.

McDonald also has other pending criminal matters. She faces six charges arising from separate alleged incidents in early June, including aggravated assault, common assault, damage to property, insulting words and wounding.

Separately, McDonald is accused of using a computer system to disseminate a false statement concerning former Commissioner of Police Chester Williams. That charge was previously dismissed but was reinstated in May 2026. In July, the Magistrate’s Court was informed that the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions had directed that the cybercrime matter proceed on indictment to the High Court rather than be tried summarily in the lower court.

McDonald remains unrepresented in the criminal matters and maintains her innocence.

World.title: Lloyd Parchue rejects 4-year sentence indication after gun allegedly found in SUV; remanded to prison
World.content:
Lloyd Parchue rejects 4-year sentence indication after gun allegedly found in SUV; remanded to prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A former security guard accused of being caught with an unlicensed 9mm pistol and eight live rounds of ammunition has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after rejecting a sentencing indication of four years and one month behind bars.

Thirty-three-year-old Lloyd Parchue, a resident of southside Belize City, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, where he was charged with keeping an unlicensed firearm and keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

Police allege that at around 3:40 a.m. on Sunday, August 23, members of the GI3 Unit were patrolling near Flamboyant Street and Croton Lane when they noticed a white SUV travelling at high speed.

Officers reportedly stopped the vehicle after it came to a halt in front of a residence on Croton Lane. Parchue, who was identified as the driver, was ordered out of the vehicle and informed that police would conduct a search for firearms, ammunition and drugs.

According to police, nothing illegal was initially found inside the glove compartment; however, officers allegedly discovered a silver 9mm pistol with a brown handle and eight live S&B 9mm rounds concealed behind the glove compartment.

Parchue was subsequently detained and taken to the Queen Street Police Station.

During his arraignment, Parchue requested a Maximum Sentence Indication (MSI) to determine the sentence he could face if he pleaded guilty.

The magistrate indicated that he would receive four years and one month imprisonment on each charge, with the sentences to run concurrently, meaning he would serve a total of four years and one month.

Parchue declined the indicated sentence and instead pleaded not guilty to both charges.

Due to the nature of the offences, bail was denied and Parchue was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 23, 2026.

World.title: Motorcyclist Jaime Catalan killed in Cayo collision; second rider detained
World.content:
Motorcyclist Jaime Catalan killed in Cayo collision; second rider detained

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a man in connection with a motorcycle collision that claimed the life of 46-year-old Jaime Haroldo Catalan of San Marcos Village.

The crash occurred shortly before midnight on Friday, August 21, between Duck Run 1 and Billy White Village in the Cayo District.

Catalan was found unresponsive on the roadway with grave injuries. Police also found his damaged motorcycle and a second motorcycle with minor damage.

Investigators believe Catalan was travelling toward Billy White when 26-year-old Javier Pinelo of Bullet Tree Village overtook him. According to preliminary information, Pinelo encountered oncoming traffic and swerved back in front of Catalan, leading Catalan’s motorcycle to collide with the rear of Pinelo’s motorcycle.

Pinelo was also injured and taken to the San Ignacio Community Hospital. Police obtained a specimen from him, detained him under police guard and issued a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

Investigations continue.

World.title: Police review Crime Fusion footage after Christopher Smith found shot dead on Arlington Drive
World.content:
Police review Crime Fusion footage after Christopher Smith found shot dead on Arlington Drive

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the murder of 23-year-old Christopher Smith, whose body was discovered in a yard on Arlington Drive in Belize City on Sunday morning.

According to police, the body was reported at around 7:00 a.m. on August 23. Investigators found Smith unresponsive with apparent gunshot injuries and recovered several expended shell casings from the scene.

Police believe Smith may have been shot at around 1:20 that morning, when reports were received of gunfire in the area. Officers who responded at that time, however, were unable to establish a crime scene.

Investigators have since retrieved surveillance footage through the Police Department’s Crime Fusion Center, and police say that footage has provided leads which are now being pursued.

No motive has been established.

Police also confirmed that Smith was known to them. He had previously been charged in connection with the 2024 double murder of Belmopan taxi drivers Marvin Cante and Juan Carlos Raymundo, whose bodies were found in a shallow grave near Hattieville. Importantly, however, the murder charge against Smith was withdrawn on November 28, 2025, on instructions from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

World.title: Sherman Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza charged in armed home invasion and theft of 2026 Wingle pickup
World.content:
Sherman Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza charged in armed home invasion and theft of 2026 Wingle pickup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have charged two men with aggravated burglary following an armed home invasion in which a resident was reportedly robbed of a 2026 Wingle pickup truck.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sheffan Hemmans, described by police as a post guard officer, and 26-year-old Alberto Arreaza, a Cayo District labourer, have been jointly charged.

Police say the complainant reported that at around 7:45 p.m. on Thursday, two masked men entered his home, one armed with a firearm, and demanded the keys to his black 2026 Wingle pickup.

Fearing for his safety, the victim complied and the men drove away with the vehicle.

Police activated operational procedures and, at around 9:45 p.m., officers in the Santa Rosa area of western Belize intercepted the stolen pickup.

Police also observed another vehicle in the area which sped away. Officers pursued that vehicle and eventually intercepted it. Hemmans was reportedly found aboard.

A search of Hemmans allegedly led to the discovery of 50 live rounds of .22 LR ammunition.

In addition to the aggravated burglary charge, Hemmans was charged with keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

World.title: Three charged after San Pedro raid turns up cannabis, cocaine and crack
World.content:
Three charged after San Pedro raid turns up cannabis, cocaine and crack

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three San Pedro residents have been jointly charged with drug trafficking following a police raid in the Boca del Rio area.

Police say an operation was conducted at a residence on August 21 and resulted in the discovery of 1,312 grams of suspected cannabis, 21 grams of suspected cocaine and 28 grams of suspected crack cocaine.

Police subsequently arrested and jointly charged three people, including 26-year-old Horace Anthony Crawford and 24-year-old Bridget Alcer, along with another 26-year-old San Pedro resident.

The trio each face three counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another.

World.title: High-speed SUV stop leads police to loaded 9mm; Lloyd Parchue charged
World.content:
High-speed SUV stop leads police to loaded 9mm; Lloyd Parchue charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man has been charged with firearm and ammunition offences after police say a high-speed SUV caught the attention of officers conducting an anti-crime operation.

Police say GI3 personnel were operating in the St. Martin’s area at around 3:40 a.m. when they observed an SUV travelling at high speed.

Officers pursued and intercepted the vehicle.

A subsequent search allegedly led to the discovery of a 9mm Smith & Wesson pistol containing a magazine loaded with eight live rounds of ammunition.

Police formally arrested and charged 33-year-old Lloyd Parchue of Croton Lane, Belize City, with keeping a firearm without a gun licence and keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

World.title: Three Belize City men charged after armed robbery caught on camera at Independence Village store
World.content:
Three Belize City men charged after armed robbery caught on camera at Independence Village store

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have charged three Belize City men following an armed robbery at a store in Independence Village over the weekend, which was caught on camera.

The robbery occurred at approximately 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 22.

Police say two men entered the establishment, one armed with a firearm, and made demands of the store owner. The robbers took several items belonging to the proprietor before fleeing.

Information on the suspected perpetrators was circulated to police formations, and officers later intercepted a vehicle reportedly connected to the robbery.

Three men were found aboard and subsequently detained.

Police identified two of the accused as Dorian Garnett, 36, and Krishna Flores, 35, and Anthony Smith.

All three have been jointly charged with robbery.

Police said the suspects are persons known to authorities in connection with activities in the Belize District, but investigators have not established that they regularly operated in southern Belize.

World.title: Fewer students drunk or high
World.content:
(Photo: Adobe stock)

THE National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) is reporting that fewer teenagers are using illegal drugs or drinking alcohol across Jamaica, but the numbers remain concerning.

According to the NCDA, its recent Global School-Based Health Survey (GSHS) — which had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools — showed that the consumption of alcohol by students in grades seven to 11 dropped from 52.5 per cent in 2010 to 38.8 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, the number of children who started consumption of alcohol before age 14 has decreased from 80.2 per cent in 2010 to 71.5 per cent this year. Also, teenagers who get drunk after the consumption of alcoholic beverages dropped from 35.5 per cent in 2010 to 21.5 per cent in 2026.

But 10.3 per cent of adolescents still attend school under the influence of alcohol, and 10.6 per cent are exposed to s about alcohol.

The NCDA — an agency of the Ministry of Health and Wellness — believes the overall message for positive trends has been working; however, it says continued action is needed to strengthen early prevention programmes, enforce underage drinking laws, reduce youth exposure to alcohol marketing, and increase parent and school engagements.

The survey also found that the use of ganja among adolescents declined from 21.5 per cent in 2017 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, a trend welcomed by the NCDA.

However, the organisation says it is concerned that 24.3 per cent of adolescents have easy access to the weed, while 5.5 per cent continued to use ecstasy, also known as molly.

Ecstasy is a synthetic psychoactive drug with both stimulant and psychedelic effects. Teens use it at parties and other gatherings, but it can cause dangerous spikes in body temperature, dehydration, high blood pressure, and heart failure.

With some students still attending school under the influence of substances because of the easy access to ganja and ecstasy, the NCDA says it will be expanding its substance-use prevention programme, aimed at strengthening prevention, delaying initiation, reducing access, and providing timely support for young people.

It also plans to improve the monitoring of emerging drugs.

In the meantime, the GSHS found that physical fights among students declined from 50.1 per cent in 2010 to 27 per cent in 2026, while injuries from fights dropped from 59.6 per cent in 2010 to 49 per cent in 2026.

In addition, the survey says bullying dropped from 40.2 per cent in 2016 to 27 per cent in 2026.

However, the survey found that 15 per cent of teenagers faced cyber bullying in the past year but there was no comparative figure with 2010. Another 16.9 per cent experienced bullying off school compounds.

The NCDA said despite a drop in physical fights among students, it will be strengthening its violence-prevention programme as it seeks to maintain safe school policies.

It added that it will be stepping up its anti-bullying initiatives to promote respect, inclusion, and a culture of kindness.

“Safe environments are essential for academic success and healthy development,” said the NCDA.

“Violence and injuries impact students’ physical and mental health, learning and well-being. Bullying and cyberbullying can lead to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and social isolation,” the NCDA added.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: More vacancies than advertised
World.content:
Numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts.

With the new academic year just days away numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts. But Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS) President Anniona Jones says the influx of s across various media do not reflect the full picture of the staffing needs.

According to Jones, while some vacancies have been caused by teachers embarking on well-earned vacation breaks, others are the result of educators leaving the system, some without proper notice.

“Some of these resignations do not reach the regional office, and sometimes we fill [vacancies] based on old resumes and not necessarily place all of it in an ad because not every school has the fiscal position to even run an ad. So what you’re seeing in the paper is the tip of the iceberg of the actual gaps in schools because many of us do not place in the national papers the s for teachers. We use a lot of social media, word of mouth, our teachers’ groups, Jamaica Teachers’ Association groups, and so on. That’s what’s happening. So we really don’t have a good picture nationally on what is really happening on the ground,” Jones told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The educator, who was responding to queries by the Observer about what accounts for the almost perennial influx of s yearly during the summer break, explained that the system itself is partly accountable.

“The education system asks all members of the academic staff to apply for their leave by November of the first term, for the following academic year. So leave applications are made almost a year in advance. Usually, by June we would get notification from the Ministry of Education indicating which teachers’ leave application is approved. This year it came a little later in July, and we see where a priority was placed on approving leave applications, certainly in Region One, which is Kingston and St Andrew, for persons who would have applied for eight months,” Jones outlined.

She said while the leave amounts might seem staggering, a little known fact is that “it takes a regular classroom teacher or vice-principal five years of service in order to qualify for four months of leave”.

“So, unlike many people’s workplace where they will get two weeks’ vacation leave, we don’t do that in education, and there are a lot of reasons for that. However, that’s how the system is set up. So teachers will get leave of four months or eight months. They’d apply for study leave, and they would know at that period of time,” she said.

Jones noted that because of the late approvals, principals were not made aware, until July, of how much their staffing levels would be affected for September.

“Usually that’s when many principals know how many of the teachers who have applied for leave have had their leave approved, and whether or not it is for four months, eight months, a year study leave, two years, or so on. So that means that July and August of every year, obviously, you’re going to see a large number of applications in the media, and we will have to fill these positions for smooth start of school for September,” Jones said.

She noted that teacher migration and not just vacation entitlements have also influenced the s of vacancies.

“There are several factors causing teacher migration. It’s not a national problem only, it’s not a regional problem only, it’s an international problem; and if you look at many of the international bodies, such as Education International, some projections go as high as 40 million teachers may be needed within the next decade globally. There are lots of reasons why teachers are leaving the education system: terms and conditions of service, salary, moving on to other interests, and so many other reasons. But we do have a significant shortage in some areas, the industrial arts [for example]. Obviously, persons can earn far more money in the private sector than in teaching,” she told the Observer while noting that Jamaican educators are in high demand by other territories.

The recruitment, she said, is also driven by the fact that there are “shortages in some areas that are undersubscribed like history, geography, the foreign languages like French, Spanish” in addition to the fact that some schools are located in remote areas, or in communities where Zones of Special Operations are in force, or areas that experience high levels of crime or violence, therefore “not many people may want to work in some of those areas”.

According to Jones, the discontinuation of a special hazard allowance — a grant that made to teachers who worked in very remote or rural situations, or in high-risk areas — as an incentive is also a contributor to some schools finding it difficult to fill vacancies.

“So there are many factors that would influence how fluid the system is. And then, of course, if we only have four months available, and that teacher gets a position that is potentially permanent, a teacher may go in that regard. So the short-term vacancies may also be difficult to fill,” the JAPSS president stated.

She said it is difficult to provide a total number of all schools with unfilled vacancies.

“If you look in the papers you will find that even schools that would have advertised before, they may have conducted interviews and even made an offer to a teacher. A teacher may rescind that offer from one school and move to another school where they did interviews because teachers are applying for multiple jobs, they’re doing many interviews, and then they’re picking once they’re offered. So, because of how fluid the system is, you may also find that you may think that you have filled a vacancy, and a teacher calls back to say, ‘I am so sorry. Instead of working at your school for four months or eight months, I’ve just been offered a position for a year, or a clear vacancy at another school, and so I’m going to take that offer instead’. So even though you may think that you filled the vacancy, it now becomes available again because the teacher is moving in the direction of what is best for them and their families,” Jones said.

Asked to say whether this meant the association still has no clear picture as to readiness for the new school year Jones said, “We have filled most of the vacancies… but many schools will have at least one or two positions that they’re hoping to fill this week, with some schools having as many as six or eight positions that are yet to be filled”.

Jones, in the meantime, had this message for parents, guardians, and students: “Every Jamaican child deserves high-quality education, and conditions of work for the teacher are conditions of learning for the children. So if it is that we want the best for our children, then it means we should want the best for the teachers. So, please help us to advocate for the conditions that will be required for us to be able to attract the best and the brightest, retain the most experienced teachers, so that our children can ultimately benefit.”

Added Jones, “Let’s celebrate those who have gone on their well-earned leave; [working] five years to get four months is a lot [and working] 10 years to get eight months is a lot. So let’s celebrate with those who are taking well-deserved breaks. But let us work together to advocate for a better education system.”

World.title: Celene Hall takes Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 crown
World.content:
Celene Hall makes her first walk as Miss Universe Jamaica 2026.

Despite winning five sectional prizes, the newly crowned Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 titleholder, Portland native Celene Hall said she had no idea that she would have emerged the winner.

Hall competed with 32 other ladies for the coveted title and to represent Jamaica at the Miss Universe finals in Puerto Rico in November.

he coronation show took place on Sunday night inside a jam-packed ballroom at AC Hotel Kingston.

“I know I received a lot of sectional awards, but honestly, it wasn’t until the crown was placed on my head that I really knew that I was Miss Universe Jamaica 2026,” Hall told the

Jamaica Observer shortly after she was crowned.

This marked the start of a new journey and the end of countless days and nights of practice, rehearsals, and training.

Hall first entered the Miss Universe Jamaica Portland pageant, which she won a few months ago.

According to Parish Director Shanique Rogers, Hall was transformed during the process.

“From the beginning, she listened, she understood what the crown represented, and, most importantly, she was willing to learn… She is not the same woman who entered the competition in Portland. The Miss Universe Jamaica Portland platform challenged her, developed her, and helped shape her into the queen she is today,” Rogers, a former Miss Universe Jamaica finalist, told the Observer.

She added: “Seeing Celene win makes me incredibly proud, because I know the amount of hard work, dedication, and behind-the-scenes effort that went into preparing her for this moment. To see that hard work pay off is truly rewarding.”

Hall concurred that the pageant challenged her.

“I knew the space would challenge me more to grow into the absolute best version of myself, and that is the reason why I entered in the first place,” she shared.

From Passley Gardens in Port Antonio, she attended Titchfield High School.

Her beaming parents, three sisters and two brothers were on hand to witness her success.

“She started modeling from primary school and she just kept going, and we have been supportive of her,” said her mother, Sonia Hall.

Father Victor said, “Celene has been a queen from ever since. I told her mother from the beginning that Celene had what it takes.”

The coronation show started more than an hour late, and once it got going there was no turning back. The 33 contestants opened the show but they were quickly reduced to a top 20.

The ladies then moved into swimwear before the top 14 were announced.

The evening gown competition resulted in the final six spots being filled.

After being interviewed, the final three were revealed to be Kadejah Anderson, Celene Hall, and Tianna McDaniel.

Hall won the Essence of Style Award, Best in Swimwear, Best in Evening Gown, Most Aware, and the Altruism Award.

Tianna McDaniel was adjudged Most Photogenic; Andrea Hill – Most Congenial; Marcie Lee Smith – Best Personality; Alanda Newman – Runway Star Award; and Marsha Roberts, Alanda Newman and Channon Smith made a three-way tie for Spirit of the Pageant award.

At the end of the night second runner-up was determined to be Anderson, while McDaniel, a medical practitioner, finished in the first runner-up position, as Hall snagged first place.

World.title: ‘Cricket isn’t dead!’
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen opener Kirk McKenzie hits the ball during the Caribbean Premier League T20 match against Trinbago Knight Riders at Sabina Park in Kingston on August 15, 2026.

JAMAICA Cricket Association President Dr Donovan Bennett believes the Jamaica Kingsmen have already made a strong impression on the island is optimistic they can play a key role in developing grassroots cricket locally.

The Caribbean Premier League (CPL) returned to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019 as the new Jamaica franchise hosted four games which concluded last Tuesday.

Tens of thousands of Jamaicans turned out for the four matches against the Barbados Tridents, Trinbago Knight Riders, Guyana Amazon Warriors and St Kitts and Nevis Patriots with some of the Caribbean’s top players on display including the Kingsmen’s own Rovman Powell and Andre Russell as well as regional stars Nicholas Pooran, Shimron Hetmeyer and Sunil Narine.

It continued the trend of growing crowd interest shown by local fans following last summer’s series between the West Indies and Australia, as well as Sri Lanka’s visit in June.

Bennett believes the Kingsmen’s home leg is a good reflection of the state of cricket in Jamaica.

“I have heard many persons who are or were cricket fans saying that cricket is dead in Jamaica but what both the Sri Lanka tour and the CPL that followed have clearly said is that cricket is not dead in Jamaica,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“In fact, cricket is still one of the most popular sports in the country and that as long as the people are fed the right diet, they get what they want to see, they will come out and support us and it was clear to everybody from the crowds. It was a fantastic atmosphere, not just the numbers, but the participation because the crowds were a behind the team with almost every ball that was bowled. It was really something electric and really a pleasure to sit and observe.”

Although pleased with action on the pitch, Bennett says he was impressed by the Kingsmen’s early investment in youth cricket.

The team’s ownership sponsored the All-Grace Shield and All-Headley Cup exhibitions tournament in July, which saw some of the best high school cricketers from the urban and rural areas go head to head in a 50 over match and a T20 match over two days. The

Observer understands the Kingsmen handed over $3.1 million to the JCA to execute the matches.

“As I made a presentation to them, it was a yes and I can tell you, the amount that was literally given to us for the two games is a significant amount of money which comfortably put both games on,” Bennett said. “I think it is something that should encourage the schools to participate on a wider basis and for players to have something substantive to look forward to at the end of the season. It should be the responsibility of ISSA but in a situation where ISSA does not have an interest, then I think the JCA has got to take up the responsibility and get those games on a yearly basis.”

While happy with the progress the Kingsmen have made, Bennett wants them to do more to help develop the next generation of Jamaican cricketers.

“As soon as the CPL is concluded, hopefully we can sit down with the Kingsmen to discuss other development programmes because I am not one of those who sees development from above downwards. I think that is one of the problems with West Indies Cricket over the years is that a lot of money has been spent at the top and very little at the bottom,” he said.

“We have had initial discussions, we haven’t had any decisions as yet. But certainly things like our under-13 programme has got to be put on the table because we really want to do an extended, comprehensive under-13 programme. Every year, we need to have an Under-13 Jamaica team and then from that, we need to extract the best players out of that group every year and put them into a specialised, continuous programme so that in a couple of years’ time, we can have a large cadre of players who, from an early age, have been taught the right things, the right attitudes and also the seriousness at which they should take the cricket, both representing Jamaica and the West Indies.”

The Kingsmen, who have four games remaining in the league stage, are currently just outside the play-off spot in fifth on four points. They return to action on Thursday against the Patriots at Warner Park in St Kitts.

World.title: Before You Book: Questions You Should Ask Your Hotel Wedding Venue
World.content:
Finding a beautiful hotel venue is exciting. You can already picture the décor, the guests arriving, the food being served and everything coming together perfectly.

But before you sign the contract or pay that deposit, there are a few important conversations you need to have.

When planning a wedding at a hotel, what you don’t ask can sometimes cost you just as much as what you do. A venue may look perfect during a walkthrough, but the details behind the scenes — from additional fees and set-up times to catering restrictions and technology — can have a major impact on your event.

Here are some things you should know before saying yes to a hotel venue.

What Exactly Is Included in the Venue Cost?

Never assume that everything you see during your tour is included in the quoted price. You should also ask about taxes, service charges, overtime charges and any additional fees that may appear on the final bill. The goal isn’t simply to know the rental price; it’s to understand the true cost of hosting your event there.

Will the Space Really Work for Your Wedding?

Capacity is about more than the maximum number of people allowed in a room. A ballroom might accommodate 300 people theatre-style but significantly fewer once you add banquet tables, a stage, dance floor, buffet stations, décor and audiovisual equipment.

Explain exactly what you’re planning and ask the hotel how many guests the space can comfortably accommodate with your preferred layout.

Think Beyond the Start and End Time

Your invitation might say 6:00 pm, but your event begins long before the first guest arrives. Decorators, florists, entertainers, photographers and production teams may need several hours to prepare. Ask when vendors can access the venue, where they can load and unload, and how much time is allowed for breakdown afterward. If additional set-up or breakdown time comes at an extra cost, that’s something you want to know well in advance.

Understand the Food and Beverage Details



If the hotel provides catering, don’t stop at choosing a menu. Ask about food-and-beverage minimums, service styles, what’s included in the per-person price and how dietary requirements and allergies are handled. If you’re hoping to bring a special cake, outside caterer or another food or beverage item, confirm whether it’s permitted and whether additional fees apply.

These small details can have a surprisingly big impact on both your plans and your budget.

Ask About Vendors, Technology and Entertainment

If you already have a favourite decorator, DJ, photographer or production company, confirm that they’re allowed to work at the hotel. Some properties have preferred or exclusive vendors, while others may require outside suppliers to provide insurance or meet specific requirements.

Technology deserves the same attention. Ask what’s available for microphones, speakers, screens, projectors, lighting, electrical connections and Wi-Fi. And before planning candles, elaborate installations, confetti, hanging décor or late-night entertainment, ask about the hotel’s restrictions. There may be rules around open flames, wall or ceiling installations, amplified music and the time entertainment must end.

Consider the Guest Experience

Walk through the experience from your guests’ point of view. Where will they park? How easy is it to find the event space once they enter the hotel? Accessibility matters too. Ask about ramps, elevators, accessible restrooms and step-free access for guests who may need them.

A beautiful venue means very little if getting into it — or moving around it — is difficult for your guests.

What Happens When Plans Change?

Guest counts rarely remain exactly the same from the day you book until the day of your wedding. Find out when the final guaranteed number is due and what happens if attendance increases or decreases.

If your wedding booking includes overnight accommodation, discuss room blocks, booking deadlines and any commitments attached to those rooms.

You should also understand the hotel’s cancellation and rescheduling policies. Are there cancellation charges? And what happens if circumstances outside your control affect the event?

Is there a back-up location secured for you if you are outdoor and it rains?

These aren’t the most exciting questions to ask, but they’re some of the most important ones to have answered in writing.

Know Who Will Be Looking After You



The person who shows you the ballroom and prepares your proposal may not be the person managing your event on the day. Ask who your main contact will be throughout the planning process and who will be responsible for your function once event day arrives. Knowing exactly whom to call when you need an answer or something changes can make the planning process considerably easier.

And Finally, Ask the Question People Often Forget



After you’ve gone through everything on your list, ask your hotel representative: “Based on the type of event I’m planning, is there anything else you think I should know before I book?”

It’s a simple question, but an experienced event professional may immediately identify something you haven’t considered.

Before You Sign



Choosing a hotel event venue isn’t only about finding the prettiest ballroom or the most attractive package. You’re choosing a partner that will play a significant role in your guests’ experience.

The right venue shouldn’t just look good in photographs. It should have the space, team, policies and resources to help your event run smoothly — from the first vendor arriving for set-up to the final guest heading home.

Because when it comes to wedding planning, the questions you ask before you book can save you from the surprises you don’t want later.

World.title: 11 years after decriminalisation, ganja use complicating mental health care
World.content:
AI image of a young man smoking marijuana. (Adobe stock)

Eleven years after Jamaica decriminalised ganja, the use of the substance features heavily among patients presenting with psychosis and schizophrenia. While there is currently no data establishing whether use of the herb is causing or contributing to the mental health problems, its prevalence is complicating treatment.

This is against the background of data from the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) pointing to an increase in high-risk usage of cannabis and the potency of the substance in Jamaica, as well as an increase in admissions for psychosis and schizophrenia over the last decade.

“What we do know is that the majority of psychiatric admissions in our public hospitals are coming from psychosis or schizophrenia. And the majority of those persons do use cannabis. So, we can look at that relationship and see that it is strong,” said Director for Treatment Services at the NCDA, Dr Kristen Robinson Barrett.

Still, Robinson Barrett noted that there is little data specifically exploring cannabis-induced psychosis.

Psychiatrist at Bellevue Hospital, Dr Brian Kazaara concurred that cannabis use has a striking presence among patients presenting with mental issues, but suggested that the substance rarely causes psychotic disorders.

“We don’t have official studies performed at Bellevue Hospital regarding cannabis use among patients, but from a cursory observation I can safely say the vast majority of patients admitted to the hospital also use cannabis,” he said.

Kazaara, who previously worked at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), pointed to a survey carried out by UHWI that revealed that the majority of persons admitted to the institution’s psychiatric ward smoked cannabis.

“What studies show is that persons with common psychiatric conditions like major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders use cannabis far more frequently than persons who do not have mental illnesses,” he said.

Despite this, Kazaara explained, “Cannabis-induced psychosis is not the norm. It is rare. At Bellevue we very, very rarely see that diagnosis. I also worked at UHWI for seven years [and] rarely saw it, almost never.”

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug and can affect the way that people perceive the world, leading to relaxation, paranoia, or other effects.

“It binds to our cannabinoid receptors around our body, but particularly in our brain, and that’s how we get the effects. It tends to create effects as it relates to emotions and feelings,” Robinson Barrett said. “They might experience changes as it relates to their time perception, so things might feel slowed down… issues with their concentration, so their attention and their awareness, their reaction time will change.”

Kazaara cautions that cannabis use can muddle the treatment of mental health issues.

“Cannabis definitely complicates psychosis, because for persons who use cannabis, they are more likely to develop an earlier onset of psychosis. So it may happen earlier than if they didn’t use it. It makes symptoms worse. It makes it harder to treat,” he explained.

Jamaica has a strong culture of recreational cannabis use, and Research Analyst at the NCDA Uki Atkinson explained that while overall population use has not necessarily changed over the last decade following decriminalisation of the drug, the potential for high-risk use has.

She supported her assessment with results from the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) which was used during surveys in 2016 and 2023.

“We were able to compare the levels of high-risk use from 2016 to 2023. In 2016, 50 per cent of the people who used cannabis in the past year were deemed to be at high risk for misusing it,” Atkinson said, noting “this has increased by 16 per cent in 2023. So, it shows not necessarily that more people are using ganja… But there’s a significant increase in high-risk patterns of use.”

In addition to high-risk usage, the potency of cannabis being consumed in Jamaica is also a concern.

According to a European study, using high-potency cannabis with a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration over 10 percent, significantly increases the risk of developing psychotic symptoms or disorders, especially with daily use.

Robinson Barrett expressed serious concern about current potency trends worldwide compared to a potency of around four per cent in the 1990s.

“As of 2024, we’re looking at potencies of 15 to 20 per cent,” Robinson Barrett indicated.

“The potency trends of cannabis in Jamaica measured between 2014 and 2020, were showing that over that decade, the cannabis potency would have moved from about one per cent to over 10 per cent across 12 parishes,” she continued. “So, we’re concerned… because we have a culture of heavy use in young age groups…it’s a very concerning picture as it relates to all young people and any other vulnerable group.”

Outside of general risks, Robinson Barrett noted that there are some who may be particularly susceptible to the effects of cannabis use, including youth.

“Generally speaking, the earlier the age of onset for any substance is going to increase your risk for addiction, and it’s going to increase your risk for its effects…for the cannabis, we’re looking at increased risk for development of psychosis, increased risk for cognitive impairment,” Robinson Barrett said.

She also highlighted people who are genetically vulnerable, or have a family history of mental illness as well as heavy users who smoke regularly.

While cannabis has many cannabinoids, Robinson Barrett explained that the main ones are Delta-9-THC, which most people know as a psychoactive component, and CBD, which can have a calming or relaxing effect.

Kazaara agreed that cannabis misuse can complicate mental health treatment.

“Yes, it does. Cannabis complicates the treatment of psychiatric conditions. For example, in the case of schizophrenia, it can worsen symptoms and also make the medication we use for it, less effective,” he explained.

In the meantime, Atkinson stressed that the NCDA was not demonising cannabis, highlighting the medicinal benefits and scope for a medicinal industry.

“We recognise the value, but we see the downside in our clients and in some of the young people who we have to treat,” she explained.

She urged that use must be balanced with ensuring that the population, especially youth and those with a predisposition to mental illness, understand the risk of use, particularly in a problematic manner.

World.title: Honorary consul to Atlanta Elaine Grant-Bryan ‘humbled’ by OD recognition
World.content:
Elaine Grant-Bryan

When Elaine Grant-Bryan settled in Atlanta in 1990, that city was long acknowledged as the mecca of black empowerment in the United States. She joined a growing Jamaican community which has made an impact in commerce and community politics.

Grant-Bryan has been Jamaica’s honorary consul to Atlanta since 2018. Currently in her third term, she has been awarded the Order of Distinction (Officer class) by the Jamaican government for service to the diaspora.

That award will be presented during the National Honours and Awards ceremony on October 19 at King’s House in Kingston.

In an interview with Observer Online, Grant-Bryan spoke of being “deeply humbled” by recognition of her work. Like New York City and South Florida, she said Jamaicans have made their mark in Atlanta and neighbouring areas such as Decatur and Stone Mountain.

“This region has grown significantly, especially after COVID-19 as Jamaicans moved from colder regions in the United States in great numbers. Our community has doubled, and many have successfully assimilated in the Georgia culture and made significant contributions to Jamaica and this region,” Grant-Bryan stated.

An educator and real estate broker, she points to initiatives started with her husband Gregory as major achievements of her tenure. These include the Elaine Bryan Foundation which drives the Jamaican Pioneer Programme and STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics).

The pioneer programme allows Americans of Jamaican heritage to gain citizenship in their family’s homeland. Once that is secured, they increase their contribution to Jamaica’s education system by mentoring and assisting needy students.

STEAM is an enrichment curriculum she developed with her husband, a programmer and Information Technology expert. It teaches coding/programming and offers career assessments, internships, entrepreneurships, and scholarships to Jamaican students completing degrees in STEAM fields.

Empowerment was a buzz word in Elaine Bryan’s home in Kingston, where she was born to a father who was an engineer and her mother, a nurse. A past student of Excelsior and Kingston Technical high schools, she was head girl at the latter.

Staying true to her profession, education is the thrust of upcoming projects by the Elaine Bryan Foundation.

“We will continue to include additional students who are completing degrees in the STEAM fields in Jamaica. The projection for 2026-7 is to extend mentorship programmes in Jamaica, study abroad and exchange programmes,” she disclosed.

World.title: ‘Long overdue’
World.content:
Minister of National Security and Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang and Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange are all smiles as they receive the keys to the third Government-run shelter for women facing domestic abuse. (Photo: JIS)

LOCAL gender advocates have welcomed news that work has been completed on a third shelter for victims of domestic abuse.

Minister with responsibility for gender affairs Olivia Grange made the announcement last Friday as she toured the facility at an undisclosed location.

“We made a commitment that we would establish three centres, safe spaces for women, and we have achieved that,” said Grange as she pointed out that prior to the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration there were no State-run shelters for women wishing to leave violent relationships.

In the last few years the Government completed, and is operating, two shelters for women. Grange said the addition of the third shelter will enable the ministry to offer up to 70 safe spaces for women and their children.

Grange said the completion of this third shelter, which is scheduled to begin providing a safe space for women after September 1, enables the Government to provide much-needed services to vulnerable females across the entire island.

“The completion of this space advances the gender agenda, because what we have been able to do now is to provide the spaces across the island, and we are now better equipped that when we get the call we are able to activate the kind of network that is necessary to move [women in abusive situations] into safe spaces,” said Grange.

On Sunday, gender and development practitioner Judith Wedderburn told the Jamaica Observer that the new shelter was long overdue.

“It is certainly very welcome because, not only from my experience but from the reports of women who do suffer, they have been beaten by a male partner and have experienced gender-based violence. The data does show us that it’s not getting better. More and more reports are coming out that it is happening,” said Wedderburn

According to Wedderburn, she became aware of plans to construct the new shelter through discussions with officials of the Bureau of Gender Affairs, however she was uncertain of the completion time.

“I am acknowledging that I have been in meetings in the last couple months where it was reported by somebody from the bureau that a third shelter was going to be built in a different part of the island, outside of Kingston. My understanding was it was going to serve the western part of the island,” said Wedderburn.

Pointing to a recent article published by the Jamaica Gleaner headlined, ‘The cop who finally listened’, Wedderburn said the presence of another shelter in the country serves as a call to action.

“Two women who recounted years of fear after ending abusive relationships are grateful to a corporal for standing with them. What it said was the woman who had been so badly abused was paying tribute to the only policeman who took her report seriously, the only policeman that supported her. And if you reflect on not just this article but other reports, on many occasions, unfortunately, a woman will not gather up the strength to go to a police station to report the incident,” Wedderburn argued.

Welcoming the initiative Joy Crawford, co-founder and executive director of female support group Eve for Life, told the Observer that the move strengthens the national response to gender-based violence (GBV) and expands access to safety for women and children leaving abusive situations.

“We recommend convening a robust, national GBV shelter working group comprising Government, NGOs, community-based organisations and other stakeholders to improve coordination, effectiveness, and accountability across the shelter system. This should include deliberate efforts to strengthen and expand non-government shelter models, recognising that Government cannot do this alone,” said Crawford.

She told the Observer that the country needs more diverse, accessible safe spaces across the island for survivors with different needs, including women with children, women with complex needs, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

“NGOs and community organisations play vital roles in victim identification, referral, psychosocial support, and sustained engagement. Formal referral pathways and partnerships can help survivors access appropriate services and safe accommodation earlier,” added Crawford.

For advocacy officer at Jamaica Coalition for a Healthy Society Philippa Davies, the provision of a third shelter by the Government is a commendable initiative but it is unfortunate that the problem of GBV exists.

“It is always better that society encourages, teaches, and supports healthy, safe relationships between men and women. As such, the family is the fundamental foundational institution of any society. The very real need for such places is evidence of family pathology, which is often passed on through generations,” said Davies.

She argued that the Government needs to establish a Ministry of the Family to address the critical role of the family and the need to prioritise its welfare.

“This would include strongly encouraging women and men to exercise discernment when choosing romantic and life partners, and to seek wise advice before and when challenges arise. It is scientifically established that the brain hormones released during sex bonds partners to the point of overshadowing danger signals such as the potential for or the occurrence of abuse,” added Davies who argued that the Government should also consider providing support for men who may be victims of abuse.

In announcing the completion of the new facility Grange said the Government-run shelters not only provide safety but also provide a therapeutic environment for women to rebuild their lives.

“We not only ensure that we protect them, but we help them to gain skills where they don’t have skills, we provide counselling, we have adequate space that we can facilitate a family — mother and children,” said Grange.

She revealed that during the last few years, one shelter hosted a mother and five of her children, while another mother gave birth while residing at another shelter.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang, acting in his capacity as chairman of the Citizens Business Group — a Government team that is mandated to manage social interventions across the country — said the establishment of Government-run shelters for women has been a big part of a programme to seek to impact, in a positive way, a number of vulnerable communities in Jamaica and, in particular in this case, women who have suffered abuse.

Chang noted that in the past few years the ministry has established domestic violence intervention centres at selected police stations as part of the strategy to eliminate domestic violence.

World.title: Costa tours the capitals — while Merz rallies the penny-pinchers
World.content:
António Costa is kicking off a tour of EU capitals to find out what leaders want from the bloc’s next seven-year budget — and what they might accept in return for a deal. His first stop is Bratislava, with Slovakia among the countries pushing to protect cohesion and agricultural funding. Later this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will gather like-minded northern countries in Berlin to argue for a much leaner budget and major cuts to the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal. Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart look at the competing campaigns as negotiations head into a crucial period.

Next, an argument inside Europe’s socialist family over Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and her cooperation with Giorgia Meloni on migration has raised questions about whether the tensions could spill into the Socialists & Democrats group in the European Parliament.

Plus: Greece is trying to turn the buzz around Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey into tourist money. With parts of the film shot in the Peloponnese, regional authorities are building an “Odyssey Route” — hoping the movie can leave the kind of lasting tourism legacy Mamma Mia! did on Skopelos.
