World.title: From 10% to 100%: Aviation ministry weighs annual dope tests for all pilots
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The aviation ministry is considering mandating dope tests for all pilots at least once a year, civil aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu Kinjarapu said on Tuesday.

The current rules require dope testing of 10 per cent of the overall pilot network, but the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is examining whether testing can be expanded to cover every pilot at a random time during the year.

âThere are multiple ways of approaching this dope test. Right now, the rule says 10% across the overall pilot network. DGCA is engaging, and one of the opinions from our side is that everyone has to go through it in the year at a random time,â Naidu told reporters.

The minister added the government would need to balance aviation safety with the operational impact of implementing 100 per cent testing.

âWe have to see how all the stakeholders are going to respond to this because one is the safety aspect of it, and the second thing is the operational impact, which also has to be taken into consideration,â he said.

Meanwhile, addressing the recent Delhi-Phuket flight incident, Naidu said the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) is investigating the incident and a preliminary report is expected soon.

The minister said the flight data recorder and the aircraft are intact and in the possession of the investigating agency, which would help in the probe.

âAAIB is presently taking up the investigation. Because everything is intact, the flight data recorder and everything is intact, and the plane is also in their possession, I believe that we can expect a preliminary report very early from now,â he said.





Naidu also said the DGCA is holding consultations with stakeholders on existing regulations concerning substance use and ways to strengthen the policy.

âMore importantly, in terms of substance use and everything, DGCA is also having stakeholder consultations right now on what the regulation says today and how we ensure there is a strict policy around this in the future as well. So, this consultation is going on right now,â he said.

The AAIB is examining the circumstances surrounding the incident, while the DGCA consultations are focused on reviewing existing regulations and strengthening safeguards related to substance use in aviation.

The development comes after Air India flight AI2379, operating from Phuket to Delhi on August 4, experienced a sudden 300-foot altitude drop over Odisha, leaving 20 passengers and four cabin crew members injured.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The Airbus A320, bearing registration VT-EXO, subsequently stabilised and landed safely in Delhi. The aircraft was carrying 137 passengers, including three infants, and eight crew members, comprising two pilots and six cabin crew.

A purported post-flight maintenance report has also revealed a series of technical warnings involving the aircraftâs hydraulic systems, flight controls and autopilot during the journey.

The report lists repeated low-pressure alerts across the green, blue and yellow hydraulic systems, along with low fluid levels in the yellow and blue reservoirs. Autopilot disconnections were also recorded twice.

World.title: ‘Grain’ revolution: How lost varieties of rice are coming back
World.content:
Biryani made with Kaima instead of Basmati, payesh made with Badshahbhog, risotto made with Assamâs Bora. With heirloom rice vanishing from Indian kitchens faster than they could be documented, this seemed, until not very long ago, nothing more than nostalgia.

The Green Revolutionâs push for high-yield monoculture had, over the years, pushed out many old types of rice. But now, several of those varieties, thought long gone, are staging a comeback â thanks to the efforts of farmers, conservationists, NGOs, restaurateurs, and a bit of help from some state govts.

Guardians of the grain

In coastal Karnatakaâs Nettanige village, Padma Shri awardee Sathyanarayana Beleri â everyone calls him âSeeding Sathyaâ â nurtures more than 100 traditional paddy varieties in grow bags outside his house.

Itâs a small selection from his vast collection of over 650 seed varieties, collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.

He has strains of flood-resistant Edekunhi and Nereguli, the medicinal Dodda Byra Nellu, and Kalanamak (also called âBuddha Riceâ). Heâs distributed seeds to hundreds of farmers across Karnataka and Kerala, as well as to agricultural universities nationwide. âRiceâ, he says, âcan be cultivated in grow bags, just like vegetables at home.





As climate change reshapes agriculture, conserving traditional, climate-resilient varieties is no longer a choice.

It is a necessity.â

Sathyanarayana Beleri with some of the more than 650 seed varieties he has collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.

Further inland, entire families have turned conservation into a generational commitment. In Belthangady taluk, the Rao family has conserved 180-190 traditional varieties on 5.5 acres since B K Deva Rao started a seed bank in 1988. His son, Parameshwar Rao, points to a benefit beyond biodiversity.

âPaddy cultivation is among the best forms of groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting,â he says. âStrong field bunds can retain water for nearly a week.

Even two cropping cycles can substantially improve the groundwater table.â Their prized variety, Kayame â a red rice â âhas a flavour rarely found in modern commercial varieties,â he adds.

Some 1,300km away in Chhattisgarh, Khemlal Dewangan, a maths teacher in Rajnandgaon district, started farming traditional paddy around 15 years ago.

Dewangan started with a handful of desi strains. He now has a collection of around 70 varieties.

His seed collection has grown through a nationwide network of farmers â brought together on WhatsApp â who test small quantities in their fields. âI now receive 10-15 enquiries a day from social media and word of mouth,â he says.

For him, the appeal goes beyond the market: he says traditional varieties are healthier, as they take longer to mature, absorbing more soil nutrients.

Roots of a revival

None of this happened by accident. Back in 2004, the UNâs second International Year of Rice, Kerala-based NGO Thanal decided something had to be done about Indiaâs vanishing rice varieties. They launched the Save Our Rice campaign through a workshop in Kumbalangi village. Thanal teamed up with Tamil Naduâs CREATE (a non-profit organisation) to run it, and the campaign took root in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Bengal, later spreading into Chhattisgarh.

Members of CREATE educate farmers about heirloom rice varieties on a farm in Tamil Nadu.

India had over one lakh varieties of rice in 1966, but by the time the campaign started, that number had dropped to around 30,000 â most locked away in university seed banks, rather than growing in farmersâ fields. The campaign has had a big impact on southern states. âIn the last 15-16 years, there has been a revival of traditional seeds in these states,â says Jayakumar C, executive director at Thanal. âToday, there are more than 25 or 30 farmers or groups doing traditional seeds in different parts of Kerala.

Thanalâs own centre in Wayanad now holds around 320- 330 varieties of rice.â

That demand has started showing up in the market. Thanal runs a regular shop now in Thiruvananthapuram. Jayakumar says Kaima (also called Jeerakasala or Jeeraga Samba), a traditional variety, has become popular for biryani. Brands have caught on, too. Thondi, from a Wayanad farmer-producer company, sells online and via courier across Keralaâs cities, even as Mappila Chamba has built a following.

âTraditional rice tends to be more filling,â says Jayakumar. You feel full after eating less, unlike white rice hybrids. Also, the longer shelf life and taste after cooking is winning over urban households, especially the older people.â

When state stepped in

In Tamil Nadu, govt push gave the revival momentum. According to Suresh Kanna, project director at CREATE Trust, state govt began promoting six native varieties some 10 years ago under the State Heritage Rice Mission: Mappillai Samba, Karuppu Kavuni, Thooyamalli, Poongar, Kaattuyaanam and Kichili Samba.

âToday, they are liked by consumers and can be seen in organic shops across the state. They also fetch good income for the farmers.

A Kavuni farmer can get up to Rs 200 for a kilo. My calculation is that more than one lakh farmers in the state are now cultivating traditional paddy varieties,â Kanna says.

Even in Karnataka, grassroots efforts are now finding institutional backing. KVK Dakshina Kannada has begun field trials of 10 traditional varieties sourced from Beleri, aiming to identify strains suited to the coastal region, and reintroduce them into local food systems.

Karnatakaâs agriculture department has documented 2,164 traditional landraces (local, traditional varieties that evolved through natural and human selection to adapt to a specific geographic and climatic environment) across 20 crops, with paddy topping the list at 1,469 varieties, under its Conservation and Promotion of Landraces Programme.

Rs 1.3 crore in incentives went to 490 farmers in 2025-26 for viable seed samples.

The effort centres on custodian farmers who âcontinued cultivating them on small patches of land,â as department director GT Puthra puts it.

The department is now supporting GI registration for varieties including Kagga paddy, Rajmudi paddy, Bijapur Jola, Joni Bella and Kumbi Mudli, and plans incentives for 15 âforgotten treasureâ shops.

Farm to fork, fork to fame

A few restaurants are actively championing rare, indigenous rice over commercial varieties.

Edible Archives in Goa works with regional grains like Thavala Kannan from Wayanad (a red rice from Palakkad, whose name means âfrogâs eyesâ in Malayalam), and Pokkali, which brings a distinct coastal terroir.

The Kolkata-based Amar Khamar, both a heritage-grain retail brand and restaurant, is entirely built around Bengalâs native rice. Its signature is âChhuti-r Bhatâ, an 11-course meal following the traditional sequence of a Bengali meal, centred on heirloom varieties like Sugondhi Chine Kamini Aatap.

âChhuti-r Bhatâ in Kolkataâs Amar Khamar, which is an 11-course meal centred on heirloom rice varieties.

That influence has spread to other restaurants in the city. Sienna Cafe sources Chine Kamini, Radha Tilok, Kanakchur and Tulaipanji Atop from Amar Khamar; Yokocho, a Japanese alleyway-inspired bar and BBQ, draws on Kanakchur, Tulaipanji Atop and Karpurkanti; Red Bari incorporates Shatia, Mallifulo and Khejur Chhari.

Juhi Punwani, head of kitchen operations at Amar Khamar, has built a career around collecting the many myths and stories behind Bengalâs native rice varieties.

âGobindobhog is not the only heritage rice in Bengal,â she says. A rice called Radhuni Pagol literally means âthe cook gone crazyâ, after lore that its fragrance once filled a kitchen so completely that the cook couldnât think of anything else.

Tulaipanji of North Bengal gets its name from how the cooked rice turns light and airy like cotton (tula); Khejur Chhari is named for the date palm its grains resemble; Radha Tilokâs dark-tipped grain evokes Radhaâs tilak mark.

âEvery rice here has a beautiful story and a journey, and thatâs what weâre trying to showcase,â says Punwani, whose team has worked to bring back over 100 varieties, keeping around 50 in active rotation.

A look at select traditional rice varieties and the regions they are associated with across India.

This past summer, that ambition crossed continents, as Amar Khamar toured France and Germany. In Paris, working with sommelier Rajat Parr, the team built an 80-guest, 10-course tasting menu entirely around rice.

Kanakchur turned up as fritters with brown butter hollandaise, Sundarbansgrown Karpurkanti and Chine Kamini appeared as aatapan alongside a jackfruit-seed mung dal, Barddhamanâs Mohansal was served boiled, the meal closing with a Jhargram Fine Black Rice phirni.

In Stuttgart, the team built a fully vegan Bengali tasting menu, rice carrying the meal from a humble jhal muri to a coconut-milk Badshahbhog payesh for dessert.

A separate 200-guest winery event tested whether the format could scale â from Karpurkanti-paired lentils, a Chine Kamini peas pulao to Sunday lamb curry and Badshahbhog milk-rice. âNone of this would be possible without the relationships we have built with a network of farmers,â says Punwani, who executed the menu in Europe.

The traceability problem

But as heritage rice travels from the farm into retail shelves, a different problem emerges: knowing whether whatâs being sold is really what it claims to be.

One store has built its entire business around solving exactly that. In Chennaiâs Mylapore sits a store unlike any other. Spirit of the Earth calls itself a âretail store and experience centreâ, where customers come to see, touch, feel and know the story of every rice.

Opened in 2017, itâs the retail face of a project that Sheela Balaji, chairperson of NGO AIM For Seva, began over a decade ago, built on a principle she believes the heritage-rice surge often misses: traceability.

âUnfortunately, certain grains are being sold as certain varieties, which is inaccurate,â says Balaji.

âThe minute you say heritage rice, people will just come and buy it. But who is taking accountability? How do you know if itâs really diabetic friendly? So, I started this project more than a decade ago, first and foremost by building a seed bank. All the rice that you see in our store is grown from our farm in Manjakkudi, a village in Tiruvarur.â

The 40-acre operation has grown as neighbouring farmers joined in, alongside a seed bank built from years of Balajiâs fieldwork with growers in Manipur, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.

For Balaji, the mission is beyond nutrition or nostalgia. âRice in our culture is Lakshmi,â she says. âAnd reintroducing its forgotten names and forms, one customer at a time, is as much about restoring that reverence as it is about the grain itself.â

World.title: 'Dog-barking' remark on students: Tejashwi says BPSC official 'mirrors CM's language'; demands removal
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Bihar leader of opposition and

leader

has demanded an apology from BPSC examination controller Rajesh Kumar over his "dog-barking" remark against protesting students.

While RJD scion also took a sharp dig at chief minister Samrat Choudhary, alleging official's language "mirrors the CM's language.

"

Tejashwi said immediate action should be taken against the official, warning that such comments could set a wrong precedent in Bihar and encourage officials to speak disrespectfully to students and the public.

Speaking to news agency ANI, Tejashwi criticised the Bihar government over the ongoing protests linked to the 70th BPSC examination.

He said the examination controllerâs remarks reflected the âlanguage of the chief ministerâ.

âThis official should be removed immediately and made to apologise,â Tejashwi said. He alleged that students and young people were being ignored and that repeated exam-related controversies had not led to anyone being held accountable.

Tejashwi also accused the government of failing to fix responsibility for repeated cancellations, alleged paper leaks and irregularities in competitive examinations.





'Elephant walks, dogs bark'

Responding to questions, Kumar reportedly said: âHaathi chale bazaar, kutta bhaunke hazaarâ - meaning, âAn elephant walks through the market while a thousand dogs bark.â

The remark angered protesting students, who raised slogans against the official and intensified their criticism of the commission.

Students have been protesting at Patna's Gardanibagh over the 70th BPSC examination, demanding its cancellation over alleged irregularities and paper leaks.

Their protest has also focused on the proposed Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 (TRE-4). Students are opposing the plan to hold the examination in two phases across Bihar and are demanding that the official TRE-4 notification be released.

World.title: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay flags off 250 new buses for MTC, TNSTC
World.content:
Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay flagged off 250 new buses for the Metropolitan Transport Corporation (MTC) and Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation (TNSTC), procured at a cost of ₹290.8 crore, at the Secretariat in Chennai on Tuesday (August 25, 2026).

According to an official release, with the objective of reducing environmental pollution in Chennai, 625 low-floor electric buses, procured at a cost of ₹697 crore, are currently being operated through five depots of the MTC. Further, the State government has planned to procure 750 new low-floor air-conditioned electric buses at a cost of ₹1,337 crore. As the first phase of the initiative, Mr. Vijay flagged off 130 new low-floor air-conditioned electric buses at a cost of ₹234.50 crore.

Similarly, the TNSTC has planned to introduce 1,614 new buses at an estimated cost of ₹756 crore. As the first phase of the initiative, 120 new buses at a cost of ₹55.58 crore were flagged off by the Chief Minister, the release said.

#TamilNadu Chief Minister C. Joseph #Vijay flags off new MTC and SETC bases at the Secretariat in #Chennai on Tuesday.



Photo: B. Jothi Ramalingam (@bkjothi) pic.twitter.com/CaKP4v9jOv — The Hindu - Chennai (@THChennai) August 25, 2026

During the event, Mr. Vijay also boarded a low-floor air-conditioned electric bus and inspected the facilities in the vehicle. Minister for Transport A. Vijay Tamilan Parthiban, Chief Secretary M. Sai Kumar, Transport Secretary L. Nirmal Raj, MTC Managing Director D. Mohan, and senior officials were present.

World.title: Video showing Karnataka BJP MLA’s daughter slapping woman police official at temple goes viral
World.content:
Days after BJP MLA Suresh Gowda’s daughter Aishwarya was booked for allegedly assaulting Police Sub-Inspector Savitha B. Patil at a temple in Srirangapatna taluk of Mandya district, a video purportedly showing the MLA’s daughter slapping the woman police officer has gone viral.

The video, apparently from a CCTV camera, shows Ms. Aishwarya slapping Ms. Savitha, who is standing next to her at the temple, prompting an immediate response from the officer, who strikes back.

An argument had broken out between the MLA’s daughter and the police officer over the former’s attempt to enter the temple’s sanctum sanctorum. Soon after the exchange turned physical, bystanders stepped in and separated the two.

Karnataka MLA's daughter slaps female cop

Complaint and counter-complaint

A police official at the jurisdictional Kyathanahalli police station in Srirangapatna told The Hindu that an FIR has been registered against Aishwarya, daughter of Tumkur Rural MLA Suresh Gowda, based on a complaint filed by Ms. Patil.

Though a counter-complaint has also been lodged by Aishwarya, police said they are still examining it. As of now, only one FIR — based on the complaint filed by the police officer on duty — has been registered, a police official said.

Sources said the incident occurred on August 12 during Bhimana Amavasya rituals at the Aarti Ukkada Temple in Srirangapatna taluk. Ms Aishwarya, who arrived at the temple, objected to Ms Patil — who is attached to the Mandya Women’s Police Station and was posted at the temple — blocking her entry into the temple.

In her complaint, Ms. Patil said Aishwarya verbally abused and slapped her while she was carrying out her duties. Aishwarya, who is also married to a police officer, has been booked under various sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita (BNS).

World.title: Andhra Pradesh special TET for in-service teachers from October 11, results on November 15
World.content:
The Andhra Pradesh School Education Department has issued a notification for conducting a special Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) for in-service teachers in the State, in accordance with the directions of the Supreme Court.

As per the notification, teachers who were appointed before 2011 and are currently working as teachers are required to qualify in the TET.

The special TET is being conducted for in-service teachers working in schools under various government managements, including government and local body schools, AP Residential Educational Institutions Society (APREIS), residential schools, welfare residential schools, AP Model Schools, private aided and other government schools.

AP Special TET convenor M. Venkata Krishna Reddy issued the notification on August 24, 2026, which, along with the information bulletin and syllabus, has been made available on the official School Education Department website.

Candidates can pay the examination fee and submit their applications online from August 25 to September 24, 2026. Hall tickets will be available for download from October 5. The Special TET examinations will be conducted from October 11 to 21, 2026, in morning and afternoon sessions through the computer-based test (CBT) mode.

The initial answer key will be released on October 24, with candidates allowed to submit objections from October 25 to November 1.

The final key will be released on November 10, followed by the declaration of the final results on November 15. The department has also set up a help desk at the Director of School Education’s office to address candidates’ queries, which will function on all working days from 10 a.m. to 5.30 p.m. Candidates can contact the help desk at 8121947387, 7995649286 and 6281704160.

World.title: Rahul Gandhi, Kharge write letter to PM Modi; asks for current census questionnaire to be cancelled
World.content:
Congress leaders Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) over the caste census issue.

The letter said the government has opted for open-ended question format to record caste details in census, which is misleading. The letter further asked for the current questionnaire to be cancelled.

In a post on X, the Congress leaders said, “Your govt has opted for open-ended question format to record caste details in census, which is misleading”.

Briefing reporters on the letter written in Hindi by Kharge and Gandhi on August 20, Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the government’s current efforts towards a caste census are just a “whitewash”.

Mr. Kharge’s post further said, “It is not possible to accurately count castes through open-ended questions. If the same caste is recorded under different names and sub-castes, the data will be scattered, and the biggest loss will be to OBCs, most backward, and deprived communities. Our demand is clear - the current questionnaire should be canceled, a new questionnaire should be prepared based on a verified list of castes, and extensive consultation should be done with political parties, experts, and the public.”

Like the caste surveys in Telangana and Bihar, conducting the count based on a pre-prepared and verified caste list is its practical solution, Mr. Kharge added. “The caste census should not only be done, it should also be done correctly.”

World.title: Keralam’s SOP for euthanasia of rabid, dangerous stray dogs | Explained
World.content:
The story so far: The Keralam government on Saturday (August 22, 2026) approved standard operating procedures (SOP) for the euthanasia of rabid, incurably ill or demonstrably dangerous stray dogs, following a Supreme Court order in May this year allowing euthanasia in such cases.

Following an alarming increase in stray dog bite cases and deaths due to rabies, the State government in July 2025 allowed local bodies to carry out euthanasia of diseased or dangerous stray dogs by making use of the provisions of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Animal Husbandry Practices and Procedures) Rules, 2023. However, the Kerala High Court soon deferred the implementation of the order. Since then, there have been occasional demands from various quarters for decisive action to control stray dog bites, while animal rights activists have argued against drastic action such as euthanasia.

What led to the framing of the SOP?

In 2025, Keralam reported a total of 3.69 lakh dog bites, compared with 3.17 lakh dog bites in 2024. A total of 33 people succumbed to rabies in the State in 2025, while the number of rabies-related deaths in 2024 was 26. Though the Animal Birth Control (ABC) programme is being carried out across most local bodies in the State, the pace of sterilisation of stray dogs has not kept up with the increase in their population. For instance, the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation sterilises an average of 1,200 stray dogs annually, while the ideal number required is 4,000-5,000 sterilisations to control the rising stray dog population.

What did the Supreme Court say?

The SOP, now approved, relies on the Supreme Court’s order of May 19, 2026, allowing euthanasia in cases involving rabid, incurably ill or demonstrably dangerous stray dogs. The Supreme Court, while underscoring that when the safety and lives of human beings are weighed against the interests and welfare of sentient beings, the “constitutional balance” must necessarily tilt in favour of the preservation of human life, also permitted municipal authorities to adopt legally permissible measures, including euthanasia in cases involving “rabid, incurably ill or demonstrably dangerous or aggressive dogs”.

As per the relevant portions of the Supreme Court judgment quoted in the SOP, “In areas where the population of stray dogs has assumed alarming proportions and where incidents of dog bites or aggressive attacks have become frequent and pose a continuing threat to public safety, the authorities concerned may, subject to due assessment by qualified veterinary experts and strictly in accordance with the provisions of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023 and other applicable statutory protocols, take such measures as may be legally permissible, including euthanasia, in cases involving rabid, incurably ill or demonstrably aggressive dogs, so as to effectively curb the threat posed to human life and safety.”

How will euthanasia be carried out? What are the safeguards?

A stray dog management committee, which will be formed in every local body, will bear the responsibility of deciding whether euthanasia has to be carried out in a particular case. The stray dog management committee, which will have the local body chairperson as its head and the secretary as the convener, will include the respective ward councillor, veterinary officer and medical officer of the local body, Animal Birth Control (ABC) centre project-in-charge officer and a representative of the Animal Welfare Board.

The procedure for euthanasia should be carried out by a qualified veterinary surgeon. Only sodium pentobarbital or thiopental sodium should be administered intravenously. Other chemicals or methods that could cause pain should not be used. All local bodies will have to maintain a separate register to record cases of euthanasia of stray dogs. The register will have information about each such dog, including the area from which it was caught, photographs and the exact reasons for deciding on euthanasia.

The dogs caught for euthanasia have to be kept for two to three days in the local body’s isolation kennels or an ABC centre. During this period, approved agencies or animal lovers who are willing to take care of the dog can claim responsibility for it. The euthanasia should not be carried out in the presence of other dogs.

The SOP cites the apex court ruling regarding legal protection for the officers carrying out the procedure. As per the ruling, the officials are “entitled to due protection for acts performed by them in good faith and in bona fide discharge of their official duties and compliances carried out pursuant to the present order and the earlier orders passed by the Court. Accordingly, no First Information Report, criminal complaint or coercive proceedings should be initiated against such officials”.

World.title: School bus overturns in Regidi mandal, 15 children injured
World.content:
As many as 15 school children received injuries when a school bus overturned near Tunivada village of Regidi mandal of Rajam Assembly constituency limits on the morning of Tuesday (August 25, 2026).

According to police, the bus belonging to Tamminaidu schools of Palakonda, overturned in the paddy fields while travelling on a narrow road which had been damaged due to rains. The driver had failed to control the bus and it led to the accident.

The school children who received injuries were admitted to government hospital of Rajam immediately. Other children are safe were sent to their homes after the incident. The incident shocked parents and family members who rushed to the hospital to the see their children. Collector S. Ramsundar Reddy and Rajam MLA Kondru Muralimohan inquired about the incident and directed the doctors to take extra for their quick recovery.

World.content:
August marks Children’s Eye Health and Safety Month, with a focus on childhood vision and myopia. Against this backdrop, The Hindu is holding a webinar, free for all, on Sunday, August 30, 2026.

The webinar will focus on refractive errors in children, particularly the growing concern over myopia, and examine whether increasing screen exposure and reduced time spent outdoors are contributing to changes in children’s vision. The discussion will also look at early warning signs, the importance of timely eye screening, and measures that can help prevent or slow the progression of myopia.

The session will be moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, senior reporter, The Hindu.

The webinar will run from 11.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.

World.title: Trump plans to impose over $100,000 fee for H-1B visas: How will it impact Indians
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Monday (August 24, 2026) released a proposed regulation to codify an unprecedented fee of more than $100,000 on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers.

The fee, first temporarily imposed by Mr. Trump in 2025, dramatically raises the cost of visas that are heavily relied on in the tech, education and research sectors, spelling bad news for Indian techies and students who aspire to work/study in the U.S.

What is H1-B visa programme?

The H-1B programme allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers with training in specialty fields. It offers 65,000 visas annually, with another 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees, approved for three to six years.

Mr. Trump, a Republican, and other critics of the H-1B program say it is abused by many companies who replace American workers with cheaper foreign labor. But business groups and many individual companies have said the visa program is needed to address a lack of qualified American workers for some jobs and to allow U.S. businesses to recruit top talent.

About 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications as ‌of late ⁠February, according to court filings, the Reuters reported

How will H1-B visa fee hike impact Indians

Those visas typically came with fees between $2,000 and $5,000 before the U.S. President’s order. The proposed rule by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, posted in the Federal Register on August 24, would make a ⁠fee of $103,265 permanent. It could be finalised by the end of the year.

Indians account for the largest share of H-1B visa holders, making up 71% of all beneficiaries in FY2024. This move will significantly impact Indian technology workers who are hired by tech companies and others on H-1B visas.

The Hindu had earlier reported that a $100,000 surcharge would, in a majority of cases match or even exceed the yearly salaries earned by Indian H-1B workers. Since Indian professionals typically report lower median wages than their peers from other countries, they are likely to be hit the hardest, both in absolute numbers and as a share of total workers.

Who are exempted from fee hike

But the fee would not apply to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, or to renewals of current visas.

Fee hike faces legal challenges

The fee hike is being challenged by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the largest U.S. business lobbying group, Democratic-led states and a coalition of unions and employers. Those lawsuits could be amended to challenge the rule proposed this week once it is finalized.

A federal judge in June 2026 ruled that the fee was unlawful and blocked the Trump administration from collecting it, much to the relief of Indian diaspora. A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing that decision while a different court considers whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by a major business group.

Amid Mr. Trump’s broader immigration crackdown, employers last year registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas, down more than 25% from 2024 and fewer than half of the 794,000 visas sought in 2023, according to data, opens new tab from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The Trump administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new ⁠visa selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers. Earlier in August, the Department of Homeland Security in a separate rule added fees of up to $4,500, opens new tab to applications to extend the stay of H-1B workers or to transfer employees based in other countries to the United States.

The U.S. administration move is aimed at protecting American workers while ensuring that companies have a pathway to hire “truly extraordinary people” and bring them to the United States.

(With inputs from Reuters)

World.title: Imran's hospital transfer: SC returns contempt plea filed by PTI founder's sister

ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court office on Tuesday returned the contempt plea filed by the sister of PTI founder Imran Khan, Dr Uzma Khan, against the violation of the court’s August 18 orders, which had directed the ex-premier’s transfer to a private hospital.
