World.title: 'Significant' fencing safety issues at pool where toddler drowned, inquest hears
World.content:
It is likely a backyard swimming pool where a toddler drowned was never required to be subject to an application for an approval, a coronial inquest has heard.

South Australia Deputy State Coroner Emma Roper is investigating the death of a 19-month-old boy after he drowned in the pool at his family's rented home in Salisbury, in Adelaide's north in November 2022.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

In his opening address, counsel assisting the coroner Darren Evans said on the day of the drowning, the boy — whose name has been suppressed — was with his mother, as well as his four siblings who he had been asking to go outside with him.

Mr Evans said it was about 5:20pm when the boy's siblings noticed he was missing.

"The family looked for him … his sister then found him floating in the swimming pool outside," he said.

Mr Evans said the girl found her brother near the pool's steps, before she "grabbed him by the hands and pulled him out".

"Their mother came and turned [the boy] upside down to drain water from his mouth," Mr Evans said.

"Neighbours heard a commotion and came over to assist, calling triple zero, and then commencing CPR with advice over the phone."

The pool gate was kept shut with a bicycle lock. (Supplied: SA Coroners Court)

The court heard when paramedics arrived, the boy had been moved onto the living room floor, and that after about 30 minutes "a return of spontaneous circulation was achieved".

He was taken to the Women's and Children's Hospital, but died seven days later, as a result of a severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy injury post cardiac arrest.

"There was no further treatment that could reverse the brain injury … it was identified that his condition was not compatible with life," Mr Evans told the court.

Ms Roper said the circumstances of the boy's death were "likely to have had and will continue to have a profound impact upon his siblings".

"It may be that it remains unknown who opened the pool gate on the day of his death, but it appears to be open at the time he's retrieved from the water," she said.

Faulty pool gate

The court heard when police attended the family's home, the boy's mother told officers the pool gate was "usually closed" and that she did not know how it came to be open or how her son got in.

It heard the top hinge on the pool gate was missing at the time, and there was a bicycle lock that had been put around it to keep it shut.

"[The boy's] father says that he noticed this was broken but did not raise it with the landlords, as he thought it was simple enough to fix himself with a new hinge," Mr Evans said.

Police commissioned a review of the pool by Salisbury Council pool inspector Jeff Shillabeer, who gave evidence that he found a number of "significant" issues with the safety of the fencing.

An inspector found several safety issues with the pool fencing. (Supplied: SA Coroners Court)

Mr Shillabeer said the "most notable" of those were the fact the gate did not close by itself, there was a gap greater than 10cm under the fence, and that there were climbable objects around the pool including a rabbit hutch and brick barbecue.

The court heard when he attended the property for a re-inspection in January 2023, all safety issues had been rectified by the property owners.

'Grand-fathered' safety compliance

The deputy coroner will consider whether improvements could be made to the regulation of older pools — particularly where the home is rented out — including whether the state government should implement a regular inspection regime, which is already in place in other states.

The court heard the pool was "likely" constructed prior to 1972, and therefore never required to be subject to an application for an approval or be entered onto the council's records.

Mr Evans said the requirement of pool fencing was only enforced under law after that time.

"The legislative regime continues to allow for grand-fathered safety compliance for pools installed in previous decades," Mr Evans said.

Mr Shillabeer said councils were only required to inspect a pool when a new one was built, and that there was no legislative requirement for an inspection after a transfer of sale.

He also told the court that, in his role as an inspector, he had carried out checks of pools following the death of a child at least five times.

The inquest continues.

World.title: 'She didn't care what anybody thought': Margaret Olley in five paintings
World.content:
In 1945, Margaret Olley — one of Australia's most celebrated painters — graduated from the National Art School, then known as East Sydney Technical College, with first-class honours.

Within two years the Lismore-born artist would win the first-ever Mosman Art Prize and join Sydney's post-war art scene, alongside artists like William Dobell, Sidney Nolan and Donald Friend.

During her life she would hold more than 90 solo exhibitions; influence artists like Cressida Campbell and Ben Quilty; establish a trust to buy paintings for public galleries; and be painted for an Archibald Prize-winning portrait not once, but twice.

Olley — who donated $30-40 million worth of her art to public galleries — pictured in her studio in 2005. (Getty Images: Patrick Riviere)

Now, she's being celebrated with a retrospective at her alma mater, titled Australia Intimiste. The intimism of the title refers to the late 19th-century art movement where artists like Pierre Bonnard and Édouard Vuillard painted intimate, domestic scenes from which Olley gathered much inspiration.

"She loved this place," curator Katrina Cashman says of the National Art School, where Olley began her career.

"She spent her whole life working towards the pursuit of beauty.

"She worked very diligently and worked very hard to maintain [her success]. She had her ups and downs. She had various health struggles over the years. She suffered from depression at times.

"But she was relentless in that pursuit of her primary passion: beauty."

Portrait in the mirror

Olley painted Portrait in the mirror in 1948 when she was just 25, living on Sydney's Lower North Shore with her friend and fellow artist Margaret Cilento.

Cashman says Portrait in the mirror shows Olley's "developing awareness of colour". (Supplied: AGNSW)

Cashman describes it as a turning point in Olley's career: "She's really establishing herself. She's recognising that she needs a space away from the National Art School to create her own work."

While she had graduated three years earlier, Olley was still a regular on campus, attending evening classes until the year she painted Portrait in the mirror.

That same year, Olley held her first solo exhibition, in Sydney, where both the Art Gallery of New South Wales and the National Gallery of Victoria purchased works.

"This painting is so special because it shows us who she is and who she's going to become," Cashman says.

Portrait in the mirror is one of many self-portraits of Olley.

"Her own image was something she could find solace in, and it expressed her interior world," Cashman says.

The dressing room table in the painting is adorned with flowers, fruit and postcards of famous works of art.

"[Portrait in the mirror is] the very beginning of her focusing on objects, on cherished items, and the classic still life study … but putting her own spin on [it]" Cashman says.

"She loved flowers as much as she loved people — they were a visual language in themselves … [And] she's surrounded her image with these beautiful pieces of art that she loves."

Spare bedroom

In 1970, Olley painted Spare bedroom in her family home of Farndon in Brisbane's West End.

"I love this work because it's actually a very rich interior," Cashman says.

In 1980, a decade after Olley painted Spare bedroom, Farndon was destroyed in a fire. (Supplied: Lismore Regional Gallery/Carl Warner)

The room depicted — in a "rusty sienna brown" — was a kind of side room, leading to a sunroom out the back.

"It's a painting of absence, but you get that feeling of presence," Cashman says.

"Even the way the chairs are positioned — you get that feeling somebody's just walked out of the room.

"You've got this beautiful, filtered light coming through from a window, presumably in the next room. You've got this feeling of spaciousness and air, like the space is well-ventilated, with a breeze flowing through it."

Cashman admires the simplicity of Spare bedroom, compared to some of Olley's more densely populated paintings.

"It has a lot to say about the idea of the intimate interior," Cashman says.

It's a style of painting unlike the abstract art or large-scale paintings that were fashionable at the time.

"Still life paintings were not de rigueur," Cashman explains.

"So, I think [Olley] was out of step in some ways with a certain part of the art sector who would not have considered this to be contemporary art with a capital C.

"But she persisted regardless. She didn't care what anybody thought of her work."

Kitchen still life

Olley would often paint in the evening with fellow artist David Strachan, who she met in the 40s.

"[Strachan] believed that the night-time was kind of pregnant with creative possibilities," Cashman explains. "There's something happening in the energy of the night."

After he died in 1970 in a car accident, she got permission from his sister to continue using his Sydney home as a studio, where, in 1976, she painted Kitchen still life.

Cashman says Olley's work asserts the domestic is "just as important as public space". (Supplied: NAS)

"It's a simple image," Cashman says. "We see the pots on the stove, the garlic, the onions, the kale, the salt and pepper, the accoutrements. We've got this beautiful dark blue panel at the back, which is the window to the evening sky outside."

Cashman likes the "strange feel" of the painting. "It's slightly menacing with the knife. They're about to cut up the onions or they're about to do the cooking, but there's something about the way that knife is placed."

The ingredients and utensils also seem to indicate there's a "person in that space" — a presence within an absence as in Spare bedroom.

"I just love the energy of this painting, knowing it's painted at night, the stillness, the quiet, that moody blue sky," Cashman says.

Homage to Manet

Often, Olley would replicate the paintings of famous artists in her work, including 1987's Homage to Manet.

The other figures in Manet's The Balcony are painter Jean Baptiste Antoine Guillemet and violinist Fanny Claus. (Supplied: AGNSW/Mim Stirling)

She painted a bowl of cherries and a jug of blue flowers in her kitchen, where she pinned a postcard of French artist Édouard Manet's 1868-9 painting The Balcony and a poster-size version of the work's seated figure: Berthe Morisot, a painter who married Manet's brother Eugene.

The Balcony itself was inspired by Spanish artist Francisco Goya's Majas on the Balcony.

"It's a self-consciously devotional act to include these works [in her art]," Cashman says.

"It's not a postmodern appropriation with any sense of irony. She's not poking fun. It very genuinely is an homage to these great painters that she knows and loves."

Cashman also admires the painting's "extraordinary" use of colour, "the richness of the patina, the focus on the female protagonist, and the focus on the delicacy of the flowers".

Incorporating famous artworks into her paintings was in some ways a means for Olley to work on her craft.

"Transcription is a part of art teaching," Cashman explains. "It's a deliberate thing to be able to transcribe another person's work and learn from it."

It was also simply a reflection of life. Olley's home was "completely strewn with images by other artists", Cashman says.

"Margaret was continually being replenished and refreshed by [other artists' work]."

The yellow room triptych

Olley continued to paint until the end of her life. She was preparing for an exhibition when she died in 2011, at the age of 88.

In her final years, she painted The yellow room triptych, a living room scene spanning 2.7 metres.

Olley died at her home in Paddington, which was once a hat factory. (Supplied: New England Regional Art Museum)

"She's choosing yellow as the colour to represent sunlight and the colour itself emits this sense of light," Cashman says.

It's that light the curator finds so compelling.

"The sunlight coming through the window is bouncing off that wall on the right-hand side and glimmering across the gold in the Chinese screen, and diffuse light is coming off those lemons.

"The energy and the mastery of colour is what makes [Olley] so special."

The yellow room triptych draws together much of Olley's practice, like the paintings by fellow artists, including Dance by French artist Henri Matisse; and the precious objects meticulously arranged beneath the window.

"We've still got that passage to the garden, just beyond, and that vibrancy of that green and the freshness of the light that's coming through and spilling onto the arrangement," Cashman says. "Then in the background she's got these very muted pinks and browns."

Like so many of Olley's still life paintings, the space also feels lived in — like someone has only just left the room.

"For me, that ripple in the fabric [of the curtains] suggests someone whose hand has just touched that," Cashman says.

Margaret Olley: Australian Intimiste is at the National Art School, Sydney, until October 24.

World.title: Mother stabbed, 10-year-old son punched in random attack outside police HQ
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaCrime Mother stabbed, 10-year-old son punched in random attack outside police HQ Alexander Darling and James Costa Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:02pm ,first published 3:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been arrested after allegedly punching a 10-year-old boy and repeatedly stabbing his mother with a pair of scissors in Melbourne’s CBD. Police said the random attack outside Victoria Police’s Spencer Street headquarters on Tuesday afternoon only ended when several passersby intervened. Police were on the scene quickly to arrest the man. Nine News Superintendent Zorka Dunstan said the woman’s two other children witnessed the violent assault. The family had been visiting the city from Phillip Island. “The man was walking south, and as he passed them, he randomly punched the 10-year-old then kept walking. He then turned around, grabbed mother in a headlock and started to stab her repeatedly with a pair of scissors,” Dunstan said.



Dunstan said she learnt of the incident while she was in her office upstairs and went immediately to the scene. Dunstan said police were horrified by the attack, and grateful that three people came to the family’s aid before police arrived to arrest the alleged attacker. “We had a citizen immediately intervene, who jumped onto him and just pulled him off the mum, and then the other two added assistance by grabbing him as well,” she said. Loading “It [was] heroic, without the intervention, it could have been a lot worse, so we are so grateful for their assistance.”



The 10-year-old is recovering at The Royal Children’s Hospital, while his 46-year-old mother is at the nearby Royal Melbourne Hospital with injuries to her back and shoulders. “She was in fairly good spirits given the circumstances,” Dunstan said. “Within a minute, we had police from the Melbourne West Police Station quickly attend and take over the arrest … and take him into custody immediately.” The mother was visiting the city from Phillip Island with her three children, aged 10, 11 and 16. Dunstan said the incident had also traumatised the family. “One of the boys was an 11-year-old, he was crying, I gave him a hug,” she said. “We took him over to the police museum just to keep him distracted while [his] mum was being treated,” Dunstan told 3AW.



The 27-year-old man from Sunshine West will be interviewed by police. Dunstan said while the attack was random, the man was known to police in Victoria, NSW and Western Australia. Liz, an eyewitness who spoke to 3AW, said that she saw a woman with “blood all over her back”. “She was with a child … [who] was getting taken into another ambulance.



“Luckily, he looked like he was okay, but clearly shaken.” One of Liz’s work colleagues saw the man getting tackled by a passerby in a citizen’s arrest, she said. “But it was right outside the cop shop, so the police were there quite quickly.” Be the first to know when major news happens. 

CORRECTION An earlier version of this story said the mother who was attacked was 30 years old. She is 46. The error was made by Victoria Police.

World.title: ‘Geeing me up’: Jai Arrow on what it means to ‘play’ 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Geeing me up’: Jai Arrow on what it means to ‘play’ 100 games for Souths Christian Nicolussi Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:02pm ,first published 11:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jai Arrow was in the South Sydney gym with teammate Latrell Mitchell when coach Wayne Bennett first approached him with the idea of “playing” two more games so he could reach 100 NRL matches for the historic club. Arrow initially thought Bennett was “geeing me up”, only to realise he was serious about reaching the milestone before the season finished. Jai Arrow at Heffron Park on Tuesday. George Chan The 31-year-old was forced to retire earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease. But with the blessing of NRL acting chief executive Peter V’landys and the Rugby League Players’ Association, Arrow will start against the Gold Coast Titans on Saturday, then the Sydney Roosters on Friday week.



The plan will be to substitute him the moment the referee blows the whistle for the kick-off. Souths will be allowed to carry seven players rather than six on the bench, and have nine interchanges instead of eight. Arrow said he was quite comfortable to finish on 98 games for Souths, but then Bennett floated the touching gesture. “It’s not your usual way to bring up a milestone, it’s unique, and I pray to God this never happens to anyone else in the future – I hope this is the first and only time this ever happens in the NRL,” Arrow told this masthead. “When Wayne came to me with the idea in the gym while I was training with ‘Trell’, I thought he was geeing me up. “Then he explained it; Wayne said it didn’t sit with him right that I finish up on 98 games for Souths.



“Once he said that, I did what I always do, which is do what Wayne tells me to do. “To be honest, I was happy finishing on 98 games, and I was proud of what I’d done in my career. My career was cut short by MND, but shit happens. Jai Arrow will take the field on Saturday. Getty Images “I’m genuinely in awe of the support I’ve received from everyone, but this is special. It’s bigger than me, it’s bigger than the game. Rugby league is a special community, and I’m forever in debt to everyone who is playing their part to allow this to happen. “Mind you, I am progressing unfortunately, I can’t run any more, so I will be walking, and I can’t control my emotions, so I’m either going to cry my eyes out or laugh my head off. I also get real stiff when I get embarrassed, so there might be a bit of a limp when I walk off, but that’s the disease. I’ll be right. If anything looks unnatural out there, blame it on the MND.



Editor's pick Updated

NRL 2026 The Broncos ruled Adam Reynolds out of his own farewell. It hasn’t gone down well “It’s going be a wild ride, but I wouldn’t have it any other way.” South Sydney teammate Cody Walker joked that he might try and trip Arrow when he walked off the field against the Titans. Another teammate, Tallis Duncan, joked the Roosters might even attempt “to take his head off one last time” before he made it to the sideline for the final-round grudge match. “He hasn’t lost his wit, he still makes everyone laugh, and walks around with a smile on his face – Jai is still Jai,” Duncan said.



One of the most emotional scenes of the year involved Arrow breaking down while being comforted by his partner, Berina, and their daughter, Ayla, before Souths and the Broncos played in round 15 at Accor Stadium. His interview with Nine’s Danika Mason when opening up about MND will not be forgotten by anyone in the game. Loading The game and its supporters have done a wonderful job supporting Arrow and raising awareness about MND through various initiatives. South Sydney chief executive Blake Solly said of the Arrow cameos: “We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Pucovski launches legal action against Brighton Grammar over first concussion
World.content:
Former Australian cricketer Will Pucovski has taken legal action against Brighton Grammar School, alleging that the elite private school mishandled the first of what became a career-ending series of concussions. Pucovski’s management confirmed to this masthead the launching of legal action on Tuesday in the Victorian Supreme Court. Will Pucovski working for Channel Seven. Getty Images Brighton Grammar declined to comment as the matter is before the courts. The statement of claim alleges that the APS school breached its duty of care when he was heavily concussed at a football training session in 2014, the first of 13 documented concussions that ultimately ended his cricket career.



He announced his retirement in April last year after a medical panel, comprising Cricket Australia and Cricket Victoria experts, recommended that he stop playing. Prominent class action lawyer and former Western Bulldogs club president Peter Gordon is representing Pucovski, and has been advising him on his legal standing for several years. Gordon also confirmed the lodgement of the statement of claim. Will Pucosvki after suffering a head knock while playing for Australia A. Getty Images Pucovski, who played one Test for Australia in January 2021 against India at the SCG, left the game prematurely after a series of blows to the head, but his problems with concussions and their related effects began in high school.



Twelve years ago he was knocked unconscious at football training, when he suffered an accidental knee to the head. Pucovski, 28, has previously spoken about how he returned to the track very soon afterwards, before suffering months of flow-on effects from the concussion. “I got sling tackled into ironically one of my best mate’s knees who was running the other way,” Pucovski said in July at a Lord’s Taverners function. “I literally got walked to the sidelines. And then my only memory was the coach coming up to me and being like, ‘Do you want to keep training?’ Will Pucovski at the age of 13, on debut for the Brighton Grammar First XI. “I am like ‘Yeah’. So I just went and trained for the rest of the day. It is probably the biggest day of my life in a weird way because I have never felt the same since that day. I went from someone who would do anything and everything to basically sitting on the couch doing nothing for an extended period.” What followed was a harbinger of many of the concussions Pucovski would suffer subsequently, intertwined with mental health struggles that at times became difficult to distinguish from the head knocks themselves.



“I got ‘foggy eyes’,” he told the Taverners function. “I’m like ‘I can’t see’, thinking I was just tired or fatigued or something, which turned out to be from the concussion. “The next couple of days I just started to feel more sick, the headaches got worse and worse. Five or six days later I started feeling really, really sick and mum and dad took me to hospital. The mental health challenges started pretty quickly.” Will Pucovski surged to 50 on debut. Getty Subsequently, Pucovski became an outstanding young top order batsman for Victoria, quickly taking him to the cusp of Australian selection – he was first picked in a squad in January 2019, before eventually making his debut two summers later. Having made a polished half-century, Pucovski ran into further concussion troubles in subsequent seasons, preventing him from returning to the Australian team.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Can Australia afford to take Labuschagne back to the land of his birth? He made a final comeback for Victoria in the 2023-2024 season, sculpting a century in a Sheffield Shield game at the SCG. But he was struck another heavy blow to the helmet in a Shield game against Tasmania in Hobart later that season, a knock that took months to recover from, and he did not play again. More recently, Pucovksi has worked as head coach of the Melbourne Cricket club, while also doing commentary work for Seven. He was part of the commentary team for the first Test against Bangladesh in Darwin earlier this month. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘The longer this goes, the harder it gets’: Industry scrambles as Labor agonises over immigration
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalImmigration ‘The longer this goes, the harder it gets’: Industry scrambles as Labor agonises over immigration James Massola and Natassia Chrysanthos August 25, 2026 — 5:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government’s sweeping changes to Australia’s migration system could be pushed back up to a month, with industry groups seizing on the delay to lobby Labor against reducing the number of temporary workers in Australia. The National Farmers Federation and the Australian Construction Association, peak bodies that represent industries that rely on imported labour, said the plan to scale back immigration appeared to be driven by politics rather than practicalities and could have damaging effects on their industries. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese are trying to steer a contentious policy package on migration. Alex Ellinghausen The intensity of their lobbying is a sign of the economic and business sensitivities that Labor is dealing with in its plan to change the migration system without jeopardising key industries. Labor will attempt to restore public confidence in the migration system as One Nation’s public support surges, although the minor party again appeared confused over its policy on Tuesday, with Senator Malcolm Roberts referring to “negative” migration rather than Pauline Hanson’s recent clarification of a 130,000 net intake.



Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke’s proposal for reducing migration levels has not returned to cabinet for debate since a discussion in the expenditure review committee, led by deputy prime minister Richard Marles, put the changes on ice earlier this month. In that meeting, ministers expressed concern the proposal was not watertight and had not worked through all the economic and budget consequences. Labor ministers have played down the dispute and the delay, but Opposition Leader Angus Taylor this week accused the government of “brawling within their team” over the issue. “They can’t agree, and that’s why the numbers have consistently come in above target,” Taylor said. Asked if the changes to migration policy were sorted during a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: “No, we won’t be finalising that today.”



“Migration policy though, we’ve finalised our numbers. We’re headed to [net overseas migration of] 225,000 in two years’ time,” Albanese said. “We have a series of plans in place. There’s more work to do and we’ll work on that and make announcements at [the] appropriate time.” This masthead reported that Burke wanted to boost compliance by sending out more immigration officers to track down and deport overstayers, while other reports from the ABC said Burke was considering restricting family visas, as well as the work and appeal rights of asylum seekers. But a keynote speech announcing those changes was cancelled just days before the scheduled address at the National Press Club on August 6. Three Labor MPs, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly, said the delay in the announcement was likely to stretch until mid-September. “Industry has gotten hold of it and said how badly this will hurt them. They are going bananas,” one MP said.



“Everyone has used the extra time to prosecute the case for why they should not be impacted. The longer this goes, the harder it gets.” A second MP said: “If you were moving quickly you could do it next week, but I’m not sure they are, as this affects so many stakeholders.” The government has since quietly paused working holidaymaker visa applications from 24 countries. Migration and travel agents have told the tourism industry they have been detecting delays in processing times, and the pause on applications was introduced without notice. National Farmers Federation president Hamish McIntyre said the agriculture sector desperately needed both working holidaymakers, who comprise up to 80 per cent of the labour that harvests fresh produce in peak times, and Pacific Island workers. Changes that scaled back either cohort would mean “we wouldn’t be able to harvest our crops … and it would drive up costs and increase the cost of living,” McIntyre said.



“Some crops only give you a week to harvest, some crops give you a couple of weeks. We are horrified at them cutting off the labour we need because of politics.” Australian Constructors Association chief executive Peter Colacino said the sector needed highly skilled labour to complete some of the most sophisticated projects in the world, ranging from tunnelling to the Snowy Hydro project through to a nascent nuclear industry. “It’s a conflicting message from government wanting the best in the world in terms of people with the right skills, but on the other hand they are looking to constrain migration,” he said. Coalition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam said Labor had “finally realised that the immigration system is a mess of their own making”. “They’ve been dragged to this point kicking and screaming … but clearly can’t agree internally on what to do.”



Burke was contacted for comment. Migration’s magic number? As recently as last October, Burke was saying there was “not a magic number” in the immigration debate, and that net overseas migration was difficult to predict because it involved levers the government did not control – such as Australian citizens’ movements – as well as those it did. But since the May budget, Labor has framed the 225,000 budget forecast for NOM as a target it intends to hit, as One Nation’s surging popularity pushes the Albanese government to offer credible policies that maintain public confidence in the migration system. Net migration was about 300,000 last year and shows signs of remaining at that level. It means Burke has been considering a suite of policy changes that will drive that number down by a further 75,000 people.





“I’ve been talking about net negative migration,” he said. “So if 220,000 people leave... you have 130,000 people coming in, that’s a net migration of minus 90,000.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Jackie O suffered PTSD after Kyle’s ‘bullying’: doctor
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWorkplace Jackie O suffered PTSD after Kyle’s ‘bullying’: doctor Calum Jaspan August 25, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jackie “O” Henderson was identified as suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder after working with Kyle Sandilands at KIIS FM, new documents lodged in her lawsuit against the radio station’s owner show. In her first remarks about working with Sandilands after the demise of their show, Henderson said his behaviour was “unpredictable and erratic”, causing her to feel “worn down over time” and unsafe in the workplace, according to excerpts of a new affidavit released by the Federal Court on Tuesday. Jackie Henderson is pushing ahead in the Federal Court despite Kyle Sandilands’ settlement. Instagram The expert report by psychiatrist Dr Jonathan Phillips, excerpts of which were included in an updated defence lodged by Henderson’s employer against her lawsuit over the termination of her $100 million contract, made a series of findings about Henderson’s health. Henderson’s contract was terminated in March after she said she could no longer work with Sandilands following an on-air bust-up two weeks prior, in which he reduced her to the point of tears.



Phillips found she was suffering from PTSD as a result of Sandilands’ bullying, the failure of KIIS owner ARN to protect her, and the publication of a statement to the ASX detailing the termination of her contract. A separate letter from psychologist Dr Emma Agnew said the pattern of belittling behaviour alleged by Henderson was consistent with “behaviours commonly described as workplace bullying”. The public nature of Sandilands’ alleged conduct, and a perceived lack of support from ARN, “appears to have contributed to a decline in her emotional wellbeing,” Agnew said in a letter dated March 27. The report from Phillips and the letter from Agnew were cited in ARN’s updated defence to a lawsuit filed by Henderson. Their full text was not made available. In her affidavit, Henderson alleges a “shift” in the way Sandilands spoke to her on air in 2023, adding that she later felt worn down by Sandilands, with his behaviour contributing to her wanting to “give up”.



“What had previously felt like humour or banter started, at times, to feel different. The comments and putdowns became more pointed and less like they were said in fun and more like they were intended to belittle or humiliate me, and this became more difficult to tolerate over time,” Henderson said. Related Article Updated

Media & marketing KIIS expected me to berate Henderson, Sandilands tells court ARN updated its defence on Tuesday, saying that Henderson was responsible for her own health and safety at work because it hired her via her company, Henderson Media. It used the examples from the expert witnesses Henderson has drawn upon to argue that case. “If (which is denied) Ms Henderson has incurred pain, suffering, hurt, humiliation, and distress […] such pain, suffering, hurt, humiliation, and distress were caused or contributed to by Henderson Media failing to ensure the health and safety of Ms Henderson whilst performing the Program Services,” it argued in the filings.



In new court filings, the broadcaster argued Henderson Media failed to appropriately notify the company of the ongoing bullying she claims to have suffered. Henderson’s own legal argument is also expected to, in part, rely on a letter written by Dr Justine Corry – a former clinical psychologist – dating back to July 25 last year, in which Corry details the sustained impact Sandilands’ behaviour was having on her. Related Article Updated

Media & marketing Full cost of Kyle and Jackie O’s legal battle revealed ARN disputes Corry’s credentials, arguing she was no longer a medical professional of any kind at this time, and had a commercial relationship with Henderson. Corry, Henderson and her manager Gemma O’Neill were working together to sell a dating and relationships course called “Red Flag Project”, the filings say. It also says that Corry’s letter was not provided to ARN at the time, and was “deployed for the first time in the context of this litigation”.



Corry also appeared regularly on Henderson’s podcast and on The Kyle and Jackie O Show. ARN also claims that Sandilands and Henderson had been in contact in the days between their on-air blow up on February 20, and when Henderson’s representatives sent the “complaint letter” three days later. That letter alleged that “direct contact with Mr Sandilands is now untenable”. The radio company claims that letter made clear Henderson and her company were refusing to provide the broadcasting services required under the $100 million contract, “even if the purported safety issues that they identified … were satisfactorily addressed”. Sandilands declined to comment. ARN and Henderson were contacted for comment. Read more on Kyle and Jackie O

World.title: Breakdown underscores archaic state of Sydney’s rail infrastructure
World.content:
NationalNSWRail Editorial Breakdown underscores archaic state of Sydney’s rail infrastructure The Herald's View Editorial August 25, 2026 — 5:51pm

August 25, 2026 — 5:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A sagging wire brought Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line to a halt and wreaked havoc on tens of thousands of commuters in another display of how, when it comes to our city’s rail network, little things can ruin the best-laid plans. The loss of tension in an overhead wire south of Chatswood station late on Monday night resulted in the cancellation of city-bound services from Gordon to North Sydney the following morning. But it did not stop there, with knock-on effects on the T9 Northern Line between Hornsby and Strathfield and a reduction in services on the T1 Western line. Maintenance staff repair faulty overhead wires near Chatswood station on Tuesday morning. Kate Geraghty The latest failure comes less than two weeks after overhead wiring fell onto a train near Redfern, causing power outages across critical sections of the rail network and major disruptions during the evening peak. Transport for NSW is investigating the cause of the failure on the T1 line. These wiring faults follow a scathing review of Sydney’s train network, sparked by another wiring fault in May 2025 that caused days of delays.



Related Article Updated

Public transport Commuters face ‘isolated delays’ in afternoon peak after Sydney train chaos Sydney’s geriatric train network – the first version of the North Shore line was built in the 1890s – is a stark contrast to the efficient, fast, new metro, which has given the city a glimpse of how good mass transport can be. The Minns government is fiscally conservative and has ensured NSW is better off than most other states. It is pushing ahead with Coalition-initiated plans for the Metro West. The major new city-shaping line is being carved out over 24 kilometres between Sydney’s central business district and Westmead, and there is the new rail line from St Marys to Western Sydney Airport. Both leave a gigantic hole in the capital works budget. It has also said it is conscious of the need to invest in old heavy rail. Incidents such as Tuesday’s suggest the government faces a significant challenge to ensure the city has the transport infrastructure it needs to ensure it can cope with bold new housing targets. Last December, the Minns government released its draft Sydney Plan, projecting 20 years ahead with 6.5 million residents around more than 40 “interconnected centres” to provide most jobs and services. Given such massive growth, the demand for new infrastructure is clear.



Commuters wait in Chatswood station on Tuesday after a wiring fault led to lengthy public transport disruptions. KATE GERAGHTY The Minns government should be able to walk and chew gum at the same time by planning for new extensions and projects while also boosting maintenance and reliability on the existing network. Tuesday’s T1 North Shore Line forced commuters, students and others forced to wait hours for emergency buses or pay Uber prices to the CBD. The best ways to prevent repetition and stop further catastrophic interruptions to service are to properly fund maintenance programs and invest in assets renewal. There is no doubt the Sydney train system remains archaic. It is incumbent on the government to explain how its vision for a bigger, modern world city can evolve with a transport network that, wedged between the old and the new, is proving so vulnerable to costly attacks by lilliputian failures. World.title: Powerful Labor mayor takes swing over ‘half-hearted’ NSW gambling reforms
World.content:
A powerful Sydney Labor mayor has criticised the Minns government’s gambling reforms as a “half-hearted” attempt to deal with the poker machine addiction, and vowed to keep up the pressure on his own party before the 2027 election. Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne’s comments came after Gaming Minister David Harris said the rollout of mandatory facial-recognition technology in pubs and clubs and a statewide gambling self-exclusion register means cutting the number of poker machines in the state would “make no difference at all”. Nearly two years after an independent panel was convened to oversee the trial of cashless poker machines, the government has also ignored calls to introduce obligatory account-based gaming, instead saying it would begin exploring a system of opt-in “account-based” gambling. Punters in NSW spent $9.3 billion on poker machines in 2025. Jason South The government on Tuesday announced the latest tranche of its gambling reforms, including a statewide exclusion register that would allow families, friends, police or venues to initiate bans for problem gamblers in hotels and clubs.





Byrne, a senior figure in Labor’s Left faction who was integral to the negotiation of the gambling reform deal, criticised the “half-hearted approach to addressing poker machine harm”, saying pressure for “real reform” would intensify ahead of the 2027 NSW election. “Labor members voted for a ‘significant reduction’ in poker machines, but based on current trends, this plan would lead to just a few hundred of NSW’s 87,000 machines being decommissioned each year,” he said in a statement. ‘The fact that the poker machine lobby has not mounted a major campaign against these changes tells you everything you need to know.’ Darcy Byrne, Inner West mayor “The fact that the poker machine lobby has not mounted a major campaign against these changes tells you everything you need to know about how limited they are.” While Harris said he was discussing taxation changes with Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, he appeared to walk away from using government policy to materially reduce the 87,000 pokies operating across about 2100 venues in NSW.



“That becomes less important once the technology is in play,” Harris said. “The most important thing is that when a person is sitting at a machine anywhere in the state, they can set how long they can play. They can set how much they can spend. Once those things are in place, the actual number of machines matters less. The rollout of mandatory facial-recognition technology is a major win for the clubs lobby, which has long campaigned for its use, instead of mandatory account-based or cashless gambling. Stu Cameron, the chief executive of Wesley Mission, said clubs had been “pushing for this for ages”. He was concerned about how the rules would govern its use, including whether clubs could use data from the technology for things such as marketing. The Herald has previously revealed some companies that sell the technology to clubs promote it as a tool to “balance commerce and compliance” by identifying potential repeat customers. “The devil is in the detail,” Cameron said. “You’re still relying on a system that will require some 19-year-old responsible-gambling officer to go up to someone and say, ‘Please, sir or madam, can you stop gambling?’ A lot of the time they’re going to tell them to get stuffed. There’s as many holes in it as a block of Swiss cheese.”



While the self-exclusion register and facial-recognition technology is expected to be in place by 2028, Harris could not provide timelines for some of the announcements. Related Article Exclusive

Poker machines Pensioner’s $500,000 pokies spree and the Wild West of club governance Tuesday’s package included a reannouncement of a plan to increase gaming machine entitlement forfeitures – meaning the number of machines that must be given up every time they are transferred between venues – from one in three to one in two. The government first announced that policy before the 2023 election but never enacted it. Harris could not give a timeline for when it would occur. “There’s a whole lot of legislation involved in bringing this forward. We’re working through all those processes now. I can’t give you a date at this time,” he said.



The reforms also included a ban on VIP programs linked to gaming, which Harris said would include schemes such as the Diamond Suite at Club Marconi in Bossley Park. The high rollers’ room requires patrons to turn over at least $500,000 a year on poker machines to qualify for entry. The Herald reported last week that a 62-year-old pensioner who lives in a home owned by the Department of Housing has played the pokies until 4am, six or seven nights a week, there since it opened a decade ago. Mark Morey, the secretary of Unions NSW who has helped lead the push for gambling reforms and is entering parliament at the next election, said the reforms “represent real and solid progress to reduce harm to problem gamblers”. A statewide exclusion register will replace a fragmented system policed by individual venues and staff.



More than 3 per cent of the adult population experience moderate-risk gambling, while nearly 1 per cent experience high-risk gambling, according to the NSW Gambling Survey 2024. In 2023-24, poker machines in NSW generated about $8.4 billion in profit for clubs and hotels. NSW government revenue generated from pokies is forecast to grow by an average of 7.5 per cent over the next four years, rising from $1.63 billion to $2.2 billion by 2029-30. World.title: Mother stabbed, 10-year-old son punched in random attack outside police HQ
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaCrime Mother stabbed, 10-year-old son punched in random attack outside police HQ Alexander Darling and James Costa Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:02pm ,first published 3:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been arrested after allegedly punching a 10-year-old boy and repeatedly stabbing his mother with a pair of scissors in Melbourne’s CBD. Police said the random attack outside Victoria Police’s Spencer Street headquarters on Tuesday afternoon only ended when several passersby intervened. Police were on the scene quickly to arrest the man. Nine News Superintendent Zorka Dunstan said the woman’s two other children witnessed the violent assault. The family had been visiting the city from Phillip Island. “The man was walking south, and as he passed them, he randomly punched the 10-year-old then kept walking. He then turned around, grabbed mother in a headlock and started to stab her repeatedly with a pair of scissors,” Dunstan said.



Dunstan said she learnt of the incident while she was in her office upstairs and went immediately to the scene. Dunstan said police were horrified by the attack, and grateful that three people came to the family’s aid before police arrived to arrest the alleged attacker. “We had a citizen immediately intervene, who jumped onto him and just pulled him off the mum, and then the other two added assistance by grabbing him as well,” she said. Loading “It [was] heroic, without the intervention, it could have been a lot worse, so we are so grateful for their assistance.”



The 10-year-old is recovering at The Royal Children’s Hospital, while his 46-year-old mother is at the nearby Royal Melbourne Hospital with injuries to her back and shoulders. “She was in fairly good spirits given the circumstances,” Dunstan said. “Within a minute, we had police from the Melbourne West Police Station quickly attend and take over the arrest … and take him into custody immediately.” The mother was visiting the city from Phillip Island with her three children, aged 10, 11 and 16. Dunstan said the incident had also traumatised the family. “One of the boys was an 11-year-old, he was crying, I gave him a hug,” she said. “We took him over to the police museum just to keep him distracted while [his] mum was being treated,” Dunstan told 3AW.



The 27-year-old man from Sunshine West will be interviewed by police. Dunstan said while the attack was random, the man was known to police in Victoria, NSW and Western Australia. Liz, an eyewitness who spoke to 3AW, said that she saw a woman with “blood all over her back”. “She was with a child … [who] was getting taken into another ambulance.



“Luckily, he looked like he was okay, but clearly shaken.” One of Liz’s work colleagues saw the man getting tackled by a passerby in a citizen’s arrest, she said. “But it was right outside the cop shop, so the police were there quite quickly.” Be the first to know when major news happens. 

CORRECTION An earlier version of this story said the mother who was attacked was 30 years old. She is 46. The error was made by Victoria Police.

World.title: ‘Geeing me up’: Jai Arrow on what it means to ‘play’ 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Geeing me up’: Jai Arrow on what it means to ‘play’ 100 games for Souths Christian Nicolussi Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:02pm ,first published 11:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jai Arrow was in the South Sydney gym with teammate Latrell Mitchell when coach Wayne Bennett first approached him with the idea of “playing” two more games so he could reach 100 NRL matches for the historic club. Arrow initially thought Bennett was “geeing me up”, only to realise he was serious about reaching the milestone before the season finished. Jai Arrow at Heffron Park on Tuesday. George Chan The 31-year-old was forced to retire earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease. But with the blessing of NRL acting chief executive Peter V’landys and the Rugby League Players’ Association, Arrow will start against the Gold Coast Titans on Saturday, then the Sydney Roosters on Friday week.



The plan will be to substitute him the moment the referee blows the whistle for the kick-off. Souths will be allowed to carry seven players rather than six on the bench, and have nine interchanges instead of eight. Arrow said he was quite comfortable to finish on 98 games for Souths, but then Bennett floated the touching gesture. “It’s not your usual way to bring up a milestone, it’s unique, and I pray to God this never happens to anyone else in the future – I hope this is the first and only time this ever happens in the NRL,” Arrow told this masthead. “When Wayne came to me with the idea in the gym while I was training with ‘Trell’, I thought he was geeing me up. “Then he explained it; Wayne said it didn’t sit with him right that I finish up on 98 games for Souths.



“Once he said that, I did what I always do, which is do what Wayne tells me to do. “To be honest, I was happy finishing on 98 games, and I was proud of what I’d done in my career. My career was cut short by MND, but shit happens. Jai Arrow will take the field on Saturday. Getty Images “I’m genuinely in awe of the support I’ve received from everyone, but this is special. It’s bigger than me, it’s bigger than the game. Rugby league is a special community, and I’m forever in debt to everyone who is playing their part to allow this to happen. “Mind you, I am progressing unfortunately, I can’t run any more, so I will be walking, and I can’t control my emotions, so I’m either going to cry my eyes out or laugh my head off. I also get real stiff when I get embarrassed, so there might be a bit of a limp when I walk off, but that’s the disease. I’ll be right. If anything looks unnatural out there, blame it on the MND.



Editor's pick Updated

NRL 2026 The Broncos ruled Adam Reynolds out of his own farewell. It hasn’t gone down well “It’s going be a wild ride, but I wouldn’t have it any other way.” South Sydney teammate Cody Walker joked that he might try and trip Arrow when he walked off the field against the Titans. Another teammate, Tallis Duncan, joked the Roosters might even attempt “to take his head off one last time” before he made it to the sideline for the final-round grudge match. “He hasn’t lost his wit, he still makes everyone laugh, and walks around with a smile on his face – Jai is still Jai,” Duncan said.



One of the most emotional scenes of the year involved Arrow breaking down while being comforted by his partner, Berina, and their daughter, Ayla, before Souths and the Broncos played in round 15 at Accor Stadium. His interview with Nine’s Danika Mason when opening up about MND will not be forgotten by anyone in the game. Loading The game and its supporters have done a wonderful job supporting Arrow and raising awareness about MND through various initiatives. South Sydney chief executive Blake Solly said of the Arrow cameos: “We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Dozens of luxury watches and jewellery worth more than $2.5 million have been seized from the inner Sydney apartment of a man who allegedly impersonated a lawyer while running a property investment scam.

The 51-year-old allegedly defrauded six people between March 2023 and June this year, swindling more than $650,000.

A 51-year-old man was charged with 30 offences relating to alleged property investment scams. NSW Police

Police raided his apartment on Bayswater Road, Potts Point about 7am on Tuesday, seizing 60 luxury watches and more than 100 pieces of jewellery.

The man allegedly produced false financial and legal documents impersonating a lawyer and financial institutions to deceive his victims.

World.title: Pucovski launches legal action against Brighton Grammar over first concussion
World.content:
Former Australian cricketer Will Pucovski has taken legal action against Brighton Grammar School, alleging that the elite private school mishandled the first of what became a career-ending series of concussions. Pucovski’s management confirmed to this masthead the launching of legal action on Tuesday in the Victorian Supreme Court. Will Pucovski working for Channel Seven. Getty Images Brighton Grammar declined to comment as the matter is before the courts. The statement of claim alleges that the APS school breached its duty of care when he was heavily concussed at a football training session in 2014, the first of 13 documented concussions that ultimately ended his cricket career.



He announced his retirement in April last year after a medical panel, comprising Cricket Australia and Cricket Victoria experts, recommended that he stop playing. Prominent class action lawyer and former Western Bulldogs club president Peter Gordon is representing Pucovski, and has been advising him on his legal standing for several years. Gordon also confirmed the lodgement of the statement of claim. Will Pucosvki after suffering a head knock while playing for Australia A. Getty Images Pucovski, who played one Test for Australia in January 2021 against India at the SCG, left the game prematurely after a series of blows to the head, but his problems with concussions and their related effects began in high school.



Twelve years ago he was knocked unconscious at football training, when he suffered an accidental knee to the head. Pucovski, 28, has previously spoken about how he returned to the track very soon afterwards, before suffering months of flow-on effects from the concussion. “I got sling tackled into ironically one of my best mate’s knees who was running the other way,” Pucovski said in July at a Lord’s Taverners function. “I literally got walked to the sidelines. And then my only memory was the coach coming up to me and being like, ‘Do you want to keep training?’ Will Pucovski at the age of 13, on debut for the Brighton Grammar First XI. “I am like ‘Yeah’. So I just went and trained for the rest of the day. It is probably the biggest day of my life in a weird way because I have never felt the same since that day. I went from someone who would do anything and everything to basically sitting on the couch doing nothing for an extended period.” What followed was a harbinger of many of the concussions Pucovski would suffer subsequently, intertwined with mental health struggles that at times became difficult to distinguish from the head knocks themselves.



“I got ‘foggy eyes’,” he told the Taverners function. “I’m like ‘I can’t see’, thinking I was just tired or fatigued or something, which turned out to be from the concussion. “The next couple of days I just started to feel more sick, the headaches got worse and worse. Five or six days later I started feeling really, really sick and mum and dad took me to hospital. The mental health challenges started pretty quickly.” Will Pucovski surged to 50 on debut. Getty Subsequently, Pucovski became an outstanding young top order batsman for Victoria, quickly taking him to the cusp of Australian selection – he was first picked in a squad in January 2019, before eventually making his debut two summers later. Having made a polished half-century, Pucovski ran into further concussion troubles in subsequent seasons, preventing him from returning to the Australian team.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Can Australia afford to take Labuschagne back to the land of his birth? He made a final comeback for Victoria in the 2023-2024 season, sculpting a century in a Sheffield Shield game at the SCG. But he was struck another heavy blow to the helmet in a Shield game against Tasmania in Hobart later that season, a knock that took months to recover from, and he did not play again. More recently, Pucovksi has worked as head coach of the Melbourne Cricket club, while also doing commentary work for Seven. He was part of the commentary team for the first Test against Bangladesh in Darwin earlier this month. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

Asked if the changes to migration policy were sorted during a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: “No, we won’t be finalising that today.”



“Migration policy though, we’ve finalised our numbers. We’re headed to [net overseas migration of] 225,000 in two years’ time,” Albanese said. “We have a series of plans in place. There’s more work to do and we’ll work on that and make announcements at [the] appropriate time.” This masthead reported that Burke wanted to boost compliance by sending out more immigration officers to track down and deport overstayers, while other reports from the ABC said Burke was considering restricting family visas, as well as the work and appeal rights of asylum seekers. But a keynote speech announcing those changes was cancelled just days before the scheduled address at the National Press Club on August 6. Three Labor MPs, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly, said the delay in the announcement was likely to stretch until mid-September. “Industry has gotten hold of it and said how badly this will hurt them. They are going bananas,” one MP said.



“Everyone has used the extra time to prosecute the case for why they should not be impacted. The longer this goes, the harder it gets.” A second MP said: “If you were moving quickly you could do it next week, but I’m not sure they are, as this affects so many stakeholders.” The government has since quietly paused working holidaymaker visa applications from 24 countries. Migration and travel agents have told the tourism industry they have been detecting delays in processing times, and the pause on applications was introduced without notice. National Farmers Federation president Hamish McIntyre said the agriculture sector desperately needed both working holidaymakers, who comprise up to 80 per cent of the labour that harvests fresh produce in peak times, and Pacific Island workers. Changes that scaled back either cohort would mean “we wouldn’t be able to harvest our crops … and it would drive up costs and increase the cost of living,” McIntyre said.



“Some crops only give you a week to harvest, some crops give you a couple of weeks. We are horrified at them cutting off the labour we need because of politics.” Australian Constructors Association chief executive Peter Colacino said the sector needed highly skilled labour to complete some of the most sophisticated projects in the world, ranging from tunnelling to the Snowy Hydro project through to a nascent nuclear industry. “It’s a conflicting message from government wanting the best in the world in terms of people with the right skills, but on the other hand they are looking to constrain migration,” he said. Coalition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam said Labor had “finally realised that the immigration system is a mess of their own making”. “They’ve been dragged to this point kicking and screaming … but clearly can’t agree internally on what to do.”



Burke was contacted for comment. Migration’s magic number? As recently as last October, Burke was saying there was “not a magic number” in the immigration debate, and that net overseas migration was difficult to predict because it involved levers the government did not control – such as Australian citizens’ movements – as well as those it did. But since the May budget, Labor has framed the 225,000 budget forecast for NOM as a target it intends to hit, as One Nation’s surging popularity pushes the Albanese government to offer credible policies that maintain public confidence in the migration system. Net migration was about 300,000 last year and shows signs of remaining at that level. It means Burke has been considering a suite of policy changes that will drive that number down by a further 75,000 people.





“I’ve been talking about net negative migration,” he said. “So if 220,000 people leave... you have 130,000 people coming in, that’s a net migration of minus 90,000.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Jackie O suffered PTSD after Kyle’s ‘bullying’: doctor
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWorkplace Jackie O suffered PTSD after Kyle’s ‘bullying’: doctor Calum Jaspan August 25, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jackie “O” Henderson was identified as suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder after working with Kyle Sandilands at KIIS FM, new documents lodged in her lawsuit against the radio station’s owner show. In her first remarks about working with Sandilands after the demise of their show, Henderson said his behaviour was “unpredictable and erratic”, causing her to feel “worn down over time” and unsafe in the workplace, according to excerpts of a new affidavit released by the Federal Court on Tuesday. Jackie Henderson is pushing ahead in the Federal Court despite Kyle Sandilands’ settlement. Instagram The expert report by psychiatrist Dr Jonathan Phillips, excerpts of which were included in an updated defence lodged by Henderson’s employer against her lawsuit over the termination of her $100 million contract, made a series of findings about Henderson’s health. Henderson’s contract was terminated in March after she said she could no longer work with Sandilands following an on-air bust-up two weeks prior, in which he reduced her to the point of tears.



Phillips found she was suffering from PTSD as a result of Sandilands’ bullying, the failure of KIIS owner ARN to protect her, and the publication of a statement to the ASX detailing the termination of her contract. A separate letter from psychologist Dr Emma Agnew said the pattern of belittling behaviour alleged by Henderson was consistent with “behaviours commonly described as workplace bullying”. The public nature of Sandilands’ alleged conduct, and a perceived lack of support from ARN, “appears to have contributed to a decline in her emotional wellbeing,” Agnew said in a letter dated March 27. The report from Phillips and the letter from Agnew were cited in ARN’s updated defence to a lawsuit filed by Henderson. Their full text was not made available. In her affidavit, Henderson alleges a “shift” in the way Sandilands spoke to her on air in 2023, adding that she later felt worn down by Sandilands, with his behaviour contributing to her wanting to “give up”.



“What had previously felt like humour or banter started, at times, to feel different. The comments and putdowns became more pointed and less like they were said in fun and more like they were intended to belittle or humiliate me, and this became more difficult to tolerate over time,” Henderson said. Related Article Updated

Media & marketing KIIS expected me to berate Henderson, Sandilands tells court ARN updated its defence on Tuesday, saying that Henderson was responsible for her own health and safety at work because it hired her via her company, Henderson Media. It used the examples from the expert witnesses Henderson has drawn upon to argue that case. “If (which is denied) Ms Henderson has incurred pain, suffering, hurt, humiliation, and distress […] such pain, suffering, hurt, humiliation, and distress were caused or contributed to by Henderson Media failing to ensure the health and safety of Ms Henderson whilst performing the Program Services,” it argued in the filings.



In new court filings, the broadcaster argued Henderson Media failed to appropriately notify the company of the ongoing bullying she claims to have suffered. Henderson’s own legal argument is also expected to, in part, rely on a letter written by Dr Justine Corry – a former clinical psychologist – dating back to July 25 last year, in which Corry details the sustained impact Sandilands’ behaviour was having on her. Related Article Updated

Media & marketing Full cost of Kyle and Jackie O’s legal battle revealed ARN disputes Corry’s credentials, arguing she was no longer a medical professional of any kind at this time, and had a commercial relationship with Henderson. Corry, Henderson and her manager Gemma O’Neill were working together to sell a dating and relationships course called “Red Flag Project”, the filings say. It also says that Corry’s letter was not provided to ARN at the time, and was “deployed for the first time in the context of this litigation”.



Corry also appeared regularly on Henderson’s podcast and on The Kyle and Jackie O Show. ARN also claims that Sandilands and Henderson had been in contact in the days between their on-air blow up on February 20, and when Henderson’s representatives sent the “complaint letter” three days later. That letter alleged that “direct contact with Mr Sandilands is now untenable”. The radio company claims that letter made clear Henderson and her company were refusing to provide the broadcasting services required under the $100 million contract, “even if the purported safety issues that they identified … were satisfactorily addressed”. Sandilands declined to comment. ARN and Henderson were contacted for comment. Read more on Kyle and Jackie O

World.title: Powerful Labor mayor takes swing over ‘half-hearted’ NSW gambling reforms
World.content:
A powerful Sydney Labor mayor has criticised the Minns government’s gambling reforms as a “half-hearted” attempt to deal with the poker machine addiction, and vowed to keep up the pressure on his own party before the 2027 election. Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne’s comments came after Gaming Minister David Harris said the rollout of mandatory facial-recognition technology in pubs and clubs and a statewide gambling self-exclusion register means cutting the number of poker machines in the state would “make no difference at all”. Nearly two years after an independent panel was convened to oversee the trial of cashless poker machines, the government has also ignored calls to introduce obligatory account-based gaming, instead saying it would begin exploring a system of opt-in “account-based” gambling. Punters in NSW spent $9.3 billion on poker machines in 2025. Jason South The government on Tuesday announced the latest tranche of its gambling reforms, including a statewide exclusion register that would allow families, friends, police or venues to initiate bans for problem gamblers in hotels and clubs.





Byrne, a senior figure in Labor’s Left faction who was integral to the negotiation of the gambling reform deal, criticised the “half-hearted approach to addressing poker machine harm”, saying pressure for “real reform” would intensify ahead of the 2027 NSW election. “Labor members voted for a ‘significant reduction’ in poker machines, but based on current trends, this plan would lead to just a few hundred of NSW’s 87,000 machines being decommissioned each year,” he said in a statement. ‘The fact that the poker machine lobby has not mounted a major campaign against these changes tells you everything you need to know.’ Darcy Byrne, Inner West mayor “The fact that the poker machine lobby has not mounted a major campaign against these changes tells you everything you need to know about how limited they are.” While Harris said he was discussing taxation changes with Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, he appeared to walk away from using government policy to materially reduce the 87,000 pokies operating across about 2100 venues in NSW.



“That becomes less important once the technology is in play,” Harris said. “The most important thing is that when a person is sitting at a machine anywhere in the state, they can set how long they can play. They can set how much they can spend. Once those things are in place, the actual number of machines matters less. The rollout of mandatory facial-recognition technology is a major win for the clubs lobby, which has long campaigned for its use, instead of mandatory account-based or cashless gambling. Stu Cameron, the chief executive of Wesley Mission, said clubs had been “pushing for this for ages”. He was concerned about how the rules would govern its use, including whether clubs could use data from the technology for things such as marketing. The Herald has previously revealed some companies that sell the technology to clubs promote it as a tool to “balance commerce and compliance” by identifying potential repeat customers. “The devil is in the detail,” Cameron said. “You’re still relying on a system that will require some 19-year-old responsible-gambling officer to go up to someone and say, ‘Please, sir or madam, can you stop gambling?’ A lot of the time they’re going to tell them to get stuffed. There’s as many holes in it as a block of Swiss cheese.”



While the self-exclusion register and facial-recognition technology is expected to be in place by 2028, Harris could not provide timelines for some of the announcements. Related Article Exclusive

Poker machines Pensioner’s $500,000 pokies spree and the Wild West of club governance Tuesday’s package included a reannouncement of a plan to increase gaming machine entitlement forfeitures – meaning the number of machines that must be given up every time they are transferred between venues – from one in three to one in two. The government first announced that policy before the 2023 election but never enacted it. Harris could not give a timeline for when it would occur. “There’s a whole lot of legislation involved in bringing this forward. We’re working through all those processes now. I can’t give you a date at this time,” he said.



The reforms also included a ban on VIP programs linked to gaming, which Harris said would include schemes such as the Diamond Suite at Club Marconi in Bossley Park. The high rollers’ room requires patrons to turn over at least $500,000 a year on poker machines to qualify for entry. The Herald reported last week that a 62-year-old pensioner who lives in a home owned by the Department of Housing has played the pokies until 4am, six or seven nights a week, there since it opened a decade ago. Mark Morey, the secretary of Unions NSW who has helped lead the push for gambling reforms and is entering parliament at the next election, said the reforms “represent real and solid progress to reduce harm to problem gamblers”. A statewide exclusion register will replace a fragmented system policed by individual venues and staff.



More than 3 per cent of the adult population experience moderate-risk gambling, while nearly 1 per cent experience high-risk gambling, according to the NSW Gambling Survey 2024. In 2023-24, poker machines in NSW generated about $8.4 billion in profit for clubs and hotels. NSW government revenue generated from pokies is forecast to grow by an average of 7.5 per cent over the next four years, rising from $1.63 billion to $2.2 billion by 2029-30. World.title: Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win
World.content:
Analysis NationalNSWPoker machines Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win Harriet Alexander August 25, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a particular feature of poker machine play that raises the pulses of reform advocates and gamblers alike, known as “losses disguised as wins”. The lights flash and the bells ring and the machine celebrates the spin like a win, but the payout is less than the amount wagered. Depending how far you wind back the time machine on this state’s slow descent into poker machine addiction, the Minns government’s long-awaited gambling reform package could be described as a loss disguised as a win. There is nothing terrible about the measures announced on Tuesday. It’s a grab-bag of things that can’t hurt, things that might work and things that are long overdue. The reforms proposed by NSW Premier Chris Minns gloss over money laundering. Sitthixay Ditthavong But it goes nowhere near addressing the social harms that have emerged as a result of NSW having the highest number of poker machines per person in the world. Starting with that metric, for example, the package includes an increased forfeiture rate when gaming machine entitlements are traded, from one in three to one in two, so that for every two entitlements traded, one machine is permanently removed from circulation. This is designed to reduce the number of poker machines over time.



NSW has about 87,000 poker machines. That is just 13,758 fewer than when the forfeiture scheme was introduced 25 years ago. The NSW Audit Office projected last year it would take 55 years to reach parity with the national average. The accelerated forfeiture rate might shave a decade off that time frame, but only if pubs and clubs do not change their behaviour. They might decide the forfeiture rate is too high and stop transferring their entitlements altogether. Related Article Updated

Poker machines Powerful Labor mayor takes swing over ‘half-hearted’ NSW gambling reforms The second big item is a statewide third-party exclusion scheme for people experiencing gambling harm. Gambling harm advocates have long advocated for this. Previously, people could ask to be excluded from particular venues, but there was nothing to stop them going elsewhere to get their gambling fix. Few will object to that loophole being closed, or the new ability for third parties to intervene to place their loved ones on the exclusion register. Similarly, the strengthened protections against harmful gambling advertising, a ban on VIP programs that reward high rollers, a ban on gambling advertising on government-owned buildings, and new transparency requirements for influencers can only reduce gambling harm. But when it comes to poker machines being used for money laundering – that is, criminals using them to disguise the origins of dirty cash – the changes fall far short.



A casual observer might forget the NSW Crime Commission’s damning 2023 report into money laundering in pubs and clubs was the original catalyst for gambling reform. That problem has not gone away. The financial crimes watchdog last year launched civil proceedings against the state’s largest club group, Mounties, for allegedly allowing criminals to launder $226 million through its pokies. The independent panel for gaming reform recommended last year the government introduce mandatory account-based gaming, which would require gamblers to provide identification and allow crime agencies to track their transactions. Loading This top-line recommendation has appeared only in ghost form. Under these reforms, the government will upgrade the Centralised Monitoring System over the next two years to allow venues to transition to account-based play, which will give players the option of playing without cash – but it will not be mandatory. Setting aside the fact they could have done this two years ago, a voluntary, ad hoc system will do nothing to reduce money laundering. Instead, the government has committed to introducing mandatory facial recognition technology at the entrance to gaming rooms – the money laundering prevention method favoured by the gambling industry – and this will also support the statewide exclusion program.



One pundit quipped the most generous thing that could be said about the package was that it was more than any other government has done, but only because the bar was so low.
